articles.title: 'It's significant': Ukraine fears US is withholding allied-funded air defense supplies to pressure Kyiv
articles.body:
'It's significant': Ukraine fears US is withholding allied-funded air defense supplies to pressure Kyiv
Ukrainian officials described the alleged delay as another example of political pressure that could put civilian lives at risk.
U.S. President Donald Trump (L) speaks as U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth looks on during a meeting in the Cabinet Room of the White House on Dec. 2, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has yet to approve the transfer of a significant batch of Patriot interceptor missiles for Ukraine, Ukrainian officials and military officers told the Kyiv Independent, raising suspicions in Kyiv that Washington is deliberately withholding the weapons to pressure Ukraine.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 19 that there are delays in providing "certain types of vital supplies," pointing a fingure at the U.S. Department of Defense.
"There are political agreements that have not been implemented at the working level," he added.
One senior Ukrainian official and two Ukrainian military officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters, say Hegseth is holding up supplies of Patriot missiles, which Ukraine relies on to intercept ballistic missiles.
"Hegseth has the contracts for Patriot missiles on his desk. He is not signing off on them," one Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent.
The official added that the missiles had already been paid for by Ukraine's allies.
The delay comes as Russia launches near-daily ballistic missile attacks on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure, leaving Kyiv dependent on its limited supplies of interceptors.
It also builds on the latest strain in relations between Ukraine and the Trump administration, which the U.S. president criticizing Kyiv's strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Ukraine has also recently experienced repeated disruptions to its early-warning systems for incoming Russian ballistic missiles, which rely on U.S. intelligence. American officials have attributed the outages, which have occurred several times in the past, to “bad weather conditions,” while U.S. State Secretary Marco Rubio has cited a software malfunction.
Ukaine has also experienced disruptions to Starshield and Starlink services, which have severely hampered Ukrainian drone operations, including the interceptor drones Ukraine uses to counter Russian jet-powered attack drones.
Ukrainian officials described the alleged delay as another example of political pressure that could put civilian lives at risk.
Patriot systems are among Ukraine's most important defenses against Russian ballistic missiles, which are particularly difficult to intercept. Any delay could seriously undermine Ukraine's defense of its cities and critical infrastructure.
A significant batch of missiles
Ukraine obtains Patriot interceptors through several channels, one senior Ukrainian military official said. One of the main mechanisms is NATO's Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), through which Kyiv's allies fund weapons purchases from the U.S.
Zelensky said the U.S. delivers only 12 Patriot interceptors to Ukraine each month.
Kyiv also seeks missiles directly from countries that may have them in stock. Ukrainian embassies contact governments to identify available supplies.
Ukrainian officials declined to disclose the country's current interceptor stocks, citing operational security.
"(Ukraine) never discloses the quantity of weapons we have on hand so that the enemy remains unaware of the situation," one Ukrainian defense official said.
Another senior Ukrainian official described the batch allegedly awaiting Hegseth's approval as "significant."
"It's hard to call this a 'monthly supply,' because there's no set amount of how much you need for a month," the official said. "But it's significant."
The status of the broader supply program remains less clear. A NATO official said PURL deliveries were continuing, including shipments of air defense equipment.
"Support to Ukraine through PURL continues to flow," the official said.
Another NATO official acknowledged that some shipments could face delays but said political reasons were unlikely to explain them.
Ukrainian officials, however, believe the hold-up is a political decision rather than a routine logistical delay.
"It looks like this is a political refusal to sign," one Ukrainian official said.
"First, it was missile early warnings. Now this. It's clear what they're doing."
The Kyiv Independent contacted the Pentagon for comment, but had not received a response. A U.S. government official disputed Ukraine's claims, calling them "not true."
As of the morning of Oct. 19, a Ukrainian defense official said there had been no change in the supply situation, and Hegseth had still not approved the transfer.
A wider dispute over Russian oil
The dispute over Patriot interceptors comes amid mounting tensions over Ukraine's campaign against Russian energy infrastructure.
Trump has criticized Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries as his administration seeks to address rising global fuel prices, driven by his war in Iran.
On Oct. 9, Trump announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin allowing Russia to supply millions of tons of diesel to U.S. and international markets despite sanctions imposed over Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Russia subsequently partially lifted its ban on diesel exports, allowing additional supplies to reach foreign markets.
With fuel prices putting pressure on U.S. consumers, Trump has increasingly blamed Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries, while denying responsibility for the situation at the gas pumps.
One senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent that the administration's approach was driven by domestic politics.
"He can't admit he was wrong about the war in Iran, so — purely for campaign purposes — he's fallen back on the old narrative of accusations against Ukraine," the official said.

articles.title: Netanyahu unveils war doctrine, maps new regional threats
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israel's Netanyahu unveils war doctrine, maps new regional threats
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has unveiled a security doctrine advocating pre-emptive military strikes and buffer zones along Israel's borders, despite the collapse of his previous security strategy during the 7 October 2023 attack, while displaying maps of supposed regional alliances just days before Israeli elections.
The three-page document, titled "Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Security Concept", was published on the Israeli government's website on Sunday and outlines the country's alleged principal security threats and 10 central principles guiding its military strategy.
The proposals drew sharp criticism from Israeli opposition leaders, who dismissed the document as superficial, filled with hollow slogans and an attempt to distract from Netanyahu's security failures ahead of the 27 October parliamentary elections.
The document was released as Netanyahu struggles in opinion polls and has recently acknowledged being "very worried" about his prospects of winning another term.
According to Haaretz, Netanyahu's previous security doctrine, unveiled in 2018, was in place ahead of the Hamas-led attack on 7 October 2023, when Israel's intelligence, deterrence and border defences failed.
An Israeli state comptroller's report last year criticised Netanyahu for failing to submit his national security doctrine for formal cabinet approval, meaning it was never translated into binding military plans or budgets.
The report found that three fundamental pillars of Israel's security strategy collapsed on 7 October: deterrence, intelligence warnings and border defences, including advanced technological barriers that were breached during the attack.
Despite those failures, Netanyahu has yet to establish an independent state commission of inquiry into the decisions that preceded the attack, instead focusing his latest presentation on Israel's subsequent military campaigns.
Pre-emptive strikes and military expansion
In the document's introduction, Netanyahu argued that the Hamas-led attack on 7 October 2023 had "forced" Israel into a wide-ranging war, claiming that Israeli military operations from Gaza to Yemen, Lebanon and Iran had averted an elleged threat of imminent nuclear "annihilation".
He also claimed that Israel had dismantled the "stranglehold" imposed by the so-called Iranian axis, despite the devastating consequences of Israel's military campaigns across the region, including its genocidal war in Gaza.
Netanyahu said the conflict had required a fundamental revision of Israel's security doctrine, prioritising offensive military action over containment and defence.
The document calls for "prioritising the prevention of threats and attacking them rather than containing them and defending against them", including pre-emptive strikes against emerging threats.
It identifies Iran, which Israel accuses of seeking nuclear weapons, as a principal threat, alongside Yemen's Houthis, Hezbollah in Lebanon and Palestinian armed groups in Gaza.
Precision-guided missiles, drones, electronic warfare and cyberattacks are also listed among Israel's major security concerns, alongside what it calls "domestic terrorism and internal enemies" and international efforts to isolate Israel.
Among its central principles, the doctrine calls for maintaining Israel's military superiority, strengthening deterrence and early-warning capabilities, and preparing for preventive attacks.
It also advocates establishing buffer zones along Israel's borders where deemed necessary, although it does not specify their locations or which neighbouring countries could be affected.
Israel has already occupied additional territory in southern Syria and maintained military positions inside southern Lebanon, while continuing its occupation of Palestinian territory.
The document also calls for strengthening Israel's domestic military industries to reduce dependence on foreign arms suppliers, including underground weapons production, while expanding technological capabilities in artificial intelligence, quantum computing and space.
Under a section titled "Spirit of the People", it advocates encouraging settlement in the "Land of Israel", despite the illegality of Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank under international law.
According to Netanyahu's office, the document was prepared with assistance from Israel's National Security Council and its head, Shmuel Ben Ezra.
Maps of regional alliances raise questions
During Sunday's presentation, Netanyahu displayed a geopolitical map depicting what he claimed were emerging regional alliances and alleged threats to Israel.
The map, which carried the logo of Germany's Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung foundation, identified Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Pakistan as the "Sunni Diamond", alongside Iran and its allies as the "Axis of Resistance", and an Israel-UAE grouping described as the "Hexagon Alliance".
Originally published in May 2026 by researchers Marc Saxer and Marcus Schneider, the graphic also categorised countries and territories considered friendly to the competing blocs.
Somaliland and Puntland were depicted as friendly to Israel and the UAE, alongside Ethiopia, Djibouti and Greece, while Somalia and its North East State were shown as friendly to the Turkey-Egypt-Pakistan-Saudi Arabia grouping.
The classifications reflect the researchers' assessment of regional alignments rather than formal military alliances.
The presentation also referred to an "Iranian-Shia axis" and a Turkey-linked Muslim Brotherhood axis as regional challenges.
Netanyahu urged Israel to take advantage of the remaining two years of US President Donald Trump's administration to expand its alliances, warning that a future American government might be less supportive.
He acknowledged differences with Trump over Turkey and claimed Israel had acted to prevent Ankara from expanding its military presence in Syria.
"I hope we don't reach a direct confrontation," Netanyahu said.
Israel recognised Somaliland as an independent state in December 2025, a move rejected by Somalia's federal government as a violation of its sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Israeli opposition dismisses 'empty slogans'
The publication of Netanyahu's security doctrine prompted fierce criticism from opposition leaders Yair Lapid and Gadi Eisenkot, who accused the prime minister of attempting to conceal his government's failures, particularly those surrounding 7 October 2023.
In a post on X, Lapid described the document as "superficial and strange", saying it appeared to have been written using a free version of an AI chatbot.
He argued that it offered no genuine national security strategy and criticised Netanyahu's refusal to establish an official commission of inquiry into the 7 October failures.
Lapid also accused the prime minister of contradicting his own security principles by allowing ultra-Orthodox Jews to avoid military service, damaging Israel's international relationships and deepening domestic divisions.
Eisenkot, who leads the opposition Yashar party, described the document as "two empty pages filled with slogans", arguing that it exposed the strategic vacuum created by Netanyahu's leadership.
He questioned why the prime minister had waited until nine days before the elections, and three years after the 7 October attack, to publish his national security vision.
Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of failing to achieve his stated military objectives, including dismantling the military and governing capabilities of Hamas and Islamic Jihad, deterring Hezbollah and maintaining stability in the occupied West Bank.
He also argued that Hamas continued to maintain armed forces in Gaza while Hezbollah was rebuilding its military capabilities.
Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of refusing to investigate the failures of 7 October or draw lessons from them.
He described the document's publication as another example of Netanyahu's political tactics, accusing him of "manipulating public consciousness, stirring fear and trying to divert attention from the series of lies and racism surrounding his election campaign".
Eisenkot pledged that an opposition-led government would prepare and approve a formal Israeli national security strategy within 150 days of taking office.

articles.title: ‘No early warning’: Zelenskyy says allies failed to alert Kyiv before Russian strikes; Rubio says US intel sharing never paused
articles.body:
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed that Kyiv received no early warning from its international partners ahead of Russia’s latest ballistic missile attack on Monday. The overnight strikes across 11 Ukrainian regions damaged more than 10 energy facilities and left at least 5,50,000 households without electricity.
The comments come as US secretary of State Marco Rubio denied that the US had paused some intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
The attack, which involved ballistic missiles and drones, also killed one person and injured eight others in Kyiv, according to local authorities. The strikes damaged residential buildings, a medical facility, a school and a metro station, highlighting the continued threat to civilian infrastructure as Russia intensifies attacks on Ukraine’s energy network.
In a post on X, Zelenskyy said Russia had launched 16 ballistic missiles in what he described as a deliberate attack on Kyiv and the surrounding region, alongside more than 200 drones, including jet-powered Shahed drones.
“Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners,” he said.
He added that the attacks extended beyond the capital, with strikes reported across regions ranging from Kharkiv and Dnipro to Volyn, Rivne and Odesa.
“Overnight and this morning, Russia attacked energy facilities in the Vinnytsia, Volyn, Kirovohrad, Kyiv, Mykolaiv, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, Kharkiv, Ternopil, Odesa, and Rivne regions,” Zelensky said.
“In this one night alone, more than 10 energy infrastructure facilities were damaged, and the lights went out for at least 550,000 families. Repair crews are working at the sites,” he added.
Rubio on Monday denied that intelligence-sharing with Ukraine had been interrupted. “There's been no pause,” Rubio told NBC in Uzbekistan, adding, "I don't know where he's getting these things or why he's saying these things to the press. You should go back and ask him. There's been no pause."
Ukraine’s Air Force said Russian forces had launched a large-scale overnight assault involving ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and 269 drones. Ukrainian air defences destroyed or suppressed 243 drones and four missiles, while strikes were recorded at 25 locations and debris fell at eight others, the force said.
According to the Kyiv City Military Administration, the attack damaged a private medical facility and a metro station in the Desnianskyi district. Educational institutions and a sports facility were damaged in the Dniprovskyi district, while a fire broke out at a medical facility inside a 25-storey residential building in Solomianskyi district. Emergency services extinguished the blaze.
Russia’s defence ministry also said it had carried out a “massive strike” using “ground-based high-precision weapons and strike drones”. It claimed to have hit military-industrial facilities, cruise missile storage sites and data centres in Ukraine, including locations in and around Kyiv allegedly linked to drone production and logistics.
Ukraine’s deputy energy minister Artem Nekrasov said Russian attacks had targeted energy facilities in 11 regions. Rolling blackouts and electricity restrictions for industry and businesses had been introduced, he said in a post on Telegram.
Zelensky also criticised what he described as inadequate support from Ukraine’s partners, particularly over air defence supplies and sanctions on Moscow.
“Ukraine never wanted this war, and we have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to bring this war to a dignified end,” he said, adding that Ukraine had responded positively to every ceasefire proposal.
“Putin not only doesn't want to end this war – he doesn't even want to take any steps toward de-escalation. EVERY ONE of our partners has experienced this firsthand when they heard Russia's refusals. And it is crucial to call things what they are. To call the aggressor an aggressor and help Ukraine defend lives. When deliveries of missiles for Ukraine's air defense are blocked while Russia is granted relief or delays in sanctions, this is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners", he said.

articles.title: Europe Weighs More Ukraine Support as Trump Waives Sanctions
articles.body:
Ukraine reported receiving no advance warning before Russia launched 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region on Monday, Oct. 19, after President Volodymyr Zelensky said US intelligence sharing had resumed.
The latest attacks damaged more than 10 energy facilities and left at least 550,000 households without electricity, Zelensky said.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
For European governments promising to maintain support for Ukraine, the attack sharpened an immediate problem: funding and weapons pledges must translate into protection while Washington eases economic pressure on Moscow and Kyiv reports delays in American missile deliveries.
Europe has outlined several responses, including further sanctions, accelerated British air-defense supplies, and Belgian fighter-jet deliveries. But Ukraine’s request for another €70 billion ($78 billion) in 2027 remains unresolved.
Intelligence resumes, but missile deliveries remain disputed
Zelensky told NBC’s Meet the Press in an interview published Sunday, Oct. 18 that US intelligence cooperation was working again after an interruption.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio disputed that account on Monday, saying Washington had not paused intelligence sharing. The competing statements leave uncertainty over which information was interrupted and why Ukraine received no warning before the latest attack.
Intelligence is only one part of Ukraine’s defense against ballistic missiles as its crews also need sufficient interceptor missiles to engage incoming threats.
Trump’s Policies Upping the Pressure on Zelensky
In a separate Bloomberg interview on Sunday, Oct. 18, Zelensky said Washington was delaying approval of some Patriot interceptors already paid for through NATO’s Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (or PURL).
“The American side approved the delivery of only some of them, but not the rest. And this is not a technical issue,” he said.
Zelensky clarified that Ukraine was receiving 12 Patriot interceptors a month, approximately one-quarter of the monthly supply under the Biden administration. His account identifies an obstacle European funding alone cannot remove: allies can finance purchases, but American approval and delivery remain necessary.
Europe rejects sanctions relief and prepares further restrictions
The dispute over military support accompanies a widening disagreement over sanctions.
Trump’s Oct. 16 executive order waived major new sanctions and tariffs under the Graham Act before the Oct. 18 implementation deadline. However, existing restrictions imposed under earlier executive orders remained in place.
The legislation gave Trump substantial powers to waive additional penalties, meaning its passage did not guarantee that Moscow would face the full measures Congress authorized.
European leaders had already criticized his earlier Russian diesel agreement and pledged to maintain their own sanctions. Their Oct. 15-16 summit conclusions expressed regret over the temporary lifting of US diesel restrictions and called for stronger measures against Russian energy revenues and sanctions evasion.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Friday, Oct. 16 that work was underway on a further sanctions package.
“We will not lift any sanctions until Russia ends the war,” she said, according to LaPresse. The package’s full contents and adoption date were not specified in those remarks.
Missiles and aircraft are pledged, while larger funding remains open
Britain has announced practical steps alongside its criticism of Moscow.
An Oct. 13 government statement outlined £45 million ($60 million) in surface-to-air missile deliveries, with £10 million ($13 million) accelerated to meet urgent winter needs. Ministers were also instructed to prepare further sanctions, military assistance, and financial measures.
The missiles include Lightweight Multirole Missiles used against drones. These can strengthen Ukraine’s defenses, but the announcement does not resolve the separate shortage of Patriot interceptors for ballistic threats.
Belgium has also pledged 10 F-16 fighter jets by the end of 2026, following Prime Minister Bart De Wever’s meeting with Zelensky in Brussels.
The Ukrainian president has urged Belgium to accelerate deliveries, saying F-16s were proving particularly effective against Russia’s jet-powered Shahed drones.
On financing, the European Commission transferred €2.86 billion ($3.2 billion) for military procurement on Wednesday, Oct. 14 through the existing €90 billion ($101 billion) Ukraine Support Loan.
The larger question is what follows. European leaders have asked the Commission to develop proposals to bridge Ukraine’s €70 billion ($78 billion) funding gap for 2027. That instruction opens negotiations over additional support. It does not constitute an agreed funding package.
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico subsequently said Slovakia and Hungary would not participate in the initiative, underlining the political obstacles to securing the money.
AfD uses Trump’s Russia deals to challenge Europe’s position
European governments also face domestic opponents invoking Trump’s approach as a model.
Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany has argued that Berlin should pursue its own Russian energy agreements rather than maintain the existing policy.
In an Oct. 15 statement, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla called for the undamaged Nord Stream pipeline to return to operation and questioned why Trump alone should be allowed to make deals with Russia during an energy crisis.
AfD and the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance also sought a joint vote in Saxony-Anhalt backing renewed Russian energy supplies, Frankfurter Rundschau reported.
Such a regional vote cannot overturn national or EU sanctions, but it demonstrates how Washington’s decisions are being used to challenge them politically.
Europe’s response now depends on adopting further restrictions, supplying promised weapons, and agreeing how to finance another year of Ukrainian resistance.
Monday’s attack exposed the urgency of those decisions, particularly where European money still depends on American authorization to become usable military support.

articles.title: Russia’s war on Ukraine ‘must be brought to an end’, Zelenskyy says
articles.body:
Russia’s war on Ukraine ‘must be brought to an end’, Zelenskyy says
Ukraine’s president says communication between Washington and Kyiv ‘virtually nonstop’, despite a spat with Trump.
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that the war with Russia “must be brought to an end” and that his country is preparing for the “next steps” of diplomacy to end the conflict.
The Ukrainian leader’s comments come amid a significant diplomatic fallout with US President Donald Trump, who on Friday night waived sanctions targeting Russia’s energy economy.
In a Sunday social media post, Zelenskyy wrote that he had a “conversation with the American president’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner”.
He added that “a lot depends” on the US position, but it’s clear there are “many things that matter to all of us”.
The Trump administration had already eased restrictions on Russian fuel imports on October 9, when it announced a deal for Russia to supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel to US and global markets in an effort to tackle soaring fuel prices
The US Treasury temporarily authorised the imports despite existing sanctions, prompting criticism that the move could provide Moscow with revenue to sustain its war in Ukraine.
Trump has also criticised recent Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure as “a disgrace”.
Nonetheless, Zelenskyy said his team is in “virtually nonstop communication” with their US counterparts and said a focus of dialogue is on the results of the talks in Florida and further steps.
US wavers on Ukraine’s access to tech
Zelenskyy also said he was “thankful” that the US had resumed intelligence sharing with Ukraine after a pause left the country particularly vulnerable to Russia’s regular ballistic missile attacks.
“It was blocked for some period of time. And then it was deblocked by the American side,” Zelenskyy told NBC, adding: “Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles. And we didn’t get it during ballistic attacks during three days.”
Kyiv has also reported restrictions on the speed of satellite service Starshield, a military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite connectivity network, provided to Ukraine by Musk’s company SpaceX.
Ukraine said its relays were experiencing a limit on how fast receivers could travel while maintaining connectivity, making it almost impossible to intercept Russia’s upgraded jet-powered long-range drones.
Musk had said any restrictions imposed on Starshield connectivity were the responsibility of the US government. The White House quickly rebuked that and in an NBC interview on Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called Zelenskyy “very reckless” for accusing the US of throttling connectivity.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Sunday that Ukraine is currently blocked from Starshield, and that a request from Kyiv to access the system for attacks deep inside Russia is “under discussion”.
US officials defend Russia waiver as Trump orders 60-day review
Meanwhile, in the US, Trump has faced bipartisan pushback for his executive order on Friday night, waiving parts of the Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.
Trump had signed the act into law in September, in honour of the late Senator Graham, a close Republican ally.
But his decision to ease sanctions and tariffs against Russia has prompted backlash even from within his own party. The penalties act was scheduled to take effect on Sunday.
Over the weekend, Trump signalled he has yet to make a final decision on easing the sanctions against Russia.
“My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” he wrote on Truth Social.
He concluded his post with further criticism directed at Zelenskyy. “He doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” Trump said of the Ukrainian leader.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that Trump wanted up to 60 days to assess the economic consequences of imposing the sanctions and tariffs that were waived on Friday.
Zelenskyy has warned, however, that the waiver could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin and prolong the war.
Rubio also defended the latest deal to import Russian diesel, saying “that diesel is going to be sold one way or the other”. He argued that the fundamental question was how much the US would secure for itself.
In a series of Sunday morning media appearances, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright also backed the arrangement.
Speaking to ABC, he called the deal a “carrot to try to end the war, not an economic lifeline” for Russia.
“If Russia can bring additional diesel to the market and export it, it would benefit American consumers,” Wright told CNN. “He’s putting pressure that would both benefit American consumers and be a step forward for peace in the Russia-Ukraine war.”
Long-range attacks continue
Also on Sunday, Ukrainian media reported that Russian strikes killed two people in the western Volyn region, near the border with Poland, and injured at least five others across the country. Overnight attacks by Russia killed a woman and injured a six-year-old in the Zaporizhzhia region.
On Saturday night and in the early hours of Sunday, Ukraine hit Russia’s second-largest city, St Petersburg, with a significant drone attack. It targeted a key oil refinery and depot, a warehouse of Russian online retailer Ozon and a data centre run by Russian social media company, VKontakte.
At least one person was killed in the attack, which Russian state media said was the largest on the city since the start of the war in 2022.

articles.title: Ukraine got 'no warning' of Russian ballistic strikes, Zelenskyy says
articles.body:
Ukraine got 'no warning' of Russian ballistic strikes, Zelenskyy says
October 19, 2026
A barrage of Russian ballistic miles struck Kyiv and the surrounding region on Monday, killing at least one person and knocking out power to over half a million homes, Ukrainian authorities said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Telegram that Russia had launched 16 ballistic missiles, targeting Ukraine's energy facilities, 10 of which were hit, cutting power to some 550,000 households.
The president also lamented the lack of warning from Ukraine's international partners.
"Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners," he wrote.
Ukraine's Air Force reported strikes, which included cruise missiles and drones, hitting 25 locations. Of the 269 recorded Shahed drones deployed in the overnight attack, Ukrainian air defenses reportedly downed or suppressed 243, as well as four missiles.
Moscow says it hit drone, missile hubs in Ukraine
Russia's Defense Ministry also confirmed the "massive strikes" on Monday, saying it had targeted Ukraine with "ground-based high-precision weapons and strike drones."
The ministry said it had hit a Ukrainian data center, a logistics hub storing components for drones and cruise missiles, a train depot storing missiles and an industrial facility involved in the production of drones.
It also said it had struck a bulk carrier in the Black Sea, some 130 kilometers (80 miles) from the port of Odesa, which the ministry said had been carrying military and dual-use cargo.
Ukraine did not confirm those targets but said that a medical facility had been hit in the capital, as well as one of the city's metro stations, according to a post by the Kyiv City Military Administration on Telegram.
Kyiv, Washington disagree over pause to intelligence sharing
The overnight strikes come amid contradictory claims by both Ukraine and the US about pauses to intelligence sharing.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that Washington had not paused some of its intelligence sharing, denying a statement Zelenskyy made on Sunday.
"I don't know where [Zelenskyy's] getting these things or why he's saying these things to the press. You should go back and ask him. There's been no pause," Rubio said during a visit to Uzbekistan.
"What he should focus on, and what we want to be focused on, is bringing an end to this war. That's what he should be focused on," he added.
Ukraine is dependent on the ability of US intelligence to spot fast-moving ballistic missiles fired by Russia. Some recent attacks have taken place without warning, Ukrainian officials have reported.

articles.title: Ukraine now gets only 12 Patriot interceptors a month
articles.body:
- Zelenskyy said the U.S. now supplies Ukraine 12 Patriot interceptors a month, about a quarter of the Biden-era level.
- He said Washington has approved only part of the deliveries Ukraine paid for through NATO’s PURL mechanism, calling the delay not technical.
The United States is now sending Ukraine only 12 Patriot air defense interceptors a month, about a quarter of what Kyiv received under President Joe Biden, and is holding back some missiles Ukraine has already paid for, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Zelenskyy made the comments in an interview with Bloomberg in Kyiv published on Oct. 18. Under the Biden administration, Patriot missiles reached Ukraine as U.S. military aid, while under President Donald Trump, Washington sells them, with the purchases funded by Ukraine and its European allies.
Ukraine paid for weapons, including interceptors for ballistic missiles, through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List, known as PURL, a NATO-coordinated mechanism under which allies finance American weapons for Ukraine, Zelenskyy said. The U.S. side approved some of those deliveries but not the rest, and he said the holdup was not a technical issue.
The Patriot is one of only two Western systems in Ukraine’s arsenal that can shoot down Russian ballistic missiles such as the Iskander-M and the air-launched Kinzhal, alongside the Franco-Italian SAMP/T, which Ukraine operates in much smaller numbers. Each Patriot battery depends on a steady supply of interceptors, and Ukrainian officials have repeatedly said missile shortages force them to choose which cities and facilities to protect.
Zelenskyy said he had offered Washington a trade: Ukraine would stop striking Russian diesel fuel facilities if the United States supplied Patriot missiles to protect Ukrainian infrastructure. Ukraine’s long-range drone campaign against Russian refineries has become a point of tension with the Trump administration, which has pressed Kyiv to halt the attacks.
In the same interview, Zelenskyy said recent U.S. steps appeared aimed at pushing Ukraine toward capitulation, while saying he was not claiming that was the goal of Ukraine’s allies. He also pointed to restrictions on the speed of Starlink satellite internet terminals used by Ukrainian forces.
Ukrainian drone units lost reliable Starshield service, the military version of Starlink, overnight on Oct. 13-14, when terminals stopped holding a connection above about 160 km/h (100 mph). Zelenskyy said earlier this month that the cap left Ukraine unable to intercept some of Russia’s jet-powered Shahed drones, which fly at more than 400 km/h, before speeds were later partly restored.
Washington has not publicly given a reason for the pace of Patriot approvals. U.S. production of the PAC-3 MSE interceptor is rising under a multiyear contract with Lockheed Martin, but the missiles are in heavy demand from the U.S. military and allies in Europe, the Middle East and Asia.
Zelenskyy said he remains in contact with U.S. officials and hopes Washington will approve the remaining paid-for deliveries.

articles.title: Ukraine has liberated more territory than Russia has captured since the beginning of fall—a trend that has persisted throughout 2026, Zelenskyy says
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces have liberated more territory since the beginning of the fall than Russian troops have captured during the same period. This trend has persisted throughout 2026, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in his 18 October address. He also reported that Dobropillia, Kostiantynivka, and five other settlements remain under Ukrainian control.
Russia systematically exaggerates its battlefield gains. A recent briefing by Valery Gerasimov, chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces, in which he claimed that Russian forces had captured 92 settlements since the beginning of September, as well as Kostiantynivka and Dobropillia, and advanced to within 5 kilometers of Zaporizhzhia, was based on “outright lies, manipulation, and exaggerations,” Ukrainian General Staff spokesperson Andrii Kovaliov said.
Ukraine also continues to defend areas near Kramatorsk, Zelenskyy said. He dismissed Russian claims about Zaporizhzhia.
“We are destroying Russians 20 kilometers from Zaporizhzhia, not five, as someone in Russia is fantasizing to Putin,” Zelenskyy said.
Ukrainian forces continue to hold back Russian assaults and destroy groups of occupying troops attempting to infiltrate Dobropillia, the president said. The Defense Forces are also defending positions elsewhere in Donetsk Oblast and in Kharkiv and Zaporizhzhia oblasts.
Zaporizhzhia axis: Russians seek to move artillery closer to the city
Russia seeks to advance on the Zaporizhzhia axis to bring the regional capital within range of its tube artillery, hold forward positions, and protect rear areas from Ukrainian strikes, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said on 18 October.
Maksym Kravchuk, spokesperson for Ukraine's Southern Group of Forces, refuted Gerasimov’s claims that Russian forces had captured Malokaterynivka, located south of Zaporizhzhia, stressing that the settlement remains under Ukrainian control, the Center for Countering Disinformation said on 18 October. Ukrainian troops recorded a video directly from Malokaterynivka to confirm this.
As of 18 October, Russian forces had advanced or infiltrated to within 24 kilometers of Zaporizhzhia, ISW said.
Dobropillia remains under Ukrainian control despite Russian assaults
Dobropillia is now a fortress anchoring Ukrainian positions along the highway leading northeast toward Kramatorsk. Russia first tried to take Dobropillia in August 2025 and is now trying again.
Russia is redeploying reinforcements to the Dobropillia axis and continues to send assault infantry through the village of Nove Shakhove despite heavy losses. Russian command will likely try to encircle or at least envelop Dobropillia and cut off Ukrainian supply routes from the direction of Bilozerske, Ukrainian military analyst Kostiantyn Mashovets wrote on 9 October.
Mashovets sees the push as the southern flank of a Russian effort to envelop the whole Sloviansk–Kramatorsk urban area.
Ukraine retook Kolodiazi north of Lyman as its drones hit 200-plus Russian vehicles in Operation Vivaldi’s last phase, Ukrainian drone officer says
Dobropillia remains under Ukrainian control, Zelenskyy said. On 18 October, footage located by analysts showed a Russian soldier hoisting a flag in the town's southeast after an infiltration, yet ISW has found no sign that Russian troops have dug in there.
Russia claimed to have captured Kostiantynivka, but ISW found no evidence
Ukrainian troops in and around Kostiantynivka are stopping Russia from locking in its gains in the city or pushing on toward Druzhkivka and Kramatorsk, ISW said on 17 October.
Russian officials claimed that capturing Kostiantynivka was an important step toward establishing control over the Sloviansk–Druzhkivka–Kramatorsk urban agglomeration and the entire Donetsk Oblast, ISW said in August. The Kremlin also claimed that Russian forces had captured the city as early as 5 July, the institute added.
A Russian military blogger claimed that Russian forces had full control over Kostiantynivka, but ISW found no evidence to support this claim, the institute said in its 16 October assessment. Russian troops had only infiltrated parts of southern and central Kostiantynivka without consolidating positions, and there was no evidence of their presence in its northern part, ISW added.

articles.title: Russia Launches 16 Ballistic Missiles at Kyiv Without Advance Allied Warning, FT Reports
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Russia Launches 16 Ballistic Missiles at Kyiv Without Advance Allied Warning, FT Reports
Ukraine received no advance warning from its Western partners before the first wave of Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv overnight on October 19, although intelligence arrived ahead of a second wave.
The Financial Times reported on October 19 that Ukraine received only partial intelligence about the Russian missile launches, raising concerns over the reliability of early-warning information shared by its allies.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat confirmed that Russian forces launched two waves of ballistic missiles, at approximately 11 p.m. and 3 a.m. While no warning arrived from Ukraine's partners before the first wave, intelligence was received ahead of the second.
Ihnat explained that Ukrainian forces continued monitoring potential missile launches through their own intelligence sources and radar systems. However, the absence of advance information from partners reduced the time available to warn civilians.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized the disruption in a Telegram statement on October 19, emphasizing that the latest attack was not an isolated incident.
"Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no advance warning from our partners," Zelenskyy wrote.
According to the Ukrainian president, Russia launched 16 ballistic missiles in a coordinated attack targeting Kyiv and the surrounding region.
Russian forces also deployed more than 200 drones of various types, including jet-powered Shahed drones, against targets across Ukraine, from the Kharkiv and Dnipro regions to Volyn, Rivne, and Odesa.
The overnight strikes targeted energy infrastructure across 11 Ukrainian regions, including Vinnytsia, Volyn, Kirovohrad, Kyiv, Mykolaiv, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, Kharkiv, Ternopil, Odesa, and Rivne.
Zelenskyy confirmed that more than 10 energy infrastructure facilities were damaged, leaving at least 550,000 households without electricity.
The strikes also damaged a medical clinic, a school, a metro station, and residential buildings. Casualties were reported, while emergency and repair crews worked to restore essential services.
The Ukrainian president linked the attacks to what he described as insufficient pressure on Moscow, criticizing restrictions on air defense missile deliveries and sanctions relief granted to Russia.
"When the supply of missiles for Ukrainian air defense is blocked, while Russia receives sanctions relief or delays, this is, unfortunately, a denial of reality by partners," Zelenskyy stated.
He also emphasized that Ukraine had responded positively to every proposal for a ceasefire, while the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, continued rejecting measures aimed at de-escalation.
The gap in allied early-warning intelligence had already surfaced days earlier, when five Russian ballistic missiles struck civilian infrastructure in Kyiv on October 13 without any advance notice from partners.
That attack was part of a barrage of more than 100 aerial weapons that also destroyed an apartment building in Kharkiv, killing four people and injuring 41 others. Advance intelligence on ballistic launches is critical because the missiles' short flight time leaves civilians and air defense crews only minutes to react.

articles.title: Lavrov In Tehran Amid Questions Over Whether Moscow Is Helping Iran In War With US
articles.body:
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov arrived in Tehran on October 19 for talks with his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araqchi and a meeting with President Masud Pezeshkian amid questions over what support Moscow is providing Iran to fight its war with the United States.
Lavrov traveled to the Iranian capital directly from Manama, where he had attended a meeting with Gulf Cooperation Council officials. Gulf states have urged Moscow to use its influence to press Tehran to halt attacks on its neighbors.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baqaei said the visit was intended to follow up on bilateral agreements. Moscow said the talks would focus on the regional crisis, which it blames on the United States and Israel, as well as on trade, energy, and transport projects.
Russian President Vladimir Putin told Pezeshkian earlier this month that Moscow was prepared to contribute to mediation efforts to help bring the war to an end.
But what's not on the public agenda will be the focus of much of the world. After battling a much more powerful adversary for almost eight months, questions about how much support Iran is getting from Russia -- which has never directly entered the war -- and in what form have simmered.
They came to a boil, however, on October 18 when US President Donald Trump said in a social media post that Russia is doing “very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran” compared to what it could do.
That came after he wrote earlier in the week on social media that he did not believe either Moscow nor Beijing were helping Iran “at all.”
"If they are, it's at a very low level, but I don't believe they are at all. They have too much to lose, and we would know about it, and know about it very fast," Trump wrote.
Trump's October 18 comment was made as part of his justification to waive sweeping sanctions planned against Russia, saying it could drive the Kremlin away from negotiations to end the war in Ukraine.
The Trump administration recently waived sanctions on Russian diesel exports, drawing bipartisan condemnation, as well as raising the ire of Ukraine and many of its international partners.
'Russian Support Has Been There'
Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the Belgium-based International Crisis Group, told RFE/RL that while it's true Moscow has withheld heavy weaponry and deals for jets such as the Su-35 fighters have stalled, Russia has still provided Iran with military intelligence enabling “precision strikes against US bases” and helped improve Iranian-made systems, including Shahed drones, through continued military-technical cooperation.
“So, it really depends on how you define support, but Russian support has been there, and it has had a tangible impact,” Azizi said.
Several analysts point to one incident they say shows how important Russia's support for Iran is.
In March, Iran attacked the Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia that wounded 12 American troops.
Experts noted its unusual precision was likely aided by Russian intelligence. Reports then surfaced that two days before the strike, 14 Russian spy satellites passed over the base. Later, US officials concluded that information from Moscow made the precision attack possible.
A senior EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak on the record, told RFE/RL that Russian assistance to Iran has always been limited because its war against Ukraine has stretched Moscow’s resources.
The official said there was “no sign at all that they are limiting it further” and described Trump's comment as "propaganda to somehow explain to the [US] public why he [is] soft on Russia and bullying Ukraine.”
Intelligence, Drones, And Missiles
Since the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28, media reports citing US, European, and Ukrainian officials have described growing Russian support for Tehran.
Several media outlets have cited people familiar with US intelligence that Russia has been passing Iran information on the locations and movements of US troops, warships, and aircraft -- much of it satellite imagery.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Kyiv had evidence that Russia was providing Iran with signals and electronic intelligence.
According to Andrea Kendall-Taylor, senior fellow and director of the Transatlantic Security Program at the Center for a New American Security, and Richard Fontaine, CEO of the Center for a New American Security, "Russia’s support for Tehran has been operationally meaningful but carefully bounded."
"Even as it fights its own war in Ukraine, Moscow has found ways to help Iran strike American targets and sustain the fight through diplomatic cover and material support while stopping short of actions that could draw Russia into direct conflict with the United States," they wrote in an analysis in Foreign Affairs last week.
Amir Chahaki, an analyst based in Germany, told RFE/RL's Radio Farda that Putin wants to use Iran as leverage in his dealings with Trump in return for the US applying pressure on Ukraine.
“The more Putin can persuade Tehran to move closer to Trump’s demands, the more concessions he can extract from Trump," he said.

articles.title: Trump can strike Iran again. He cannot bomb Hormuz open
articles.body:
A navy can control water. It can’t make a merchant captain sail through it. Warships stop missiles, sure, but no admiral can promise a shipping company that its crew, its cargo and its insurance cover will all survive the next voyage. That gap is the real problem in the US-Iran war, and airstrikes alone won’t close it.
Look at what happened this month. Kpler data shows nearly 20.8 million barrels of oil passed through the strait on 8th October, but only 2.9 million on 11th October. A single day proves little, and Washington disputes independent tracking of the strait anyway. CENTCOM says about 97 percent of ships seeking to transit have done so without being hit. Still, the drop shows how fast a recovery falls apart once crews start to wonder whether passage could be fatal. AFP counted 23 attacks in the first two weeks of October, including six on a single day, the most since the war began, and the IMO says 24 seafarers have died in the area since February. On Saturday, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said two loaded tankers caught fire after hitting mines, a claim that has not been independently confirmed.
President Donald Trump has said the US will not strike Iran before the 3rd November midterms, while insisting the blockade stays in force. Planners are reportedly readying options, including a massive ordnance air blast bomb, should he give the order. The diplomatic track is not dead, but it is stuck. Trump rejected Iran’s seven-day plan to reopen the strait last month and now speaks of “productive discussions.” On Sunday, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the offer is still on the table: if Washington accepts Tehran’s conditions, the strait would open within six days and talks would resume on the seventh. Tehran hasn’t paused in the meantime. Reuters reported that Iran has changed how it picks its targets, and UK maritime authorities have logged attack after attack on tankers and container ships this month. The election may delay the next American bombing run. It does nothing about the bill the world is already paying.
Asia pays the most. Before the war, US Energy Information Administration data showed that 89 percent of the crude oil and condensate passing through Hormuz in the first half of 2025 was bound for Asian markets. China, India, Japan and South Korea took nearly three-quarters of it. The strait also carried over a fifth of the world’s liquefied natural gas.
So when traffic stutters, the damage goes well beyond the oil price. Freight and insurance get dearer, and that lifts the cost of every barrel on arrival. Diesel runs short, which hurts trucking, farming and factories. Gas supplies lurch around, and anyone trying to plan electricity output is left guessing. The International Energy Agency’s October oil market report warned that renewed attacks were threatening the recovery in Gulf exports and that tight diesel markets were already cutting into incomes. And Reuters reported last month that marine fuel in Singapore was still more than 60 percent above prewar prices.
Gulf producers aren’t winning here either. The World Bank forecast this month that GCC economies will shrink by an average of 4.3 percent in 2026, with Qatar down 20.9 percent and Kuwait down 14.6 percent. Its rebound scenario for 2027 assumes the conflict eases by the end of this year, which is a big assumption. If it slips, the numbers get worse. Even Saudi Arabia’s workaround is under strain. Houthi attacks more than halved flows through Bab al-Mandeb in September, pushing Saudi crude back toward Hormuz, where it made up 43 percent of the strait’s oil traffic. Buyers and sellers are both being squeezed, and the Gulf partners Washington says it is defending are paying a good part of the cost.
The usual debate asks what options Trump has left. Keep the blockade and escort ships? Resume strikes? Take Kharg Island? Think about a wider ground war? That’s a list of tools, and a list of tools isn’t a strategy. The real question is whether any of them produces a waterway that commercial operators actually treat as open.
Naval escorts are the mildest option, and they do real work. They deter attacks and keep vital cargo moving. But Iran doesn’t have to beat the US Navy. A few surviving drones, missiles, small boats or mines will do, because they turn every voyage into a gamble. Guarding individual crossings for years isn’t the same as getting normal trade back.
READ: Iran’s IRGC Navy threatens to sink US warships approaching Strait of Hormuz
New air and missile strikes could wreck launch sites, command centres and coastal batteries, and things might go quiet for a while. They might also push Tehran to scatter what weapons it has left and hit softer targets around the Gulf. A Reuters investigation counted at least 135 strikes by Iran and allied forces on 84 infrastructure sites in seven Gulf countries since the war began in February. American force isn’t useless. But Iran can answer damage at home by causing trouble across a much wider regional economy.
Then there’s Kharg Island, which handles roughly 90% of Iran’s oil exports. It looks like a tempting prize, a possible bargaining chip. Yet the island sits only about 16 miles off Iran’s coast, well within reach of attack from the mainland. Take the island and you’ve signed up to defend and supply it, and that’s where the trouble starts. A full invasion would be a burden far out of proportion to the goal of keeping ships safe.
Escalation has a cost elsewhere, too. The Center for Strategic and International Studies estimates that replacing the Tomahawk missiles used in this war could take until late 2030. It doesn’t claim Washington is short of weapons for the Iranian fight. The concern is quieter: every high-end munition fired now is one that won’t be there in a Western Pacific crisis. A decision made in the Gulf ends up with a price tag in Asia.
I don’t think any of this means the United States should live with Iranian coercion of shipping. Attacks on civilian vessels have to stop. Seafarers aren’t bargaining chips. Washington and its partners have good reasons to protect navigation and keep up deterrence. But deterrence with no political way out turns into an expensive habit of managing danger without ever ending it.
So what would work? Something small and checkable, to begin with. Attacks on commercial ships would stop at once, and passage would be monitored and open to all vessels equally. Gulf states, shipowners and the relevant international maritime bodies would agree on how to report incidents and keep ships out of each other’s way. The blockade would ease in stages, each step by one side matched by a step from the other and tied to proof that commitments are being kept. Qatari-mediated exchanges show how far apart Washington and Tehran still are, which is exactly why verification and sequencing matter so much. Nuclear questions and wider regional disputes will still need negotiating. Merchant shipping shouldn’t have to wait for them.
Such a deal wouldn’t hand Iran a veto over Hormuz. It would test Tehran’s behaviour while leaving room to respond if attacks start again. And it wouldn’t guarantee peace. What it would offer is something another bombing campaign can’t: a way to tell whether the strait is getting safe enough for ordinary business to come back.
Asia and the Gulf shouldn’t sit and hope. China, India, Japan and South Korea deal with Washington and Tehran in very different ways, yet they share the same stake with the Gulf states that sit on the other side of the strait. They can press both sides in public for transit rules that can be checked, help with monitoring and incident reporting, and make clear to insurers and shipowners that the lanes will be trusted again only once the attacks end. The countries that take most of the strait’s cargo, and those that ship it, have the strongest claim to a say in how it reopens.
Trump can still order more strikes. He can turn up the pressure, grab territory or declare another tactical win. The harder test is whether he can turn military leverage into a lasting opening of the world’s most sensitive energy corridor. For Asia and the Gulf, that’s the difference between one more show of American firepower and a return to economic security.
Hormuz can’t be bombed back to normal. It has to be made safe enough for the world to trust again.

articles.title: US issues security alerts for Middle East, Yemen war rages
articles.body:
US embassies in the West Asian region issued security warnings to US citizens in the region, citing potential threats from Iran and Yemen’s Houthis on US citizens and interests
War in Yemen continues with tit-for-tat strikes between the Iran-backed Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he hopes the Islamic world can resolve its challenges and differences at an Organisation of Islamic Cooperation meeting in Baghdad, Iraq, and conducted various meetings with other country reps
Israeli attacks continue on Gaza, occupied West Bank, southern Lebanon and south Syria despite any agreements or alleged ceasefires.
And so we continue our live coverage...
Govt staff in Saudi capital told to work from home
Government agencies in Saudi capital Riyadh have told employees to work from home starting Monday, one worker and two consultants told AFP, as the city comes under repeated attack from Yemen's Houthis.
The Kingdom Centre, a 99?storey tower in downtown Riyadh that houses the regional office of the International Monetary Fund, has also requested workers in its offices to stay away until further notice.
On Sunday evening, an employee working for a government agency in Riyadh received a message saying "it has been decided to implement remote work from Monday to Thursday this week".
"We ask everyone to continue their activities as normal," it added.
Death toll of Houthi attack on Yemen govt camp over 50
More than 50 people were killed and over 200 wounded when Yemen's Houthis hit a military camp in energy-rich Shabwa province with ballistic missiles, officials and military sources said on Monday.
It marked the deadliest attack in weeks as fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognised, Saudi-supported government escalates after the collapse of a years-long truce.
"More than 53 recruits" were killed and over 200 injured, all new members of the internal security forces who were undergoing training, Shabwa authorities said in a statement.
Three ballistic missiles struck al-Alam camp in Shabwa, two military sources said. Majed al-Nuzaili, spokesperson for the Yemeni armed forces, described it as a training centre for security and police recruits.
Egypt delays Saudi military support vote until 26 October
An Egyptian parliamentary vote on whether to authorize the military to help defend Saudi Arabia, should the kingdom request support, has been postponed until 26 October.
The vote had been scheduled to take place this week.
Map of the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb Strait. [Getty]
Israel Katz boasts about wiping over 60 Lebanese villages
In an appearance on Channel 14, the far-right minister said the Israeli military had destroyed more than 60 villages across the so-called security zone that reaches deep inside Lebanon.
"Every single village, we’re talking about 23,000 homes, is in ruins. And that’s not even mentioning the underground infrastructure and the tunnels," he said to a round of applause in the studio.
"There are no residents left, 200,000 people have been displaced," he said. "This is the Gaza model. That's what we've been implementing."
Lebanese President Aoun says Israel has not adhered to the framework agreement signed in June, adding “daily violations” in southern Lebanon “do not help the Lebanese state” to implement its side of the treaty.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has unveiled a security doctrine advocating pre-emptive military strikes and buffer zones along Israel's borders, despite the collapse of his previous security strategy during the 7 October 2023 attack, while displaying maps of supposed regional alliances just days before Israeli elections.
The three-page document, titled "Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Security Concept", was published on the Israeli government's website on Sunday and outlines the country's alleged principal security threats and 10 central principles guiding its military strategy.
Russia's foreign minister has arrived in Tehran for his first visit since the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran, Russian news agencies reported on Monday, as Moscow seeks to play a mediating role.
Arriving from Bahrain, Sergei Lavrov was scheduled to meet with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
His visit comes after Russian President Vladimir Putin told his Iranian counterpart earlier this month that Moscow was prepared to contribute to mediation efforts.
Iran will respond forcefully to new US attacks: official
An adviser to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said Iran will respond forcefully to any renewed US attack.
Conservative politician Mohammad Mokhber said Iran would strike “nine countries” if Iranian bases or “petrochemical” facilities were struck again, not directly naming the nine.
“If they want to hit a base, we have to hit the bases of nine countries,” he said Monday in recorded comments posted by Tasnim, a semiofficial news agency close with the Revolutionary Guard.
Houthi rebels strike a government military camp in south
UN rights experts on Monday called on Israel to protect Palestinian farmers in the West Bank as settler attacks worsen with the annual olive harvest.
"Palestinian farmers must be protected and able to access their land safely. Yet, year after year, the violence, destruction and restrictions intensify," the experts said in a statement.
"The olive harvest should be a time when farmers can enjoy, in safety and dignity, the food and livelihoods their nature and land provide, not another season of fear, loss, violence and destruction."
The experts urged Israel to ensure that is forces protect Palestinian farmers from settler attacks and refrain from interference with their access to land. They also urged the international community to "exercise maximum pressure to protect Palestinian civilians".
Israeli violence on Palestinians is surging in the territory ahead of Israel's bitterly fought October 27 elections. The vote coincides with Palestinians' annual olive harvest which has been disrupted by Israeli settlers as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu seeks to shore up his pro-settlement right-wing base.
Govt operations continue against Houthis in Bab al-Mandeb
Sources in Bab al-Mandab told The New Arab that military operations by the internationally recognised government are continuing against the Houthis.
The sources also said that government forces are fighting two battles, the first to "clear" the Houthis and their vehicles, and the second to clear the lands of mines in very large numbers.
Israel kills 5 in Gaza over past 24 hours: health ministry
According to the Palestinian ministry of health in Gaza, since the alleged ceasefire in October 2024, Israel killed 1,522 Palestinians, wounded 5,421 and 839 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.
Over the past 24 hours, Israel killed five Palestinians and wounded 22, the ministry reported.
"In each of the previous wars, you [referring to the United States and Israel] entered battle with the slogan of overthrowing the Islamic Republic, dismembering and destroying Iran; yet today you are the ones being destroyed and overthrown while a powerful Iran still stands firm," Iran's chief of staff of the armed forces, Major General Ali Abdollahi said, in remarks carried by state-run media.
The chief of staff said "the next miscalculation against Iran" will be met with more severe responses than before.
Leaders of the Palestinian community still within the 1948 territories and hold Israeli citizenship are urging people in the community to vote in big numbers in next week's election as they seek to unseat fundamentalist Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and topple the most fanatical right-wing government in the country's history.
High turnout by the 21% 1948 Palestinian community could nudge Israel's complex coalition arithmetic in favour of an anti-Netanyahu bloc led by a former military chief, Gadi Eisenkot.
Qatar will soon announce local defence production hub
Qatar will soon announce a defence production hub, the minister of state for defence affairs told the Global Security Forum in Doha on Monday.
Against the background of the Middle East conflict, which has drawn Iranian attacks on the energy-rich Gulf countries, Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani said: "We are partnering with a regional partner, in addition to other partners such as the United States, the United Kingdom, France, to make sure either we do local protection or we are investing in some of these companies."
WFP ending aid for half million in Gaza due to no funds
The UN's World Food Programme said Monday it would end monthly assistance to 500,000 people in Gaza due to a funding shortfall, while warning that needs remained acute.
"As of this month, we're now cutting half a million people from the number of people that we're assisting," Shaun Hughes, the WFP country director, told AFP.
The reductions bring down to 1.1 million people—still roughly half of war-battered Gaza's population—the number of Palestinians receiving WFP aid either in food or cash assistance.
US President Donald Trump on Sunday offered his "complete and total" endorsement of ICC fugitive Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the country's 27 October elections.
"Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel. BIBI NETANYAHU WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
Israeli police said Monday they had arrested 10 people in the occupied West Bank after Israeli settler attacks on an US photographer for The Washington Post and a French mayor.
The police said that they raided several locations across the occupied West Bank and also seized cars and potential evidence related to the attacks, which have stepped up as Israeli settlers disrupt Palestinians' annual olive harvest.
"Following the severe incidents of violence over the past weekend, including the assault of a media worker and the suspected attacks on foreign civilians, an arrest operation was conducted before dawn," said Major General Moshe Finchi, the Israeli police's occupied West Bank commander.
"Suspects were arrested on suspicion of involvement in the violent incidents, violating a military commander's order concerning a closed military zone, and illegal construction," he said.
The attacks come after global outrage over mounting Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank.
Lebanon military delegation to try to halt Israeli attacks
A Lebanese military delegation will present Beirut's demands for an end to Israeli attacks in Lebanon at a trilateral meeting in Tampa, Florida, on 20 October, the Lebanese presidency said in a post on X on Saturday.
Under a deal reached through US-brokered Israel-Lebanon talks, Beirut vowed to disarm Hezbollah, which would in turn lead to Israeli troops gradually withdrawing from Lebanon. But Israel continues to strike the south of the country.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov will visit Tehran today, Monday, for consultations with Iranian officials and aims to follow up on the implementation of bilateral agreements, Iran's foreign ministry said in a statement.
Oil tanker on fire after hitting mine in Hormuz: IRGC
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said Monday an oil tanker caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a mine, the latest such incident since Tehran tightened its grip of the waterway.
Iran seized control of the strait after war broke out against the United States and Israel late February, choking off the vital shipping route which normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil.
The Islamic republic has demanded that all ships seek its authorisation before transiting.
"An oil tanker, which was in violation, struck a naval mine south of the Strait of Hormuz, resulting in an explosion and a fire in its engine room," Iranian state media quoted the Guards as saying.
The tanker was travelling in the strait's "unauthorized southern route" and had disabled its positioning and navigation systems, the statement said.
It came a day after the Guards said two oil tankers caught fire in the strait, both after hitting mines.

articles.title: Russia Bombards Kyiv and Surrounding Region With Missiles and Drones, Killing Two and Injuring 14
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Bombards Kyiv and Surrounding Region With Missiles and Drones, Killing Two and Injuring 14
Russian forces launched a large-scale missile and drone attack on Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight on October 19, killing at least two people and injuring 14 others, including three children.
The attack involved ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and hundreds of drones, damaging residential buildings, medical facilities, educational institutions, and transport infrastructure across the capital and Kyiv region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Kyiv City Military Administration, one person was killed and eight others were injured in the capital, where damage was recorded in the Desnianskyi, Dniprovskyi, and Solomianskyi districts.
In the Desnianskyi district, the strikes damaged a private medical facility and a metro station. Authorities subsequently announced the temporary closure of the Chernihivska and Lisova metro stations on Kyiv’s left bank.
Debris from the attack damaged both the running and power rails near one of the stations, disrupting metro operations in the affected area.
In the Dniprovskyi district, falling debris damaged educational institutions and a sports facility, while additional debris landed on nonresidential premises.
Meanwhile, in the Solomianskyi district, a fire broke out inside a medical facility located on the third floor of a 25-story residential building. Emergency services extinguished the blaze, while the attack also damaged windows in nearby buildings and a shopping center.
The missile strikes also raised concerns about the lack of advance warning for residents. According to sources cited by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty journalist Alex Raufoglu, the ballistic missile attack on Kyiv once again occurred without any warning, a situation that has reportedly happened on previous occasions.
Beyond the capital, Russian strikes caused casualties and extensive damage in several communities across Kyiv region, particularly in Irpin, Bucha district.
According to Head of the Kyiv Regional State Administration Tymur Tkachenko, six people were injured in Irpin, including three children, while three others were reported missing. Deputy Mayor Oleksandr Pashchynskyi also confirmed that a woman had been killed in the attack.
In the wider Bucha district, the strikes damaged 11 private houses, six vehicles, an industrial facility, a warehouse, and an educational institution. Windows were also shattered in several apartment buildings.
In the Vyshhorod district, authorities reported damage to a private residence, five vehicles, and an infrastructure facility.
The overnight assault formed part of a broader Russian aerial attack involving multiple types of missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles launched from Russian territory and occupied Ukrainian regions.
According to Ukraine’s Air Force, Russian forces launched Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles from Russia’s Smolensk, Bryansk, and Kursk regions, as well as Iskander-K cruise missiles from the airspace over the Kursk region.
The attack also involved 269 drones, including Shahed-type attack UAVs, S-8000 Banderol drones, Gerbera drones, and Parodiya decoys. Of the total, 59 were jet-powered drones.
As of 9 a.m. on October 19, Ukrainian air defenses had intercepted or suppressed 247 aerial targets, including four Iskander-K cruise missiles and 243 drones of various types. Among the intercepted drones were 43 jet-powered UAVs, according to the Air Force’s preliminary assessment.
The latest attack comes amid renewed attention to Ukraine’s access to intelligence needed to detect incoming Russian missile strikes. On October 18, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that the United States had resumed intelligence sharing with Ukraine following a temporary suspension, restoring a key channel of military cooperation amid concerns over the availability of early warnings about Russian missile attacks.
