articles.title: Egypt weighs sending troops to defend Saudi Arabia as Houthis warn of another Yemen disaster
articles.body:
Egypt's parliament continued deliberations Monday over whether to send military forces to Saudi Arabia to help Riyadh defend itself against attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels, as the Iran-backed group warned Cairo against intervening and invoked the disastrous Egyptian military campaign in Yemen during the 1960s.
The discussions follow a request by Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi on Saturday to convene parliament and authorize military assistance to the Saudis. In a speech, el-Sissi declared his country's full support for defending the territory of its Gulf allies and pledged to take whatever steps Saudi Arabia requested to protect its security and sovereignty. The statement was seen as an unusual signal of Egypt's willingness to become involved in the conflict.
El-Sissi's initial declaration left the exact nature of the proposed assistance somewhat unclear. However, Egyptian lawmaker Mostafa Bakry offered more details in a statement Sunday, explaining that parliament would discuss the president's decision, in his capacity as commander-in-chief of the armed forces, to send military forces to Saudi Arabia on a defensive mission.
Bakry said Egypt's National Defense Council, chaired by el-Sissi, had already approved the proposed deployment and its assigned mission before parliamentary deliberations began. The council's public statement pledged support for Saudi Arabia but did not specify the deployment of troops.
"Egypt has never abandoned its pan-Arab role or its responsibility to safeguard Arab national security," Bakry said. "For us, Saudi Arabia is an integral part of Egypt's own national security, and any threat to its security and stability is also a threat to us."
The parliamentary discussions were extended after additional lawmakers requested an opportunity to speak. Bakry subsequently indicated that a vote could take place Tuesday.
Meanwhile, Lebanon's Al-Akhbar newspaper, which is affiliated with Hezbollah and the Iranian-led axis, claimed Monday that Egypt already has military personnel in Saudi Arabia, although their presence has not been publicly acknowledged.
"Cairo is preparing to officially send forces to the kingdom after weeks of undeclared military presence, while refusing to participate in operations inside Yemen," the newspaper reported.
According to Al-Akhbar, several Egyptian military personnel arrived in Saudi Arabia weeks ago. Egyptian military sources cited by the newspaper claimed that the decision to publicly announce the move and seek parliamentary approval was prompted by rapid developments on the ground requiring additional forces, alongside consideration of supplying Riyadh with defensive weapons.
The sources said the priority in coordination with Saudi Arabia was deploying air defense batteries and providing logistical support to secure several vital facilities in the kingdom.
According to the report, the Egyptian forces would undertake defensive missions, including protecting civilians and helping reduce damage from surprise attacks. The sources insisted that Egyptian troops were not expected to participate in offensive operations inside Yemen and claimed that additional forces could begin arriving in Saudi Arabia within days.
Saudi Arabia's request for Egyptian assistance comes after weeks of significant casualties and damage caused by Houthi missile and drone attacks. The rebels say the attacks are retaliation for the Saudi air blockade of Houthi-controlled areas in Yemen and for military operations against them by forces loyal to Yemen's internationally recognized government, which Riyadh supports.
The deadliest recent attack on Saudi Arabia occurred when a Houthi missile struck Riyadh's international airport, killing 13 people and injuring more than 300.
The continuing attacks are also damaging Saudi Arabia's economy and threatening Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's Vision 2030, an ambitious program aimed at diversifying the kingdom's economy and reducing its dependence on traditional sources of revenue.
Egypt's parliamentary discussions come just over a month after Mohammed bin Salman visited Cairo on September 15 and met with el-Sissi.
Following that meeting, the Egyptian presidency said the two leaders had reaffirmed their commitment to ensuring freedom of navigation and maritime security in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, where the Houthis have recently tightened their control over nearby areas and shipping routes.
El-Sissi stressed Egypt's opposition to any attack targeting Saudi Arabia or threatening freedom of navigation along international shipping routes. The statement said both leaders agreed that the current circumstances required greater solidarity and coordination between their countries.
Egypt is among the countries most vulnerable to security developments around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Although the Houthis are currently concentrating their attacks on Saudi Arabia, Egypt, farther north, depends heavily on revenue from the Suez Canal, which is reached through the strait and the Red Sea.
Any escalation in the area can therefore cause substantial economic damage to Cairo.
For that reason, although Egypt is generally reluctant to enter military alliances and prefers to maintain a neutral position as a regional mediator, it has a clear interest in ending the confrontation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis as quickly as possible.
The Houthis, who are closely following developments in Egypt, have already begun issuing warnings to Cairo.
Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthi political bureau, told Qatar's Al-Araby television that the Egyptian military carries bitter memories of its involvement in Yemen between 1962 and 1968, and said he could not imagine it repeating that experience.
Al-Bukhaiti was referring to the events following a military coup in Yemen in September 1962, when Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser decided to support the republicans fighting royalist forces and sent some of Egypt's most elite military units into the country.
Egypt paid a heavy price for that intervention. Over the course of the conflict, it deployed approximately 70,000 soldiers to defend the new government and became trapped in a prolonged war fought under difficult conditions, with mountainous terrain and few roads.
The campaign, which ultimately forced Egyptian troops to withdraw, is still sometimes referred to as "Egypt's Vietnam."
In his interview with Al-Araby, al-Bukhaiti also mocked Saudi Arabia's leadership, claiming that el-Sissi's remarks exposed the depth of the kingdom's humiliation.
The Saudi leadership, he said, had reached a point where it was begging other countries to defend and protect it, even though, in the Houthis' view, Saudi Arabia itself was the aggressor. "We do not expect Egypt to become involved in aggression against Yemen. Egypt is bigger than that," he said. He added that such an intervention would place Egypt in the same camp as the United States and Israel.
Meanwhile, Al-Akhbar reported Monday that Houthi intelligence was monitoring movements by foreign forces that had allegedly arrived in Jizan, in southwestern Saudi Arabia, near the Yemeni border. According to the newspaper, the area has become a staging ground for planning attacks against Yemen.
The report claimed that Pakistani forces were also present, following a defense alliance recently signed by Pakistan and Turkey with Saudi Arabia. It further alleged that Ukrainian personnel had arrived in the area several days earlier aboard a military transport aircraft. Those reports have not been independently verified.
The Houthis have threatened to target foreign forces involved in military operations against them, raising the possibility that Egyptian, Pakistani or Ukrainian personnel could come under attack if they participate in the campaign.
Fighting inside Yemen is also continuing between the Houthis and forces loyal to the internationally recognized Yemeni government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.
On Monday, reports from Yemen described a major Houthi attack on the al-Alam military base in Shabwa province, allegedly carried out during a training exercise. Dozens of Yemeni government troops were reportedly killed or wounded.
Houthi missile and drone launches toward Saudi Arabia have also continued. Early Monday morning, an alert was issued in Jizan following reports of another launch.

Ukraine Exposes Foreign-Made Components Behind Russia’s Anti-Jamming Tech Used in Missiles and Drones
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate (HUR) has identified foreign-made components used in the production of Russia’s Kometa anti-jamming navigation modules, which are installed in Russian missiles, attack drones, and guided aerial bombs.
According to HUR from Ukraine’s military intelligence, the modules are designed to protect onboard navigation systems against electronic warfare interference, allowing Russian weapons to maintain navigation capabilities in contested environments.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Kometa system uses controlled reception pattern antennas, which can suppress interference by adjusting the antenna’s reception pattern and applying signal-processing algorithms.
According to HUR, a standard Kometa module used in modern Russian missiles, unmanned aerial vehicles, and guided aerial bombs consists of two main components: an antenna array containing a specified number of patch antennas and a signal-processing module based on a programmable logic device.
The system’s resistance to electronic interference depends on the number and arrangement of its patch antennas, as well as the algorithms used to process incoming signals.
By combining signals received through multiple antennas, the module can determine the direction of incoming interference and reduce its impact on the navigation system.
Ukrainian intelligence reported that Russian forces are already widely deploying Kometa modules equipped with 16 patch antennas, while efforts are underway to establish serial production of more advanced 20-element antenna arrays.
HUR also identified the Russian company VNIIR-Progress as the developer and primary manufacturer of various Kometa modifications. The enterprise belongs to the ABS Electro group of companies, which Ukrainian intelligence linked to sanctioned Serbian pro-Russian politician Nenad Popović.
According to the intelligence agency, another company within the same group is responsible for procuring components needed to manufacture the navigation modules. The supply network includes Chinese distributors and sellers of microelectronics, as well as Russian intermediaries involved in obtaining foreign-made electronic components.
To fulfill orders from Russia’s defense industry, VNIIR-Progress uses both its own manufacturing facilities and the production capacities of other companies within the ABS Electro group. HUR also identified the principal customers for Kometa modules as Russian manufacturers of cruise and ballistic missiles, attack drones, guided aerial bombs, and glide munitions.
In a separate investigation published on October 14, The Insider reported that Chinese technology company Shenzhen Xingkai Technology was prepared to supply mesh communication modems to a Russian drone manufacturing facility despite being informed that the equipment was intended for military use.
The investigation found that the company was willing to deliver communication systems to a drone production facility in Alabuga, Russia, where the equipment could be used to support long-range drone attacks against Ukraine.

articles.body:
Trump accuses Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion
President Trump said Sunday that he is "in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," and he accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the conflict sparked four and a half years ago by Russia's full-scale invasion.
In a Truth Social post on Sunday, Mr. Trump criticized Zelenskyy for targeting Russian diesel refineries and said, "he doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did."
"He could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now. His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded, and/or dead," Mr. Trump wrote.
The comments come amid a deepening rift between Mr. Trump and Zelenskyy, with the U.S. president criticizing his Ukrainian counterpart for attacking Russian oil infrastructure — a tactic Ukrainian forces have focused on in recent months in a bid to deprive Putin's forces of both cash and fuel to continue their brutal offensive.
Mr. Trump said Sunday that he had decided to hold off on implementing new sanctions against Russia because he doesn't "want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table."
Mr. Trump asserted on Truth Social that "great progress is being made, and that includes current hostage negotiations," adding that, regarding the additional sanctions, "I can sign it later, or any time that I want!"
Zelenskyy earlier said that while he trusted Mr. Trump, siding with Moscow would be a tragedy and a "historic mistake" for Washington.
"People want to forget what's going on. But we can't give this possibility to forget, or to change reality, or to change the truth," Zelenskyy said. "We can't compare me and Putin. He's aggressor. He occupied us. He killed adults and children, his soldiers. He's a terrorist, and that's why I hope that President Trump will be very clear with this position."
Speaking Sunday on NBC's "Meet the Press," Zelenskyy said waiving sanctions against Russia, which Mr. Trump has already done to enable Russian diesel exports, would strengthen Putin's war effort. He also said U.S.-Ukraine intelligence sharing had resumed after being "blocked for some period of time."
Asked Sunday about reports, including by CBS News, that the U.S. may have intentionally withheld early warnings from Ukraine last week of deadly Russian missile strikes, and Zelenskyy's assertion that data sharing was blocked for a period of time, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday that he was "not sure Zelenskyy knows what he's talking about, but it wasn't deliberate."
"We have nothing to do with that," said Rubio.
Regarding separate but linked claims from Ukrainian officials that crucial satellite data from Elon Musk's Starlink network had been constrained last week, inhibiting Ukraine's offensive and defensive drone operations, Rubio said, "The United States, nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down. It sort of happened, but my understanding is it's been restored. It's back to where it was before."
Later Sunday, Zelenskyy said on social media that he had spoken with U.S. presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner about the results of an Oct. 9 meeting between U.S. and Ukrainian negotiating teams in Miami, as well as "next steps in diplomacy."
Ukraine and Russia continued trading strikes over the weekend. Russia's Defense Ministry said Sunday it had intercepted more than 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, as well as Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula and the Black Sea.
At least one person was killed and five others wounded in an attack on St. Petersburg that also sparked fires at the Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchi oil depot, according to local government authorities.
A logistics center belonging to Russian retailer Ozon and a data center operated by Russian tech giant VK were also targeted, the companies confirmed.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency Tass that Kyiv was "resisting" Moscow's invasion but could not "change the current course of events."
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, a woman was killed and a 6-year-old girl was among at least two other people wounded in two Russian attacks on the southern city of Zaporizhzhia, local officials said Sunday.

articles.title: Rubio says there was no US pause in intelligence sharing with Ukraine
articles.body:
Rubio says there was no US pause in intelligence sharing with Ukraine
Ukraine relies on US intel provided through Starshield system to spot fast-moving ballistic missiles that Russia fires at its cities.
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has denied any suspension of intelligence-sharing with Ukraine after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Washington has resumed providing critical intelligence to help Kyiv defend against Russian missile strikes.
“There has been no pause,” Rubio told reporters while on a visit to Uzbekistan on Monday. “What [Zelenskyy] should be focused on and what we want to be focused on is bringing an end to this war.”
Ukraine has relied on US intelligence through Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite service, to detect the fast-moving ballistic missiles that Russia has fired in waves at its cities.
Asked about a possible meeting between US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to negotiate an end to the more than four-year Ukraine war, Rubio said: “There’s been talks of a meeting. I don’t know whether it’s been finalised, but the president [Trump] has been clear. He’d like the war in Ukraine and Russia to end.”
The comments were made after Ukrainian officials said some Russian strikes had occurred without warning. Speaking to the NBC TV network’s Meet the Press programme on Sunday, Zelenskyy said intelligence-sharing had been interrupted but was later “deblocked”.
“We are very thankful for this,” he said. “Now it works.”
Waiving sanctions on Russia
Zelenskyy also said other US actions, such as signing a deal to import Russian diesel and waiving sanctions on Russia that had been slated to take effect this week, will hurt Ukraine.
“If the United States will officially take the side of Russia, of course if these two countries will be together, of course, we will not prevail, and we will not be able to stand,” he said.
Trump on Sunday defended his decision to waive some sanctions on Russia while accusing Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war.
“My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
He claimed that “Zelenskyy doesn’t care” about ending the conflict. “Frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him … he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.”
Trump has temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel, allowing large quantities to flow into global markets in a bid to lower fuel prices.
The US president also reiterated his accusation that Ukraine was purposefully targeting Russian refineries to try to hurt Trump’s Republican Party in the November 3 midterm elections.
Polling has suggested Trump’s party is heading for a likely defeat in the elections as many voters are upset by fuel costs, which have soared since the US and Israel launched a war on Iran in late February.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent spoke with Meet the Press after it aired Zelenskyy’s interview, saying the Ukrainian president “presents a false binary this morning that Ukraine must win”.
“The war must end, and that will be with some kind of a negotiated settlement,” he said.
Bessent slammed the claim that the US government was behind the slowing of the SpaceX satellite communications. “President Trump and Secretary Rubio have categorically said that no one in the Trump administration did that,” he said. “And I think it is very reckless for President Zelenskyy to make such a charge.”
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, a Russian missile attack killed a woman and wounded several people in the capital, Kyiv, overnight, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram on Monday.
The attack also damaged a metro station, a medical facility, an educational institution and a nonresidential building, according to the State Emergency Service.

articles.title: Zelensky speaks to US envoys as Trump lashes out
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Zelensky speaks to US envoys as Trump lashes out
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky spoke with top US envoys Sunday to try to ease tensions, as Donald Trump accused his counterpart of not wanting to end the war with Russia.
Zelensky spoke to US officials Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as both Russia and Ukraine hit each other's energy sites, with Moscow leaving thousands without power and Kyiv carrying out the largest drone attack on Saint Petersburg since the start of the war in 2022.
Trump and Zelensky have clashed as the US president blocked new sanctions on Russia and struck a diesel deal with Moscow, fuelling fears in Kyiv and Europe that the White House was steering towards Moscow.
On Sunday Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform that he was in the process of negotiating a peace between Russia and Ukraine and making "great progress," but claimed: "Zelenskyy doesn't care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him... he doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did."
"Zelenskyy is using Diesel Refineries in Russia as a target, knowing that these attacks are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States," Trump said.
Earlier, after speaking to Trump's business partner Witkoff and son-in-law Kushner, Zelensky said "a lot depends" on the US position in the war but that "it is clear that there are many things that matter to all of us and that this war must be brought to an end."
Ukraine was ready to work "constructively" and "honestly", he said. "We expect exactly this approach from all our partners -- both from the Europeans and, of course, from the American side."
He said he discussed deliveries of US Patriot air defence systems, as Kyiv struggles to counter Russian missiles.
Zelensky earlier told US broadcaster NBC it would be a "historic mistake" if Washington formally supported Russia and that he hoped Trump would "change his decisions."
But he also said he was "thankful" the US resumed intelligence sharing after a pause that left his country vulnerable to Russian missile strikes.
Thousands without power
A US-led push to end Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II has so far not brought about a breakthrough and Trump has in the past grown frustrated with both Zelensky and Russia's Vladimir Putin because of their lack of progress.
Zelensky spoke to the American officials as he accused Russia of breaking Trump's "energy ceasefire" 76 times and warning Moscow planned to deprive Ukrainians of heat and electricity before winter.
Russian strikes left "tens of thousands" without power in several regions, he said, with Ukrainian officials reporting three people had been killed.
Ukraine's army launched drones at Putin's hometown of Saint Petersburg late Sunday, setting an oil refinery ablaze and killing one person, Moscow said.
Rising smoke was visible from Saint Petersburg's historic city centre on the banks of the Neva River, with Russia saying Ukraine struck an oil refinery and depot.
Saint Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov said one person was killed and five hospitalised in the city.
Authorities were fighting fires at the Saint Petersburg oil terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot and industrial warehouses, he said.
Russia's VKontakte social network said its data centre was hit and Ozon -- Russia's second largest retailer -- also reported a strike on its logistics centre.
The head of the wider Leningrad region, Alexander Drozdenko, said air defence shot down 144 Ukrainian drones, with state media saying this was the largest attack on the city since the start of the war.
'Dreadful routine of war'
The Kremlin, however, said Ukrainian attacks on its cities will not change its war aims.
Putin has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine and, in a fifth year of war, few see a way out of the conflict.
"There's a general feeling: they're attacking, we're attacking -- it's become the dreadful routine of war," 58-year-old Galina told AFP in Saint Petersburg.
Moscow has rained drones and missiles on Ukrainian cities daily and Kyiv says its strikes are fair retribution.
Sergei, another Saint Petersburg resident who is also 58, said he felt his apartment block shake and quickly realised it was a drone attack.
"I don't know if I was scared, what must be will be," he said.
Ukrainian strikes caused nationwide fuel shortages in Russia earlier this year.

articles.title: Zelensky seeks further US talks as strikes continue
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky spoke with U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on Oct. 18 about efforts to end the war and Ukraine’s air defense needs, as Kiev and Washington remained divided over strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.
Zelensky said they reviewed recent talks between Ukrainian and American teams in Miami and were preparing their next diplomatic steps.
“A great deal depends on America’s position here. Ukraine remains ready to work constructively, honestly, and for real results,” he said.
Trump has demanded that Ukraine halt attacks on Russian refineries and waived new sanctions against Moscow. Zelensky has said Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy facilities continued despite an energy ceasefire announced by the U.S. president.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended Washington’s approach in an Oct. 18 interview with NBC’s “Meet the Press,” accusing European allies of helping finance Russia’s war through continued purchases of Russian goods.
Bessent put U.S. imports from Russia at $4 billion and said European purchases were more than 10 times higher. He also said European allies had rejected his request to join Washington in imposing tariffs on China and India over their purchases of Russian energy.
“So why should the U.S. bear the burden?” he asked.
Bessent also questioned why European NATO members were not supplying Ukraine with more Patriot air defense systems.
Zelensky separately told Bloomberg that Washington was delaying deliveries of Patriot interceptor missiles already paid for through a NATO-coordinated purchasing program. He said he had proposed suspending attacks on Russian diesel infrastructure in exchange for additional missiles to protect Ukrainian facilities.
The exchanges coincided with further attacks on both sides. Ukrainian drones struck an oil terminal and a fuel depot in St. Petersburg early on Oct. 18, causing fires, Russian officials said. Russian technology company VK said its data center in the neighboring Leningrad region was also targeted.
Russian officials reported one person killed and nine injured in and around St. Petersburg. Zelensky said Russian overnight strikes on Ukraine killed two people and injured 12, while attacks on energy facilities left tens of thousands of households without power.
Further Russian missile strikes hit Kiev late on Oct. 18 and early on Oct. 19. Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that a woman was killed in the first attack. Debris from the subsequent strike damaged metro infrastructure and a residential building, prompting the temporary closure of two stations.

articles.title: Denmark Buys More NSM Missiles, Also Used by Ukraine
articles.body:
Denmark is purchasing an additional batch of Naval Strike Missile (NSM) anti-ship missiles to strengthen the country’s coastal defense.
The Norwegian company Kongsberg announced the deal.
The contract, worth approximately €34.5 million, covers the delivery of an undisclosed number of missiles.
Denmark first acquired NSM-equipped coastal defense systems in 2025, becoming the fifth NATO country to field them, alongside Poland, the United States, Romania, and Latvia. Meanwhile, the Danish Ministry of Defense also ordered these missiles to arm its frigates.
The ordered coastal defense system includes a Kongsberg-developed fire control system, NSM missiles, and launchers.
The Norwegian company Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace began developing the Naval Strike Missile in the 1990s to replace the aging Penguin anti-ship missile. In 2012, the Royal Norwegian Navy officially took the NSM into service.
Over time, NSM missiles have been integrated into the arsenals of the US Navy and Marine Corps, the Polish, Romanian, Latvian and Ukrainian navies, as well as the Royal Navies of the United Kingdom, Canada and Australia.
The NSM is a precision-guided, subsonic, low-observable anti-ship cruise missile by design. It is designed to engage surface vessels with advanced air defense capabilities, as well as land-based targets.
The missile weighs 410 kg and measures 3.9 meters, with about 120 kg in its penetrating blast-fragmentation warhead. The missile’s airframe incorporates radar-absorbing materials to minimize its radar cross-section.
The missile’s propulsion system consists of a solid-fuel booster and a Microturbo TRI 40 turbojet sustainer engine. Its operational engagement range exceeds 500 km.
The NSM’s key feature is its multi-mode guidance system. During the midcourse phase, it uses an inertial navigation system, GPS satellite navigation, and terrain-referenced navigation. In the terminal phase, a passive infrared imaging seeker provides guidance.
Because of its passive infrared seeker, the missile does not emit radio-frequency signals, making it highly resistant to electronic-warfare countermeasures. Its target-recognition algorithms enable the missile to autonomously identify specific vessels, fly at extremely low altitudes, and perform evasive maneuvers during the terminal phase of its flight.

articles.title: US Treasury chief rebukes Zelensky for saying Ukraine must win
articles.body:
US Treasury chief rebukes Zelensky
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has rebuked Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky over his insistence that his country must defeat Russia, rejecting his all-or-nothing stance as a “false binary” and insisting that the conflict must end through a negotiated settlement.
Speaking to NBC’s ‘Meet the Press’ on Sunday, Zelensky said Ukraine must win the conflict with Russia, calling victory essential to preserving the country’s independence, geopolitical alignment, and national identity. He lamented that Ukraine “will not prevail” if the US sides with Russia.
“Zelensky presents a false binary this morning that Ukraine must win,” Bessent told the show shortly after Zelensky’s appearance, arguing that the priority should be ending the conflict rather than determining a winner. “The war must end, and that will be with some kind of a negotiated settlement.”
Bessent stressed that Trump made it clear “he wants to end this war,” noting that the president’s decisions are aimed at securing a negotiated settlement.
Zelensky’s remarks came amid a growing spat with Trump over sanctions on Russian and Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities. Last week, Trump invoked a national-interest exemption to suspend the sanctions he signed into law last month, including 500% tariffs on Russian imports and 100% tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.
The move followed Trump’s decision days earlier to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports to ease rising fuel prices. According to US media reports, Trump eased the restrictions after Zelensky refused to halt strikes on Russian energy facilities, which the president blamed for global fuel shortages and soaring prices at the pump – a critical issue just weeks before the US midterm elections. The moves sparked outrage in Kiev, where they were seen as a betrayal of Ukraine’s efforts to maintain Western pressure on Russia.
In a Truth Social post on Sunday, Trump defended the moves, saying Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries are driving up prices, while stressing that he is focused on brokering a peace deal and does not want to “do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.” Trump also argued that Zelensky does not want to end the conflict and probably never did, despite receiving billions in Western aid.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov echoed his criticism, suggesting on Sunday that Zelensky has “no desire” to reach a settlement because his government would collapse if Ukraine signed a deal that’s acceptable to both the US and Russia.
Zelensky, whose presidential term expired in 2024, has refused to hold a new election, citing martial law. Moscow maintains that Zelensky is illegitimate; Trump recently called for his resignation, saying Ukraine should get “a new president.”
Since returning to office, Trump has revived talks with Russia, which were largely suspended under his predecessor, Joe Biden. His efforts to broker peace have produced some results, including POW exchanges, but the diplomatic push has been overshadowed by the US war against Iran and has yet to yield a peace deal.
Moscow has said it would prefer a negotiated settlement. Last month, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia expects to hold trilateral talks with Ukraine and the US in the foreseeable future. President Vladimir Putin, however, stressed that the conflict must end on terms that are acceptable to Russia – stressing that a settlement must address the root causes of the conflict and include the withdrawal of Ukrainian troops from Russian territory, protection for Russian-speakers in Ukraine, as well as denazification and neutral, non-nuclear status for Ukraine.

Trump Eases Russia Sanctions “for Peace” as Zelenskyy Warns of Forced Ukraine Capitulation
US President Donald Trump has defended his decision to suspend sanctions against Russia as an effort to preserve peace negotiations, even as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warns that Washington’s recent actions increasingly resemble pressure on Kyiv to capitulate to Moscow.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to BBC News on October 19, Trump blocked several sanctions against Russia just two days before they were scheduled to take effect, arguing that imposing additional restrictions could drive Moscow away from negotiations.
“I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding that he did not want to “do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table”.
The decision effectively delayed sanctions previously approved by the US Congress and signed into law in September. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described the move as a 60-day suspension intended to assess the potential impact of the restrictions on the American and global economies.
Moscow welcomed the decision. Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev called it “an important and truly historic moment,” claiming the sanctions would have caused serious damage to the US and global markets.
While the Trump administration presents the suspension as a diplomatic measure, Zelenskyy has raised concerns that Washington’s broader approach could leave Ukraine facing increasing pressure to accept Russian demands.
In an interview with Bloomberg on October 18, Zelenskyy said recent US decisions appeared to be pushing Ukraine toward surrender. “I believe steps were taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate,” Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian president clarified that he was describing the apparent consequences of Washington’s actions rather than accusing American officials of deliberately seeking Ukraine’s surrender.
“I don’t want to think that our American partners believe the war can be ended faster at Ukraine’s expense. But that is what it looks like,” he added.
His concerns extend beyond sanctions policy. Zelenskyy cited restrictions on Starlink satellite connectivity, delays in deliveries of Patriot interceptor missiles already purchased by Ukraine, and interruptions in intelligence sharing as examples of decisions affecting Kyiv’s ability to defend itself against Russian attacks.
Trump has rejected accusations that Washington deliberately restricted Starlink services or stopped sharing defense intelligence with Ukraine.
The disagreement has also deepened over Washington’s decision to purchase Russian diesel amid rising energy prices linked to the war involving Iran.
Zelenskyy criticized the arrangement, arguing that American purchases of Russian fuel would effectively contribute revenue to Moscow while its forces continue attacking Ukraine.
Despite international sanctions, Russia remains a major oil exporter. According to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, China purchases approximately half of Russia’s crude exports, while India accounts for around 37%.
Trump has also accused Zelenskyy of obstructing negotiations, claiming that the Ukrainian president “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did”.
Zelenskyy, meanwhile, has maintained that Russia must face sustained international pressure to reach an agreement that does not come at the expense of Ukraine’s sovereignty.
Zelenskyy also said that recent US decisions, including restrictions on military assistance and Starlink connectivity, appeared to be aimed at pressuring Ukraine into capitulation to Russia.
“I believe steps were taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate,” Zelenskyy told Bloomberg, while clarifying that he did not necessarily believe Washington intended that outcome.
Zelenskyy also said the US is currently supplying Ukraine with just 12 Patriot interceptor missiles per month, roughly four times fewer than under the Biden administration, while delaying approval for additional weapons Kyiv has already paid for.

articles.title: Ukrainian Engineers Develop Drone Detector That Reveals What Russian Drones See

Ukrainian Engineers Develop Drone Detector That Reveals What Russian Drones See
A Ukrainian team has developed an SDR-based drone detector that can identify radio signals from unmanned aircraft and convert intercepted transmissions into video that an operator can view.
DOU reported on October 17 that the system, called D·Vision SDR, was developed by Kyiv-based communications equipment company CODE380. The company was founded about three months ago, while development of the detector itself began roughly a year and a half earlier.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to DOU, the device scans radio frequencies from 500 to 8,700 MHz for signals characteristic of drones. Unlike conventional detectors that rely on analog receivers to receive video transmissions, D·Vision SDR uses Software-Defined Radio technology to analyze the radio spectrum in software.
The developers told DOU that the detector can identify a drone signal and convert it into a video feed, allowing an operator to view imagery transmitted by the aircraft. The team also claimed the system scans its entire stated frequency range without "blind spots" and offers greater sensitivity than competing detectors.
DOU noted that four people worked directly on the project, while CODE380 currently has eight employees and involves another six specialists in testing and design. The detector's lead developer previously worked on similar systems and used that experience to build the new SDR-based platform.
The system has undergone field testing with Ukrainian military personnel during combat missions, according to DOU. Feedback from those trials was used to refine the device, while the developers continue releasing software updates approximately twice a month.
Software-defined detection systems offer a different approach to fixed analog receivers because signal processing can be adjusted via software as drone communication and operating frequencies change.
Ukrainian-developed detection technology is also drawing interest beyond the front line.
In early October, Lithuania announced it was deploying the SkyFortress system, which identifies low-flying drones and cruise missiles by their acoustic or electromagnetic signatures and uses artificial intelligence to track them in real time.
The deployment came weeks after NATO fighter jets shot down an unidentified drone that had entered Lithuanian airspace from Belarus.

articles.title: Massive overnight Russian attack leaves over half a million Ukrainians without power, Zelensky says
articles.body:
More than half a million people across Ukraine are without power due to a massive Russian strike against energy facilities and other critical infrastructure overnight, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on X/Twitter on Monday.
"Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners," Zelensky wrote. "They again targeted energy facilities and infrastructure, but a medical clinic, a school, a metro station, and ordinary residential buildings were also damaged."
"In this one night alone, more than 10 energy infrastructure facilities were damaged, and the lights went out for at least 550,000 families. Repair crews are working at the sites."
Zelensky added that Russia had launched 16 ballistic missiles and more than 200 drones of various types, including jet-powered Shahed drones.
"Unfortunately, there are casualties," he stated, sending condolences to their families.
Ukraine never wanted war, responded positively to peace attempts
"Ukraine never wanted this war, and we responded positively to literally EVERY attempt by our partners to end this war honorably—to EVERY ceasefire proposal, our answer was positive," Zelensky continued. "Ballistics, 'Shaheds,' and killings are, again and again, Russia's responses."
"Putin doesn't want not only an end to this war, but even any de-escalatory steps. EVERY one of our partners has faced this personally when hearing refusals from Russia. And it's very important to call things by their proper names. To call the aggressor an aggressor and to help Ukraine protect lives."
Earlier in the day, the Russian Defense Ministry said on Monday its forces had carried out a "massive strike" on targets in Kyiv and Ukraine's capital region, targeting military-industrial facilities, storage sites for cruise missiles and drones, and data centers.
Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Lavrov in Iran as Moscow looks to mediate in war
articles.body:
This file photo shows Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov (R), and Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi (L) shaking hands during a meeting in Moscow, Russia.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov arrived in Iran on Oct. 19 in his first visit since the outbreak of the Middle East war as Moscow seeks to play a mediating role.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said that the trip would focus on “regional and international developments.”
Lavrov was scheduled to meet Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and hold talks with his counterpart Abbas Araghchi.
The veteran diplomat has said Moscow’s efforts are “aimed at preventing the return of a large-scale war,” with talks stalled between Tehran and Washington.
His visit comes after Russian President Vladimir Putin told Pezeshkian in early October that Moscow was prepared to contribute to mediation efforts.
Russia and Iran, two of the most heavily sanctioned nations in the world, maintain close ties. Their military and economic cooperation has only increased since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
In January 2025, Pezeshkian and Putin signed a 20-year strategic partnership treaty in Moscow, covering cooperation in defense, security, energy, trade and transportation.
The agreement also provides for closer coordination on regional and international issues, although it does not establish a mutual defense obligation.
The Middle East war began in February with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. Despite a ceasefire in April, followed by a U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding in June, hostilities in and around the Strait of Hormuz have not stopped.
Iran claims control over the strategic waterway — through which one-fifth of the world’s hydrocarbons pass in normal times — and regularly targets vessels that cross without its authorisation.
In response, Washington has been maintaining a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.
The Russian Foreign Ministry said discussions during Lavrov’s visit were expected to focus on “ways to resolve the acute international crisis triggered by the unlawful aggression of the US and Israel against Iran.”
The ministry said the war had been a blow to stability and security “not only in the near and Middle East, but also on a global scale.”
Iran-backed Houthis have declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and captured territory around the Bab al-Mandab strait, the Red Sea chokepoint and vital export route for Saudi oil since Iran blockaded the Gulf’s Strait of Hormuz.
The hostilities were the focus of a meeting on Oct. 18 between the Russian and Saudi foreign ministers on the sidelines of a summit between Gulf states and Russia in Bahrain’s Manama.
They discussed “regional developments, particularly the escalation in Yemen, as well as the persistent threats to shipping in the Straits of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab”, the Saudi Foreign Ministry said on X.
The Houthis have hit Saudi targets including tankers in the Red Sea, oil facilities and Riyadh’s King Khalid International airport.
A Houthi projectile injured at least six people in southern Saudi Arabia on Oct. 18 after it struck a residential area in Najran near the border with Yemen, according to the kingdom’s civil defence agency.
The Saudi-led coalition also said two ballistic missiles were intercepted in the kingdom’s south. Threat alerts for Najran city and As Sulayyil governorate in Riyadh province were issued but quickly cancelled on Oct. 18.

US Sends Ukraine Just 12 Patriot Missiles a Month, Holds Back Paid-For Supplies, Zelenskyy Says
The United States is supplying Ukraine with only 12 Patriot air defense interceptor missiles per month—roughly four times fewer than under former President Joe Biden—while withholding approval for additional weapons Kyiv has already paid for, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Bloomberg on October 18, Zelenskyy accused Washington of delaying critical air defense supplies and using restrictions on military assistance to pressure Ukraine into accepting unfavorable terms to end Russia’s war.
“We have paid for the weapons,” Zelenskyy said, referring to purchases that include anti-ballistic missile interceptors under the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative. “A part of the supplies has been authorized” by the US side, “while the rest haven’t been. And this is not a technical issue.”
The Ukrainian president said the current delivery rate represents approximately one-quarter of the number of Patriot interceptors supplied during the Biden administration. Unlike previous US military assistance, which provided interceptors to Ukraine without charge, the Trump administration is selling the missiles to Kyiv.
The restrictions come as Ukraine faces continued Russian ballistic missile attacks targeting cities and critical infrastructure, increasing demand for interceptor missiles capable of countering such threats.
Zelenskyy also proposed suspending Ukrainian strikes against Russian diesel fuel production facilities in exchange for additional Patriot interceptors.
“My latest model was: We don’t target Russian diesel, you give us missiles for Patriot systems to protect our facilities. But they just want us to stop attacking diesel. And if we strike that, they will disconnect us from something,” Zelenskyy told Bloomberg.
The proposal follows US demands that Ukraine halt attacks on Russian oil refineries, which the Trump administration has linked to rising global diesel prices. However, Zelenskyy suggested that Washington’s actions extended beyond disagreements over energy infrastructure.
“I believe steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate,” he said. “I am not saying that this is the goal our partners are pursuing. I don’t want to think that our American partners believe the war could be ended sooner at Ukraine’s expense. But that’s how it looks.”
According to Bloomberg, the restrictions on Patriot deliveries have coincided with disruptions to Ukraine’s Starlink satellite communications and the absence of advance US warning ahead of a Russian ballistic missile strike on Kyiv on October 18.
Despite the current disagreements, Zelenskyy expressed hope that relations with Washington could improve following the November 3 US midterm elections. “Politics is very aggressive during election time,” Zelenskyy told Bloomberg. “I think it is agony now, but after elections, life will continue and I believe it will be calmer.”
Earlier, on October 16, Zelenskyy warned that Ukraine was facing a severe shortage of PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptor missiles, noting that most available supplies had been redirected to the Middle East.

articles.title: Netanyahu warns Israel could lose US support, seeks 450 billion shekels in extra defense spending
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned Sunday that Israel could face a hostile U.S. administration in the future, potentially threatening its military assistance and strategic relationship with Washington, and said the country must develop new international alliances. At the same time, he announced plans to allocate approximately 450 billion shekels in additional defense spending over the next decade.
Netanyahu made the remarks during an event at which he presented his security doctrine, nine days before Israel's October 27 election. Just hours later, U.S. President Donald Trump publicly endorsed Netanyahu's reelection bid for the first time during the current campaign.
"In two years, a president, man or woman, could come to power who is very hostile to Israel," Netanyahu said. "How would you deal with that? How would you operate in relation to the United States? And beyond that, what solutions would be necessary?"
His remarks came against the possibility that a future U.S. administration could suspend military assistance to Israel or even join international sanctions and an arms embargo against the country.
Netanyahu said Israel must use the remaining years of Trump's presidency to strengthen its position while preparing for a potentially dramatic shift in American policy.
"First, we must do everything we can during these two years, and during the following two years, in the American arena, through good times and bad," he said. "The second thing is to create other alliances. That is what I am working on now with many countries in our region and outside it. India is not a small country, and there are many others."
He pointed to political developments in Latin America as another opportunity to expand Israel's network of allies.
"There is a major shift in Latin America, and there could be an enormous change in Brazil in just a few days," Netanyahu said. "We must expand our pool of alliances and develop capabilities that make us valuable to everyone."
He also addressed Israel's strained relations with European countries, accusing some governments of publicly condemning Israel while continuing to seek cooperation with it.
"Countries that condemn us, and they have some nerve, by the way, condemn us and then come to us," he said. "I tell them: It depends on you. It depends on how you behave."
Netanyahu argued that Israel still possesses diplomatic leverage but would need considerable international expertise to navigate changes in Washington and other capitals.
In a separate social media post Sunday, Netanyahu appeared to acknowledge the possibility of a change in U.S. leadership, describing Trump's remaining time in office as an opportunity to advance Israel's strategic objectives.
"We have another two years of my friend President Trump's term, and this is exactly the time to complete our major missions on every front," he wrote.
On defense spending, Netanyahu said he intended to allocate approximately 450 billion shekels over the coming decade to strengthen Israel's military capabilities. An additional defense spending package of approximately 350 billion shekels had previously been agreed upon, according to earlier reports.
Addressing the future size of the Israel Defense Forces, Netanyahu said the military would have to expand, although technological advances, particularly artificial intelligence, could reduce some of its manpower requirements.
"As for a large army or a small army, the IDF definitely needs to grow," he said. "It will grow, but not at the rate we might have expected because AI reduces many requirements. Still, it needs to grow, and for that, of course, you need to allocate both funding and personnel."
He added: "I am putting about 450 billion shekels into this so that we have the capabilities and the teeth."
Turning to Iran, Netanyahu said the regime remained a threat despite what he described as severe military and economic damage inflicted on it. He warned that Tehran would seek to rebuild its nuclear program, develop other unconventional weapons and restore its regional network of allied armed groups.
"Like cancer, this will not end as long as that regime remains in place," he said. "It will try to recover, renew its nuclear program, renew other unconventional weapons programs and rebuild the axis."
Netanyahu claimed that Israel had already accomplished approximately 90% of its objectives against Iran and described the Iranian leadership as severely weakened.
"Why aren't people taking to the streets? Because right now they are being killed. Simply killed. They are killing or wounding tens of thousands of their own people. That is the nature of this regime," he said.
He then explicitly stated that his policy was aimed at bringing down the Iranian government. "Our plan is very comprehensive and very determined, to bring about the downfall of the regime," Netanyahu said. "That is my plan. That is the directive I have given all the security agencies, and that is what will happen."
Netanyahu also discussed Israel's relationship with Russia, describing it as one based on competing national interests rather than consistent cooperation.
"We speak when necessary," he said. "But Russia has its interests, and we have the interests of the State of Israel, and they do not always overlap. Sometimes they even clash."
He cited Russia's cooperation with Iran during the war in Ukraine as an example of conflicting interests and also raised the issue of anti-Israel bot networks spreading what he described as extreme antisemitic content.
"We raise all these issues, and we do so very clearly," Netanyahu said. "And when there is an opportunity to cooperate, we do that as well."
Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of the opposition Yashar! party and a former IDF chief of staff, sharply criticized Netanyahu's presentation, describing it as an empty political exercise rather than a serious national security strategy.
"Nine days before the election and three years after the gravest failure and disaster in Israel's history, with every war front still open, Netanyahu decided to present his 'security doctrine' to the public," Eisenkot said.
"Two hollow pages, full of slogans that have nothing whatsoever to do with a security doctrine, reveal more than anything the strategic vacuum Netanyahu has left the State of Israel in and his disregard for the security of Israeli citizens."
Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of attempting to manipulate public opinion and spread fear ahead of the election.
"This is Netanyahu's method: manipulating perceptions, frightening people and trying to divert attention from the parade of lies and racism surrounding his campaign tonight," he said.
