articles.title: The war of attrition with Iran: What happened to US patriots?
articles.body:
The issue is not only the missiles the US military has consumed on the battlefield, but the time it needs to replace them; a time that can affect Washington's ability to confront potential crises in other regions, especially East Asia.
According to a report attributed to the Center for Strategic and International Studies, in seven months of confrontation with Iran, Washington used approximately the equivalent of 19 years of Patriot missile purchases of these interceptors. In the same assessment, restoring US missile stockpiles to prewar levels has been stated to take at least three years. These figures indicate the gap between the speed of munitions consumption in an intense conflict and the ability of the US defense industry to compensate for it.
The importance of this issue increases when we know that military power is not measured merely by the number of aircraft, ships, or advanced systems. The ability to sustain operations in a prolonged conflict and to quickly replace consumed equipment is also a determining factor. An army may possess advanced technology and extensive firepower, but if its munitions stockpiles decrease at a rate faster than production capacity, it will face more serious limitations in continuing operations.
Patriot; An Important Link in US Air Defense
 
The Patriot system is one of the important air defense equipment of the United States and its allies, used to counter certain aircraft and missile threats. The interceptor missiles of this system play an important role in protecting forces, bases, and military facilities. The extensive consumption of these missiles can force commanders to make more difficult decisions about how to allocate munitions, the priority of defending targets, and the level of risk acceptance.
Compensating for this reduction in stockpiles is also not simply a matter of increasing government orders. The production of advanced missiles depends on specialized components, raw materials, skilled manpower, and industrial capacity. Developing production lines and increasing delivery speed is a time-consuming process, and one cannot expect an increase in demand to immediately lead to a proportionate increase in supply.
For this reason, even after the intensity of the conflict decreases, pressure on the US military can continue. Washington must simultaneously meet the needs of forces deployed in the Middle East, maintain its commitments in Europe, and be prepared for potential crises in East Asia. The longer the rebuilding of stockpiles takes, the more difficult it will be to manage these commitments.
A Window of Vulnerability for Washington and a Possible Opportunity for China
 
One of the most important strategic consequences of the reduction in US munitions stockpiles is its connection to the competition between Washington and Beijing. China is considered America's most important strategic rival, and any potential conflict in the Indo-Pacific region could require extensive consumption of precision munitions and defense systems.
Under such circumstances, the reduction in interceptor stockpiles can complicate US military planning. Washington will be forced to strike a balance between meeting current needs in the Middle East and maintaining readiness for potential crises in East Asia. This situation may be what analysts refer to as a "window of vulnerability"; a period in which the replacement of consumed munitions has not yet been completed, but America's security needs in other regions still persist.
Of course, these conditions do not mean China's definitive superiority or America's inability to defend its interests. Washington's military power is not limited to Patriot missiles, and this country still possesses a naval fleet, air force, base network, and regional allies. However, in a prolonged confrontation, the depth of stockpiles and the speed of replacing munitions can become as important as technology and the quality of weapons.
A Cost Beyond the Battlefield
 
The consequences of this situation are not limited to the US military either. Washington's allies, who depend on American systems and munitions for air defense, may face delays in the delivery of orders if demand increases. Under such conditions, the US government must prioritize between the needs of its own forces and the requests of its security partners; a decision that can affect military relations and the security calculations of allies.
For Iran too, this issue has strategic importance; because it shows that the assessment of a military confrontation should not be made only on the basis of the number of equipment or the firepower of the parties. The capacity to withstand pressure, the continuity of operations, and the cost of replacing weapons also play a role in determining the course of a conflict. Of course, the reduction in US interceptor stockpiles alone is not sufficient to prove this country's military defeat and must be examined alongside the operational results and the extent to which the declared objectives of both sides have been achieved.
Ultimately, the extensive consumption of Patriot missiles and the time needed to rebuild America's stockpiles will be the possible restriction of Washington's strategic freedom of action in the post-conflict period. The war may end on the battlefield, but its effects on weapons stockpiles and military readiness will remain for years; an issue that takes the real cost of a prolonged confrontation beyond the days of military operations.
MNA

articles.title: World will face a serious energy crisis if US launches another war against Iran
articles.body:
World will face a serious energy crisis if US launches another war against Iran
IRGC spokesman says Tehran has not yet fully closed the Strait of Hormuz, and could extend that closure to Bab el-Mandeb and the Suez Canal
TEHRAN – More than seven months have passed since the United States, together with Israel, launched its war against Iran. What was meant to be a swift campaign to topple the Islamic Republic has instead left American bases across the region in ruins, the Strait of Hormuz still closed, and Washington without an answer to the energy crisis it helped create. With the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding in tatters and American midterm elections approaching, the question now is whether the US will risk another escalation — or accept defeat.
In an exclusive interview with the Tehran Times, IRGC spokesman General Hossein Mohebbi discussed the course of military operations over the past months and what may lie ahead. He also assessed the current state of Iran's armed forces, and spoke personally about succeeding his assassinated predecessor, Martyr General Ali-Mohammad Naeini — and about duty and loss within the faith that sustains Iran's forces on the front lines.
Below is the full text of the interview:
A question that's on a lot of people's minds these days — both in Iran and around the world — is whether the United States and Israel are once again heading toward an escalation of war and conflict, or not. How would you respond to this?
As military forces, we consider every scenario in this regard possible, and from where we stand, no possibility is off the table. That said, based on our assessments, America is definitely not in a position to want to start a new conflict in order to gain some fresh achievement from it. In the past, America came in with everything it had — it had well-equipped bases and vast amounts of equipment at its disposal, it brought fresh, ready-to-fight forces into the field, it pulled out all the stops and drew on every capacity it had — and yet it still couldn't achieve a single one of its declared or undeclared objectives. Not only did it fail, it suffered numerous strategic defeats, the least of which was the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Despite everything America has done so far, it still hasn't been able to reopen that strait, and on top of that, it's suffered enormously significant strategic defeats.
So at this point, America no longer has those capabilities, and it can't use those bases the way it once did. Most of those bases have been shut down, their equipment has been destroyed, and the countries that were most cooperative with America back then no longer offer that same cooperation. American forces today are tired, worn-out forces, and they've pulled back hundreds of kilometers from us. Before the war started, there were at least thirty to forty warships inside the Persian Gulf; but today, not only do they have no ships inside the Persian Gulf, they've also withdrawn roughly seven hundred kilometers away from the Strait of Hormuz. The forces that were stationed at those regional bases have now been moved to distant bases, and even at those distant bases — like Al-Azraq and Al-Tanf in Jordan and Syria — they're no longer safe, because those locations too are within our crosshairs.
So from a military capability standpoint and from a technical perspective, America doesn't have what it takes to carry out a new operation or conflict. But there is a possibility that, with the American elections coming up, it might want to manufacture some kind of achievement — for example, carrying out a limited action so it can exploit the results for the elections. That possibility exists, and since we don't dismiss any possibility, we're ready to respond to any action. Our response this time will be far more severe and will land America in far bigger trouble, and will confront the world with even bigger challenges too. In any case, if America takes a new action — even a limited one — the world will face a serious energy crisis. What's happened so far, in our view, hasn't yet reached the stage of a crisis, and we haven't yet brought all our capacity to bear on fully closing the strait. If America wants to make a new move, it will definitely be facing a massive crisis, and it will also confront the world with a new energy crisis.
With the cold season coming up in Europe, and with America itself and many countries needing energy for heating and daily life, the world will face a new crisis, and a global consensus will form against America — a country that creates problems for the whole world by starting fires. Global public opinion is already against America, and if there's any new move, that opposition will only grow, and America will pay a very heavy price. In our view, rationality dictates that they shouldn't do such a thing; but if one day, based on some illusion or delusion of gaining a new achievement, they want to take action, they'll pay a very heavy price. We haven't yet linked up the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab al-Mandab Strait, and the Suez Canal, and we haven't yet used all the capacities of our region — our material and spiritual potential, our popular strength, the capacity of the resistance front, and the other tools that could create a major challenge for America.
So if we look at the story from America's point of view, this scenario seems unlikely, but it's still possible, and it's precisely on the basis of that possibility that we've prepared our scenarios.
That said, when it comes to the Zionist regime, the matter is different. The Zionist regime is, in any case, looking to take advantage of America's companionship and to act even more aggressively. This possibility is worth thinking about from that angle, and this is where the American people need to think. The letter we wrote to the American people has, in part, this very dimension: Are the American people willing, for the sake of following Zionist policies and helping them reach their vile ambitions, to create massive troubles and enormous challenges — like an energy crisis and even a food crisis — for their own country and for the world? I doubt the American people would be willing to accept such a thing, and we pointed to this in that letter as well.
So if I wanted to sum up my words in one sentence, the answer to your question is that the possibility of any operation — even a limited one — is not entirely ruled out, but our assessments show that they simply don't have the capability needed to carry out an effective operation and achieve their goals. Their capability has become so weakened and scattered that they certainly won't get the results they want, and they'll only box themselves into bigger constraints. They might one day take action for the sake of a limited, tactical gain on the eve of the elections, but they'll certainly run into bigger defeats and constraints, global public opinion will mobilize against them, and there are plenty of options available to deter America. The best path and the best proposal for America is to accept Iran's conditions and declare its defeat by accepting those conditions; that would be the best path for the United States.
The enemy is trying to make it seem as though it was Iran that, by attacking several oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, caused the Islamabad MoU to fall apart. They even claimed that a few rogue forces acted without coordination on July 7. Can you tell us what exactly happened that day?
America is doing a forward escape and resorting to sophistry, when in fact the main violator of this agreement was the United States itself. This breach of promise first happened when, right after the meeting where the memorandum of understanding was concluded and sessions were held to implement its provisions, the US Secretary of State took a trip to the region and issued a statement with the leaders of regional countries that was clearly at odds with the provisions of the memorandum. On the other hand, under Article Five of the memorandum, it had been stipulated that the passage of ships would be conducted according to Iranian arrangements, but America, by threatening certain regional countries, opened a new illegal route through the southern part of the strait and along the coast of Oman in order to effectively nullify that article. Not only did they open a new passage, they also forced ships to pass through it and ignored the Iranian arrangements.
This behavior showed that America had once again broken its word — an approach that had precedent. They once carried out the attack of June 13, 2025 during the negotiations, another time they carried out the attack of February 28 in the middle of the negotiation process, and for a third time — not during the talks but after the Islamabad memorandum was concluded and at the stage of implementing it — they violated the agreement. What should the logical response to such a blatant breach of promise be? A logical, powerful, and fitting response. Any fair and reasonable person, if they look at this sequence, will acknowledge that in the face of America's repeated violations, we were compelled to show our decisiveness and strength — something that, praise God, was achieved.
As was seen, during the 17-day clashes, the greatest losses were inflicted on America. In an interview with the Tasnim News Agency, I announced the exact figures for human casualties, destroyed equipment, and demolished bases, because heavy blows were dealt to them as a result of their latest breach of promise. The claim that the actions taken by our forces were rogue is absolutely untrue. In military structures around the world, discipline and adherence to the organizational chain of command is the first principle, and no one can take unilateral action on a sensitive matter like war without coordinating with the higher levels. So our response was carried out with full coordination and as a decisive reaction to America's breach of promise.
The world needs to know that breach of promise is rooted in the very nature of the United States' statecraft, and that this country doesn't adhere to its signatures and commitments. The America that trampled the JCPOA despite the signature of its then-president and five other countries; the America that, during negotiations, assassinated senior commanders, national leaders, and scientists, and massacred thousands of innocent people — has once again proven that violating agreements is part of the fixed procedures of this country's governance. Breach of promise and disrupting agreements have, as it were, become part of the unwritten doctrine of America's ruling establishment.
On this basis, I declare with certainty that our response to the United States' breach of promise — whether in connection to the JCPOA or the recent agreements — was a strong, powerful, fully appropriate, and timely response. If time were to turn back to the 16th of Tir [July 7] we would do exactly the same thing again, and if such actions are repeated by the other side, our response will be even more crushing than before.
Let's talk a bit more about the events of July 7. Some domestic and foreign experts, attempting to corroborate the United States' claim that the attacks that day were rogue, argue that — given Iran's mosaic defense structure, in which commanders of each unit can act without coordinating with higher authorities if necessary — the occurrence of such an incident is not far-fetched. How would you respond to this analysis?
These two matters are completely different from each other. When we talk about a rogue action, we mean an individual acting without orders and without coordinating with higher bodies, and in conflict with standing directives — something that has absolutely no place in the armed forces. But the matter of mosaic defense and delegating authority to commanders in conditions of severed communications or the martyrdom of a senior commander is a defined doctrine and system, not disorder. In this structure, the chain of succession is precisely specified; that is, if the first commander is martyred or organizational communications are cut off through radio, telephone, or communication networks, the next commanders make decisions based on the requirements of the battlefield and a precise assessment of the enemy's situation. This approach is a military measure, and it isn't called rogue action.
Such measures are even rooted in our epistemic and religious foundations; just as in historical military traditions, specific successors were appointed for conditions in which commanders' communications were severed. So a distinction has to be made between the word "rogue action" and "wartime measure." The enemy raising such claims is part of psychological operations aimed at creating a rift between the body of the armed forces and the country's senior officials, or at suggesting a disagreement between the government and military institutions. They've repeatedly raised these rumors to suggest that the decision-making structure in Iran is unclear, but such atmospherics are merely media tricks whose nature is completely clear to experts, and others too have come to understand this reality well over recent months.
You probably meet with field commanders and also visit military headquarters. What's your assessment of the morale of Iranian forces after more than seven months of war?
Honestly, whatever I say about this might seem unbelievable to you, your colleagues, and your listeners, but the reality is that the morale of our combatants — from commanders to operating forces and equipment crews — is at the highest level; to the point that when we go to visit them, we feel weak and ashamed before their will and character. They're present in difficult conditions, despite certain shortages, in hot and humid weather above fifty degrees and in an insecure environment with minimal welfare facilities, with exemplary morale, and they don't utter a single word of complaint or grievance. We, who have ourselves lived through the era of the Sacred Defense [Iran-Iraq war] and have been in this system for years, feel small before the greatness of their morale, and this situation is truly indescribable. We're ready to arrange the preliminaries for a trip so that you and your respected colleagues can go to those areas in person, talk with them, conduct interviews, and tell their stories to the people. Anyone who's gone to these areas has been astonished by their will, their morale, and their interesting and creative initiatives in the areas of defense and offense. Even foreign journalists who are sometimes sent to visit are deeply amazed by this level of sacrifice, patriotism, love for the people, and idealism.
What's your assessment of Iran's missile, drone, and air defense capabilities compared to the beginning of the war?
Our capability has undoubtedly increased greatly, both quantitatively and qualitatively. Just this morning I was in a meeting where they were reporting that our capability has increased at least one and a half times compared to the past; because we never halted our production — never. The enemy, in its foolish imagination, comes and targets some of our centers and facilities and claims, "I destroyed their air force, their navy, and their missile industries," but that's not the case, and the enemy's imagination is foolish. We never stopped producing missiles, drones, and whatever else we needed in this war and will need in the future; not only did we not stop, we expanded it. Today we've brought many other centers into our organization for producing more weapons, creating greater precision in targeting, increasing destructive power, extending the range of weapons, and producing entirely new armaments. We've brought all our capacity to bear, and praise God, we've succeeded very well.
A very important point that I think many people have experienced is that in special conditions, talents emerge. What we've witnessed and experienced firsthand in this war is that in special conditions we achieve things that might be unbelievable even to ourselves, and are certainly unbelievable to others. This is divine grace, and it's due to the sincerity our forces have — those who have come to the field with all their being and selflessly, and have brought their strong will against the enemy. They fight with will, they fight with sincerity, and naturally divine grace helps too. God Almighty says that whoever strives in Our path, We will surely show him the way. God Almighty has shown and continues to show our combatants ways that are unbelievable — ways a person might not have even imagined before. In bottlenecks, in special conditions, in emergency conditions, and in conditions of connection to the infinite divine source, ways, paths, initiatives, and innovations are found that are wonder-making, and if the war continues or escalates again, these wonder-makers will certainly reveal themselves, God willing.
So, given all this, can we conclude that we possess weapons that we have not yet used?
Yes. Naturally, no country reveals all its weapons in the very first stages of battle. To this day, we have also long used weapons that were produced decades ago, and what has been employed during this period has mainly been older reserves and productions. We never use a weapon that should be reserved for more special conditions in less special conditions; naturally, that is how it will be.
Why do some regional countries, even knowing that American bases on their soil will be targeted if used against Iran, still grant the US this permission?
The first and most important point is that these countries have realized that the bases that were supposed to help their security have not helped at all — they have actually endangered their security. That is, what has the existence of a base, for example in Kuwait or Bahrain or any of them, done for that country so far? Nothing! That base has not even been able to defend itself. For example, what benefit has the so-called American naval headquarters and its Fifth Fleet stationed in Bahrain brought to Bahrain so far? No benefit at all — it has actually been to their detriment. They themselves have realized that these bases cannot provide their security, and beyond that, they have understood that America also cannot provide their security; even America cannot provide security for its own forces, and they have come to this truth.
But your question is: now that they have reached this conclusion, why do they not cut off their relations and abandon them? Naturally, they have contracts with them and have given commitments to America — perhaps as reciprocal commitments — and maybe in the back of their minds they still have some hopes regarding America that stop them from acting quickly; but they will do it, and they will do it gradually. What was the first step in this regard? The Mecca Pact. This pact was concluded among three countries — Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan — without foreign interference; this itself shows that they have become disappointed with pacts with foreign countries like America and have seen that they are of no use to them, and so they have turned to a regional pact.
Such regional pacts, and the possible desire of other countries to join them or even to conclude new pacts, stem from the fact that they have concluded that a foreign country thousands of kilometers away cannot provide their security. So, to answer you specifically: they have concluded that they must gradually separate from America and have these bases removed from their countries; but because of their commitments, their not-so-great hopes regarding America, and the limitations they currently have, they cannot do this quickly — but they will gradually bring it about. If the current generation does not do it — which in my view it certainly will — the next generation will one hundred percent accomplish it.
This is a logical, rational, and experienced process. Based on this understanding, new decisions must certainly be made and we must turn to the regional countries themselves. We too, truly, based on the guidelines of the martyred Imam and the esteemed Leader of the Islamic Revolution, have always wanted to be friends, allies, and to have exchanges with these countries. We have many commonalities in this region — generational, religious, cultural, historical commonalities, historical exchanges, and in some cases a shared destiny.
Now, for example, suppose this region becomes insecure for Iran — will security be created for those countries? Never! There will be absolutely no security in this region without Iran's security, and it will not come about. No security pact will take shape in this region without creating security for Iran; this is a logical matter, and empirical processes have proven it.
So we once again declare to the regional countries — we have fifteen neighbors, apart from those somewhat farther away — that these countries must themselves come together, resolve minor differences, and provide their own security. We too are ready to conclude joint pacts with every single country in which American bases are located, and to provide security regionally and locally, and we certainly have this capability.
Recently, the IRGC published a detailed letter addressed to the American people. What was the purpose behind publishing this letter?
In the first place, our goal was to enlighten and inform the American people. We feel that the American people are unaware of many realities; and the reason for this unawareness is that their leaders and ruling establishment lie to them and do not tell them the truth. Their media too are heavily controlled and subservient to the ruling establishment and cannot express other truths contrary to their views. We have numerous examples of this; even in the case of this very letter's publication, many [Western] media outlets boycotted and opposed it, and this shows that they do not allow the facts to reach the ears of the American people. So we wanted through this letter to clarify part of the realities and explain that the American people themselves are also oppressed by their ruling establishment.
That is, the actions America takes, the aggressions it commits against various countries, the massacres it carries out, the numerous bases it has around the world, and the enormous costs it spends to run these bases and forces and equipment — all of it is paid from the pockets of the American people; but the benefit does not reach the American people — rather, it goes into the pockets of the ruling establishment and the main capitalists of America. In other words, the American people today are in the service of American capitalists and Zionist thinking, and we are certain that a large portion of the American people are unaware of this reality.
By the way, what war or enmity do the American people have with the people of Iraq, that a million human beings should be killed over a lie? What enmity do the American people really have with the people of Iran — or conversely, what enmity could the people of Iran possibly have with the American people — that from thousands of kilometers away, they should martyr our leaders, commanders, and scientists, threaten our country with disintegration, plunder our underground resources, threaten to occupy our islands, and target our missile capability? We truly consider it unlikely that these are the wishes of the American people. What real enmity can our two nations have with each other? These actions are in fact carried out by the leaders and ruling establishment of America, and because of their many lies and their concealment of realities from their own people. Our primary goal was in fact to enlighten, inform, and raise awareness among the American people.
You became the successor to General Ali-Mohammad Naeini, who was assassinated by the US and Israel during the 40-day war. Did this cause any doubt for you, or any opposition from your family, regarding accepting this responsibility?
For me personally, such doubt has never existed and doesn't exist; because we've concluded in our school, religion, Quranic teachings, and religious knowledge that we must carry out whatever duty is created for us. When this matter was proposed to me and I felt it was my duty, I didn't hesitate at all and I said to myself: right now this is my duty and I must carry it out. If, on the path of carrying out this duty, God Almighty grants us martyrdom, that's a great triumph; meaning I've lost nothing — rather, I've attained eternal felicity.
So, based on that well-known teaching in our religious knowledge — "one of the two best outcomes" (one of two good things, both of which are good) — if I can carry out my duty well at this juncture, I've attained one of those good things, and blessed be I; and if I'm martyred on this path, I've attained the second good thing, and again blessed be I. That is, in both cases I've lost nothing and in both cases I've gained something; carrying out one's duty well is one felicity, and martyrdom on its path is another felicity, and whichever befalls me is one of those two good things.
Truly, for my family too there was no doubt whatsoever; because my family is far more revolutionary, stronger, and more spirited than I am myself, and in fact, in many of these arenas, they've been our encouragers from the very beginning until now. So martyrdom for me is felicity, and if it befalls me I'll be very happy; and I advise the survivors too to be happy and to take pride.

Russia Caught Shipping Weapons and Suspected Undercover Spies to Africa Aboard Civilian Vessels
Russia has been using civilian cargo ships to transport military equipment and suspected undercover intelligence operatives to Africa, with investigators identifying 28 passengers believed to have traveled under fabricated identities aboard vessels carrying supplies for Russian military operations on the continent.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to a joint investigation published on October 19 by the Dossier Center, Follow the Money, Süddeutsche Zeitung, Danwatch, and Delfi, the suspected operatives traveled aboard seven Russian cargo vessels transporting military equipment primarily intended for Russia’s Africa Corps, a Defense Ministry-controlled formation that replaced the Wagner mercenary group.
Journalists identified 28 passengers whose names, dates of birth, and identity document numbers could not be found in publicly available records or leaked databases. A source within European intelligence services suggested that the individuals were likely Russian intelligence personnel operating under cover identities.
The investigation found that the passengers used Russian passports without biometric chips. Several documents differed only in their final digits, while two carried consecutive numbers, suggesting they may have been issued together as part of a coordinated operation.
Former Danish intelligence officer Stig Wæver assessed that the documents displayed characteristics associated with passports used in intelligence operations. Analysts at US-based security research organization C4ADS also concluded that the passengers’ personal information appeared to have been fabricated.
One of the shipments involved the Russian cargo vessel Sabetta, which arrived at the port of Conakry, Guinea, on March 19. The ship reportedly delivered approximately 50 military and support vehicles, including armored vehicles and fuel tankers.
The equipment was subsequently transported overland to Mali, where Russia’s Africa Corps maintains a military presence. Four passengers aboard Sabetta had identity details that investigators could not verify through other available records.
The vessel is owned by Severny Proekt, a Russian company involved in state defense contracts and special projects for the state nuclear corporation Rosatom.
The investigation also identified three roll-on/roll-off vessels—Adler, Ascalon, and Baltic Leader—operated by MG-Flot, a Russian shipping company sanctioned by the United States and European Union over activities linked to Iran and supplies supporting Russian drone production.
Three additional cargo ships—Mikhail Britnev, Mys Zhelaniya, and Siyanie Severa—were also identified as part of the maritime network. Siyanie Severa had previously transported grain from temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories.
According to the investigation, the vessels frequently switched off their Automatic Identification System (AIS) transponders during voyages to Africa, making their movements more difficult to track.
A source within a European intelligence agency suggested that Russia may have deployed personnel from the Federal Security Service (FSB) or military intelligence agency (GRU) to accompany the shipments because of the sensitive military cargo.
Michelle Bockmann, a senior analyst at maritime intelligence company Windward, suggested that the suspected intelligence operatives could have been tasked with monitoring crews and preventing vessels from complying with potential orders to stop issued by European authorities.
Russia’s expanding military presence in Africa has also drawn Ukrainian involvement. According to CNN on September 12, approximately 15 Ukrainian drone specialists have been operating in Mali, providing training and operational support to local forces fighting Russia’s Africa Corps.
Ukrainian personnel have also reportedly conducted drone operations in Sudan and Libya, targeting Russian-linked military and maritime activities.

articles.title: Dozens killed in Houthi attack on Yemeni gov't military camp
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Dozens killed in Houthi missile attack on Yemeni government military camp
More than 30 soldiers for the internationally recognised Yemeni government were reportedly killed and dozens wounded on Monday after Houthi forces launched a ballistic missile attack on a military camp in Yemen's southern Shabwa province, according to military and medical sources.
The attack targeted Al-Alam military camp near the city of Ataq while soldiers were taking part in a training course.
Yemeni armed forces spokesperson Majed al-Nuzaili said the Houthis had fired three ballistic missiles at the camp.
The Houthis, officially known as Ansar Allah, have not yet commented on the attack.
The camp belongs to Shabwa's emergency forces and was hosting recruits from a newly formed military brigade at the time of the strike.
A source at a government hospital told The New Arab that the number of casualties was high, while other sources reported that Houthi drones had been flying over the area on Sunday evening, hours before the attack.
A Yemeni military source told Germany's DPA news agency that more than 30 soldiers had been killed and dozens of others wounded.
Social media users also circulated footage purportedly showing dead and wounded soldiers scattered across the military camp following the strikes. The New Arab could not independently verify the footage.
The attack comes amid an escalation in Yemen's conflict, with fighting continuing between government forces and the Houthis on several fronts, accompanied by increasingly hostile rhetoric and threats from the warring sides.
Fighting intensifies in Taiz
On Sunday evening, warplanes belonging to the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognised government carried out airstrikes on Houthi positions in the Dhi al-Birah and Najd Qasim areas of Al-Misrakh district, south of Taiz province.
Two additional strikes targeted Al-Wazi'iyah district in western Taiz.
The airstrikes coincided with an escalation in fighting around Jabal Sabir, where government forces and local resistance fighters have been attempting to repel Houthi attacks and infiltration attempts.
Sources told The New Arab that local resistance fighters from the village of Al-Rahn were engaged in fierce clashes with Houthi groups attempting to advance from the villages of Khurayshah and Al-Ma'yanah towards Al-Najjadah and neighbouring communities.
The sources said the Houthis were seeking to reach the summit of Jabal al-Arus and cut off a road connecting several villages and districts across the Sabir mountain area.
The clashes coincided with heavy Houthi attacks on the Al-Sina'a position on the opposite side of the front, following the group's reported loss of several positions in Al-Sanamat, Al-Sarari and Ambiyan.
Elsewhere in Taiz, an 11-year-old Yemeni girl was wounded by shrapnel to the head on Sunday evening after Houthi shelling struck the village of Al-Shaqab in Sabir al-Mawadim district, south of the province.
The latest violence comes as Yemen's long-running war continues to intensify, with renewed clashes and missile attacks threatening to deepen the country's humanitarian and security crisis.

articles.title: The Russian shipyards Britain has placed under sanctions
articles.body:
Britain has designated Russia’s largest shipbuilding corporation on the grounds that it supplied frigates and other warship classes deployed in Crimea, and the sanctions list now names 645 individual ships under the Russia regulations, according to the UK Sanctions List published by the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office.
Public Joint Stock Company United Shipbuilding Corporation was designated on 24 February 2022, the day Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The statement of reasons sets out the naval case against it.
It reads: “Public Joint Stock Company (PJSC) United Shipbuilding Corporation (USC) is a Russian state-owned enterprise. USC is the largest shipbuilding corporation in Russia, uniting shipbuilding, repair and maintenance subsidiaries. This includes the supply of several frigates and other warship classes that have been deployed in Crimea since Russia illegally annexed the region in 2014, and have conducted drills in the Black Sea in 2021. Therefore USC has been involved in destabilising Ukraine or undermining or threatening the territorial integrity, sovereignty or independence of Ukraine. USC also operates in a sector of strategic significance, specifically, the Russian defence sector.”
USC carries an asset freeze, trust services sanctions and the director disqualification sanction imposed in April 2025. It is the holding company that owns most of Russia’s major yards, including Sevmash at Severodvinsk where the ballistic missile and cruise missile submarines are built, the Admiralty Shipyards and Severnaya Verf in St Petersburg, and Yantar at Kaliningrad.
Two individual yards carry designations of their own, the first of them JSC Zelenodolsk Shipyard in Tatarstan, designated on 15 March 2022, with the department recording that it “is a Russian shipbuilding enterprise that has constructed more than 1500 sea- and river-going ships and vessels” and that it therefore carries on business in sectors of strategic significance to the Russian government. The yard builds the Buyan-M class corvettes that have fired Kalibr cruise missiles into Ukraine, and the Gepard class frigates.
JSC Zaliv Shipyard at Kerch in occupied Crimea was designated earlier, on 31 December 2020, and for a different reason. The statement of reasons says it “actively participated in the construction of new railway approaches to the Kerch Bridge, connecting Russian to the illegally annexed Crimean peninsula. Therefore, it is supporting the consolidation of the illegally annexed Crimean peninsula into the Russian Federation.” The yard has since taken on the two Ivan Rogov class amphibious assault ships, the largest warships Russia has laid down in decades.
The list reaches down into the supply chain that serves those yards. Forss Technology Ltd of St Petersburg was designated on 4 May 2022 as a company “providing engineering services in shipbuilding, machine building, electrical technology, instruments manufacturing and high-tech products development”. Kranark LLC went the same day, on the grounds that it “has provided equipment for the construction of the Zvezda shipbuilding complex, a strategically important project for the Government of Russia”, the Far Eastern yard built to produce ice-class tankers and gas carriers for the Arctic routes.
On the commercial side, Sovcomflot, the Russian state shipping company, was designated on 18 May 2023. The 645 named vessels sit alongside it under shipping and transport sanctions, which bar a specified ship from entering a British port, allow it to be detained or given a movement direction, and permit its registration on the UK Ship Register to be terminated. Most of those listings carry the same wording, that the vessel “is involved in carrying oil or oil products that originated in Russia from Russia to a third country”.
Naval officers appear alongside the companies and the hulls, among them Rear Admiral Denis Berezovskiy, designated on 31 December 2020, who was appointed commander of the Ukrainian Navy on 1 March 2014 and swore an oath to the Crimean armed forces, breaking his oath to the Ukrainian Navy, before becoming Deputy Commander of Russia’s Black Sea Fleet and later of the Pacific Fleet. Rear Admiral Valery Kulikov, a former Deputy Commander of the Black Sea Fleet, is listed as responsible for commanding forces that occupied Ukrainian sovereign territory.

articles.title: Zelensky: US Supplies Ukraine With Just 12 Patriot Missiles a Month
articles.body:
The US supplies Ukraine with only 12 interceptor missiles for Patriot air defense systems per month – approximately four times fewer than under President Joe Biden’s administration.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said this in an interview with Bloomberg.
Meanwhile, Washington is delaying approval for the transfer of some supplies that Ukraine has already paid for.
According to Zelensky, Ukraine has already paid for weapons, including missiles designed to intercept ballistic targets under the PURL programme. However, the US has approved only part of the deliveries.
“We paid for the weapons. The US side approved some of the deliveries, but not the rest. And this is not a technical issue,” the president said.
Separately, Zelensky also proposed a deal to Washington. Ukraine would halt strikes on Russian facilities linked to diesel fuel production in exchange for supplies of Patriot missiles to protect Ukrainian cities and infrastructure fromRussian ballistic missiles.
However, despite these delays, Ukraine was given the opportunity in September to allocate approximately €3.2 billion to purchase Patriot interceptor missiles under the €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan programme for 2026–2027.
Overall, the European Commission has approved the use of €6.1 billion to purchase air defense missiles, including US-made PAC-3 interceptors, as well as drones.
Ukraine is also contracting for the supply of around 1,000 Patriot missiles using funds from a European loan, according toUkrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara.
However, most of these missiles are expected to be delivered over the coming years.
Separately, in June, Germany announced $400 million in funding to purchase interceptor missiles for Patriot systems,primarily PAC-3 missiles.
Half of the amount will be allocated through the PURL programme, which finances purchases of US weapons forUkraine, while the other half will be provided through the JUMPSTART mechanism.
In September, the United Kingdom allocated £100 million for an air defense package that included Patriot missiles, artillery ammunition, and drones.

Egypt's top security body agrees to help Saudi Arabia defend itself against Houthi attacks
Egypt's top security body said Sunday it has agreed to support close ally Saudi Arabia in the major escalation of fighting between the kingdom and Houthi rebels in Yemen, which has marked the latest front in the Iran war.
Saudi Arabia has been pressing allies for military assistance. The Houthis have repeatedly attacked airports and oil infrastructure across the kingdom with drones and missiles that can change direction during flight, posing a challenge to interceptors. At least 19 people have been killed, thousands of flights have been affected and global markets have been rattled.
Also on Sunday, the Saudi defense minister was meeting with the United Arab Emirates president about ways to strengthen cooperation, according to the UAE’s news agency WAM. The countries have had tense relations in the recent past as they backed different factions in the Yemeni coalition fighting the rebels.
The Egyptian announcement on military assistance came a month after a visit by the Saudi crown prince. Chaired by President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi, the National Defense Council decided to provide “all possible forms of support” to enable Saudi Arabia to defend its security, according to a presidential statement.
It didn’t provide details. El-Sissi on Saturday called for parliament to grant him the authorization to deploy troops and military equipment abroad.
The surge in fighting has threatened civilians in both Saudi Arabia and Yemen, which has seen a return to civil war. The interim capital of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, Aden, has seen its airport and a palace used by the government attacked in the past week.
On Sunday, an airstrike killed at least nine people, including five children and two women, in Yemen’s rebel-held northern province of Saada, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said.
Spokesperson Anees al-Asbahi said the strike hit a house in Sahar district and wounded 19 others, including 11 children. Some were in critical condition, he said.
Al-Asbahi blamed Saudi Arabia. There was no immediate comment from the kingdom. The Houthi-run al-Masirah satellite channel aired footage of people clearing debris with their hands and pulling two young people out of the rubble.
The rebels said attacks by Saudi-led forces had killed or wounded over 30 people in the past 24 hours. Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the Houthis' military spokesperson, said 110 missiles or airstrikes were carried out against civilian sites in Sanaa and other cities. The Associated Press could not independently verify the claim.
Across the border in Saudi Arabia, a Saudi helicopter gunship crashed near the city of Najran in the southwest, killing its two-member crew, a Saudi military spokesperson said, citing a technical malfunction. The Houthis earlier claimed to have downed it.
Later, Saudi Civil Defense authorities said a projectile fired by the Houthis landed in a residential area of Najran province, wounding six people.
The Houthis have resumed attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent weeks because the kingdom has supported Yemen’s internationally recognized government in the civil war. The rebels recently seized more territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
The Houthis’ chief negotiator on Sunday blamed Saudi Arabia for the escalation. Mohamed Abdulsalam said on social media that the rebels had warned the kingdom against striking the rebel-held Sanaa airport in mid-July.
That strike prevented the landing of an Iranian flight carrying a Houthi delegation returning from the funeral of Iran’s supreme leader, who had been killed in the opening strikes of the war in February.
The Houthis, angry over the longstanding Saudi blockade on them, declared their own blockade on the kingdom.
Oman had offered a five-day truce during which the two sides would meet and settle their dispute, Abdulsalam said. He said the Houthis agreed to stop attacks if Saudi Arabia agreed to “humanitarian demands.” He didn’t elaborate.
He said Saudi Arabia didn’t show “any indication that it is ready to deal positively” with the demands. The rebels shortly after that launched their offensive down the Red Sea coast.
A Saudi diplomat last week in a rare briefing said the kingdom had called for a meeting in Oman with the Houthis in July “to resolve outstanding differences and bring an end to this escalation,” but the rebels refused to participate.
On Sunday, the Sunni Muslim world’s foremost religious institution, Al-Azhar in Egypt, called for the formation of an “urgent mediation committee” to end conflicts across the Arab region.

articles.title: Strait of Hormuz scoured for spilt cargo after Iran attacks container ships
articles.body:
People have been scouring the strait of Hormuz for spilt cargo after Iran attacked at least 15 container ships traversing the crucial waterway in the past 10 days.
Some ships have been hit by drones, others by mines. On Sunday, a ship was struck by a rocket-propelled grenade launched from a small boat 120km (75 miles) north-east of the Saudi port of Jubail.
The rise in Iranian attacks appears to have helped resolidify Tehran’s disputed control over the strait, as well as pushing up the price of a barrel of Brent crude oil close to $108 a barrel on Monday morning.
Last Wednesday a ship travelling from Karachi to Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates sunk after hitting a mine, according to Iranian state TV. All 21 crew members were evacuated and no injuries were reported. Dozens of its 2,500 containers were seen floating in the water. Rumours that iPhones and other expensive goods were among its cargo – fuelled by fake AI-generated photos published on social media – prompted fishers and others to investigate.
One fisher told an Iranian reporter: “The Arab boatmen, who were closer to the ship, arrived earlier than the Iranians. They used stonecutters to cut the container and took whatever was there.”
Col Javad Mokhtar Rezaei, the deputy head of cultural and social affairs for Iran’s cyber police (Fata), told the Tasnim news agency: “In some cases, the phones offered may actually exist, but exposing electronic components to saltwater and extreme humidity can cause corrosion of internal components, damage to the boards, battery and display, and cause hidden malfunctions in the device’s performance.”
Meysam Doost-Mohammadi, a spokesperson for the Iranian mobile association, said it would be unusual for valuable phones to be transported by ship.
The bulk of the recent spate of attacks have occurred close to the coast with Oman, a route that Iran regards as unauthorised. In the seven days to Friday 16 October, 12 vessels were attacked, according to the UK Maritime Agency (UKMTO).
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it has the right to attack any ship that seeks to traverse the strait without its permission or with its transponders off. The officials have also ordered local fishers not to pillage the sea for luxury items, saying the goods are the property of the state.
Two oil tankers were hit on Saturday, including a supertanker carrying 2m barrels of oil, according to the IRGC. The Fars news agency also published a video that appears to show the tanker burning, but which cannot be independently verified. A third tanker was hit late Sunday.
It is disputed how many ships have been hit by mines or IRGC shelling. UKMTO’s weekly overview recorded 254 transits of the strait (125 outbound, 129 inbound) in the week to 14 October, approximately 70% below pre-conflict levels.
Dr Devaraj Asir Ramesh of Anna University in Chennai, India, warned that the region’s marine habitats faced threats from toxic debris and oil spills, while noise might have disturbed marine life. Iranian strikes on the Emirates, he said, were likely to have contaminated seagrass beds with hydrocarbons and caused auditory damage to cetaceans – marine mammals such as dolphins and porpoises – which are sensitive to loud noise that travels through the sea.
Ramesh also said oil released by attacks on tankers at Fujairah could have caused ecological harm. “Oil spills, chemical leaks and acoustic disturbances have impaired biodiversity, fisheries, aquaculture, desalination, and eco-tourism,” he wrote in the International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Sciences.
On Friday the Iranian president said the conflicts in Gaza and the wider Middle East had inflicted a significant toll on nature that extended beyond borders and required “international solutions”.
“What has occurred in our region as a result of wars of aggression is ecocide, or environmental genocide, and it must be condemned,” Masoud Pezeshkian said. He argued that countries subjected to economic sanctions or military aggression should not be forced to shoulder the financial burden of environmental damage resulting from conflicts they did not initiate.
Successive studies, mainly by US universities using satellite imagery, have warned of the dangers facing the strait.
The renewed concern over the environmental impact of the war in the strait came as the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, visited Tehran offering to act as an intermediary between Iran and Donald Trump, especially over the issue of Iran’s nuclear stockpile, an issue that the US president insists must be addressed before he lifts his threat to attack Iran again.
Iran has offered to open the strait in six days in return for sanctions relief.
Russia has offered to take Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium, but Iran is reluctant to make a commitment on its nuclear programme and has not given the International Atomic Energy Agency access to its bombed nuclear sites since June 2025. Lavrov also proposed a trilateral summit between China, Russia and Iran to agree new security architecture for the strait. He said the region was on the verge of a full-scale crisis.
Tehran is braced for another attack soon, especially after the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, launched a new national security doctrine on Sunday that included a new emphasis on prevention and offence, including pre-emptive strikes on potential threats.

articles.title: Israel to Supply PULS Systems and EXTRA-MR Missiles to Unnamed European Country
articles.body:
Israeli company Elbit Systems has signed a contract worth approximately $235 million to supply EXTRA-MR missiles and PULS multiple launch rocket systems to a European country.
The developer’s press service reported the deal.
The contract is scheduled to be completed over three years.
Under the agreement, Elbit Systems will supply EXTRA-MR medium-range missiles, PULS launchers, associated artillery platforms, and a logistics support package.
EXTRA-MR is a precision-guided missile designed to effectively engage high-value targets at ranges of up to 80 km. It is fully integrated with PULS launchers and existing C4I systems.
The development of the PULS (Precise & Universal Launching System) began with the Lynx rocket artillery system, developed by Israel Military Industries, which was later acquired by Elbit Systems. Israeli engineers sought to create a universal, modular platform that could launch a wide range of munitions without extensive technical modifications.
The system’s key conceptual feature is its use of a container-based design. PULS is equipped with two standardized transport-launch containers, each loaded with a specific missile type based on mission requirements, ranging from unguided rockets to precision-guided ballistic and cruise missiles.
The artillery system can employ AccuLAR-122 rockets (18 rockets per launch pod, with a range of up to 35 km), AccuLAR-160 rockets (10 rockets, with a range of up to 40 km), EXTRA missiles (4 missiles, with a range of up to 150 km), as well as Predator Hawk ballistic missiles (2 missiles, with a range of up to 300 km).
The EXTRA (Extended Range Artillery) missile has a 306 mm caliber, a length of about 4.7 meters, and a total weight of nearly 450 kg. It carries either a high-explosive fragmentation warhead or a penetrating warhead weighing up to 120 kg.
The high accuracy of the EXTRA and EXTRA-MR missiles is achieved through a combined guidance system that integrates GPS satellite navigation with an inertial navigation system, providing a circular error probable of less than 10 meters at maximum firing range.
The PULS launcher can be mounted on a variety of wheeled chassis with a payload capacity of 10 tonnes or more, including those manufactured by Tatra, MAN, and Scania. The system can transition from march configuration to combat-ready position in less than three minutes.
PULS’s versatility and advanced technical capabilities have made it highly sought after on the international market. In addition to the Israel Defense Forces, where it is in service under the designation Lahav, the system and its variants have been selected by the Netherlands, Denmark, Germany (MARS 3), and several other NATO and Middle Eastern countries.

articles.title: Ukraine turns its Bars strike drone into a Shahed hunter
articles.body:
- Video shows a ground-launched interceptor version of Ukraine’s Bars jet drone destroying a Russian Geran-5 jet-powered attack drone.
- Russia launched 3,177 jet-powered drones at Ukraine in September, and Ukraine has fielded several new interceptors against them.
Video published online shows Ukraine using an interceptor version of its Bars jet-powered drone to destroy a Russian Geran-5, the first footage of the Ukrainian missile-drone being used against Russia’s own jet-powered attack drones.
The clip, shared by the Ukrainian military, shows the interceptor launched from a ground launcher before it strikes the Geran-5.
The interceptor is based on the Bars strike drone, a small turbojet-powered weapon that Ukraine has used for long-range attacks on Russian targets, including oil refineries. Upgraded strike versions of Bars can reportedly fly at up to 700 km/h (435 mph) and travel up to 1,000 km (620 miles), carrying warheads of 22, 60 or 105 kg (49, 132 or 231 pounds).
The Geran-5 is a Russian jet-powered strike drone that looks and flies more like a small cruise missile than the propeller-driven Shahed-type drones Russia launches in large numbers. It can fly at up to about 600 km/h (370 mph), and at higher altitudes than older models, which makes it hard to catch for the small quadcopter interceptors Ukraine relies on against slower Shaheds.
Russia launched 3,177 jet-powered drones at Ukraine in September alone, and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that month that Ukrainian forces were shooting down only 57% of them.
Ukrainian manufacturers have rushed several faster interceptors into service in response. Wild Hornets’ Sting S, SkyFall’s P1-SUN JetKiller and a jet-powered interceptor supplied by the Serhiy Prytula Charity Foundation have all been shown destroying Geran-5s since late September, and former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said on Oct. 12 that a new interceptor developed by his team had downed two Geran-5s heading toward Kyiv.
Many of those interceptors were hit by a speed cap that SpaceX placed on Starshield satellite terminals used by Ukrainian forces overnight on Oct. 13-14, which cut connections on drones moving faster than about 160 km/h. A larger, faster jet interceptor such as Bars, launched from the ground against fast targets, could give Ukraine another option for reaching Geran-5s before they reach cities.
In July 2026, Germany and Ukraine signed an agreement on joint production of Bars drones.

articles.title: Lavrov’s pivotal Monday visit to Tehran with a mediation flavor
articles.body:
Lavrov’s pivotal Monday visit to Tehran with a mediation flavor
Arman-e-Emrooz analyzed Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov’s upcoming visit to Tehran on Monday. Reports suggest that the trip is part of Russia’s ongoing mediation efforts between Iran and the United States. In recent months, Moscow has sought to position itself as a facilitator in reducing tensions between Tehran and Washington.
The timing of the visit coincides with US review of sanctions and measures related to the so-called shadow fleet, highlighting the complexity of the current situation. On one hand, the United States faces domestic pressure to lower energy prices ahead of elections. On the other, Iran is seeking meaningful economic relief. These circumstances have created an environment in which both sides may be inclined toward tactical flexibility. The meeting between Lavrov and Araghchi could represent an important step in that direction, provided both parties enter discussions with a shared understanding of existing realities and align their expectations with practical possibilities. The outcome of the visit could influence developments in the coming weeks.
Khorasan: Trump, the mother of all lies
Khorasan addressed Trump’s recent claim about using the “Mother of All Bombs” in a future strike against Iran. Trump is making such threats at a time when the economic consequences of tensions in the region have significantly increased costs related to energy and essential goods for American families and other countries, putting additional pressure on his administration. The paper described Trump as a gambler seeking a face-saving exit from the Iran war quagmire. After previous efforts, including military deployments to the region and severe economic pressure campaigns that were expected to quickly force Iran into submission, failed to achieve their goals, Trump has now turned to the rhetoric of the “Mother of All Bombs.” The article contends that the purpose of such statements is to create psychological pressure inside Iran and gain leverage in ongoing exchanges of messages between the two sides.
Shargh: An open-ended American policy or an open-ended Iranian one?
Shargh devoted its editorial to decision-making regarding the current conflict. The newspaper argued that decisions made today are linked not only to the future of 90 million Iranians but, in some respects, to global developments as well. The editorial proposed moving beyond the simple pro-war versus pro-peace divide and distinguishing among three separate positions: first, ending the war at any cost; second, negotiating an end to the conflict while preserving core national red lines; and third, continuing resistance until specific political and security conditions are achieved. This conceptual distinction is important for policymaking. A person who favors negotiations does not necessarily support surrender or territorial fragmentation, just as someone who considers resistance necessary is not necessarily indifferent to its human and economic costs. The paper argues that recognizing this distinction prevents an “open-ended American policy” from automatically being interpreted as an “open-ended Iranian policy,” which it describes as the key issue.
Ettelaat: Possibility of a longer conflict process
Ettelaat examined possible future scenarios for the conflict. US demands have shifted from redefining Iran’s regional role to focusing on the nuclear issue and the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, Iran’s demands have reportedly evolved from direct compensation by Washington to a conditional investment fund financed by other parties. Nevertheless, the newspaper argued that two major ambiguities remain unresolved and may even have deepened as a result of the conflict. Continued American pressure is said to intensify divisions among Iranian elites and increase their reluctance to take the first step. Washington, however, may interpret this hesitation as evidence that pressure is working and therefore warrants further action. According to the analysis, diplomacy has reached a deadlock. As US midterm elections draw closer, there remains a possibility that the conflict will add another chapter to the historical memories each side holds of the other, extending a process that has already lasted for more than four decades.
Hamshahri: The impact of war and economic tensions on US elections
Hamshahri focused on concerns influencing American voters. The newspaper argued that economic conditions and the conflict involving Iran have become major public concerns. Rising prices for gasoline, diesel fuel, and essential goods, along with inflation and growing concerns about living costs, have increased pressure on the Trump administration. The paper noted that these concerns are reflected in public opinion polls and political analyses. At the same time, the Iran conflict remains among voters’ principal worries. Hamshahri also linked these concerns to allegations regarding corruption and the financial interests of individuals close to Trump in connection with the conflict. As a result, the newspaper concluded that the economic pressures associated with the conflict cannot be ignored in assessing the US political climate. According to its analysis, these pressures have fueled public dissatisfaction and could present a significant challenge for Republicans in upcoming elections.

articles.title: US reacts to Kyiv's claim it received no advance notice of Russian ballistic missile launches
articles.body:
US reacts to Kyiv's claim it received no advance notice of Russian ballistic missile launches
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he could not confirm reports that Ukraine received no advance warning before Russia's ballistic missile attack on Kyiv on Oct. 19, citing a lack of information, as he spoke to reporters during a visit to Samarkand, Uzbekistan.
Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty journalist Alex Raufoglu asked Rubio during a press briefing to comment on Kyiv's statements that it had received no advance warning of Russian missile launches.
"I don't know. I mean, where did it happen last night? I don't know exactly," Rubio told reporters on Oct. 19.
In the Oct. 19 attack on Kyiv, at least one person was killed, and eight others were injured as Russian missiles struck Kyiv in multiple waves overnight. Explosions were reported shortly before 11 p.m., followed by further attacks around 3 a.m. and 7 a.m. local time.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on X on Oct. 19 that Ukraine had not received early warning from its partner countries, including the U.S., ahead of the attack. He added that Russia launched 16 ballistic missiles, with Kyiv and the surrounding region as the primary targets.
Later in the day, Ukraine's Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said on national television that Ukraine received no advance warning from its partners before the first wave of ballistic missile attacks at around 11 p.m., but that information about the second wave, at around 3 a.m., was provided.
He added that a similar situation had occurred during previous attacks, including the one overnight on Oct. 14.
Alerts did sound before the overnight strikes overnight on Oct. 19, though the warnings were unusually short. The first explosions were simultaneous with the blaring of air raid sirens, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground.
The U.S. provides Ukraine with intelligence to help its military detect and track Russian missile launches and other aerial threats.
Rubio said on Oct. 19 that "a few nights ago" there was a software problem involving the Ukrainian early warning system.
"I know that EUCOM (U.S. European Command) had been involved in looking at, and that's the report they gave us back. I can't comment on what happened last night," he said.
A senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent that the first overnight wave followed a similar pattern.
"The 'warning' about a ballistic threat came through only after the strike had already happened," the official said. "They're up to something again."
It can be common for Russia's high-speed ballistic missiles to hit with very little advance warning.
The attack came just hours after Zelensky said the U.S. had resumed intelligence sharing with Ukraine about Russian missile launches.
The president's announcement came as a relief after Kyiv endured "massive explosions" on Oct. 12, when five Russian S-400 missiles struck the Ukrainian capital. Air raid sirens and mobile alerts sounded only after the attack.
The Oct. 12 attack came after the U.S. threatened to withhold intelligence from Ukraine unless Kyiv stopped attacking Russian refineries, sources told the Kyiv Independent.
Ukrainian officials have previously explained that satellite surveillance of launch sites can be vulnerable to transmission delays. Bad weather may also cause interference with the Space-Based Infrared System (SBIRS) satellites, a surveillance network U.S. forces use to monitor Russian launch sites.
But the senior official who spoke to the Kyiv Independent said although bad weather had affected warnings before, this number of strikes with little to no warning "has never happened before."
"Now we're seeing 'bad weather' three times in a row," the official said. "When nothing comes through on any channel... well, we get it."

articles.title: Kremlin hawks savour Trump-Zelenskiy rift — if it lasts
articles.body:
Kremlin hawks savour Trump-Zelenskiy rift — if it lasts
MOSCOW, Oct 19 - Kremlin hawks are savouring a public rift between Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskiy after a damaging week for Ukraine's president and a beneficial one for Russia, but the champagne is still on ice in Moscow.
While welcoming strains in Kyiv's relationship with its most important ally, Moscow regards the US president's behaviour as unpredictable and European leaders rallied behind Zelenskiy at a summit last week.
There has also been no end to Ukrainian drone attacks on Russia, most US sanctions remain in place on Moscow over Ukraine and Trump's actions can be seen in the light of November's midterm elections to Congress.
On the surface, there was plenty for Russian hawks to revel in after Trump repeatedly criticised the Ukrainian leader, who hit back at him, prompting the US president to say "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president".
"The ‘Man of the Year’ and the ‘new Churchill’ has been branded by his former master as a hindrance to peace and to US interests. After all, he bit the hand that fed him until it bled," former President Dmitry Medvedev, now deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, wrote sarcastically on Telegram.
Kirill Dmitriev, President Vladimir Putin's point man for economic deals with Washington, reposted an image showing a bear symbolising Russia alongside an eagle representing the US and both creatures confronting Britain — in the form of a lion — and the European Union.
The image was captioned "Things Have Changed."
Dmitriev said he believed Zelenskiy's decision to criticise Trump had backfired, adding on X: "Zelensky overplayed his hand, and his hubris and attacks on President Trump will have significant consequences."
SCEPTICISM
Trump said on October 9 he had reached a deal with Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian fuel and import Russian diesel and last week skipped new sanctions on Russia's oil buyers. In Kyiv, Ukrainian complaints about disruption to US intelligence sharing prompted talk of US betrayal.
But there appears to be a consensus in Moscow that the Trump-Zelenskiy rift has not yet delivered significant benefits.
Sergei Mironov, parliamentary leader of the pro-Kremlin Just Russia party, saw the rift as an attempt to "play to a domestic audience ahead of the Congressional elections."
"The US President needs cheap fuel prices for his voters. He also needs a scapegoat – someone onto whom he can shift the blame for price rises," he said. "But the point is that all this has little to do with Russia’s interests.”
Some Russians are also wary of what they see as frequent U-turns by Trump.
Moscow initially saw Trump's hosting of Putin in Alaska last year as a breakthrough that might lead to a peace deal in Ukraine on Russia's terms. But, like Trump's first term in office, the summit is increasingly seen as a disappointment.
The impact of the diesel deal may also be limited, as the export volumes — at least initially — are relatively small and Moscow taxes fuel production rather than exports, limiting the uplift for Russia's budget.
Trump’s decision to skip sanctions on Russian oil buyers — primarily China and India — is also not seen in Russia as a great gift, or as surprising, as such a move would increase oil prices at the very moment he wants to lower them.
A more tangible benefit to Russia may be Kyiv's complaints that it has not received recent warnings of Russian missile strikes and that there have been limits on the US Starshield system, which Ukraine uses for battlefield communications.
Writing for state media outlet RT, commentator Sergey Poletaev said Russia must be patient.
"For Russia, the task is to recognise this developing reality without mistaking it for an immediate victory," he said. "Zelenskiy has made his choice, the only question left is how long Washington will tolerate the consequences." REUTERS

articles.title: Most Ukrainians reject giving Russia all of Donbas. Support for resistance on rose to 62% after new US pressure, poll finds
articles.body:
A majority of Ukrainians reject handing all of Donbas to Russia in exchange for US and European security guarantees. Some 62% are ready to endure the war for as long as it takes, a survey by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology shows.
Russia has spent the fall hammering Ukrainian cities, and Washington has eased sanctions on Russian diesel and cut Ukraine’s intelligence and Starlink speed, both apparently aimed at wearing Ukrainians down toward a capitulation. Instead, the majority calls the withdrawal of troops from Donbas categorically unacceptable, with 35% willing to accept it and 4% undecided, a position essentially unchanged since late summer.
The pressure campaign tracked the other way. Among those polled on 8-9 October, before the diesel deal and the pressure that followed, 57% were categorically opposed. Among those polled on 10-16 October, the figure rose to 62% afterward, KIIS reports.
In every region, at least half reject the trade. Resistance is firmest in Kyiv, which has borne a relentless campaign of ballistic and jet-drone strikes, where 66% are categorically against, the highest figure of any region. Even in the east, around Kharkiv, where the most are open to a compromise at 45%, 51% still rule it out.
Bracing for a long war, and ready for it
Few Ukrainians expect a quick end. Only 10% think the war will end by the close of 2026 and 13% in the first half of 2027, while 56% expect it to run into the second half of 2027 or beyond, the institute reports.
Who Ukrainians blame for blocking peace
The poll also measured who is seen as the obstacle. Asked to choose, 78% said Russia’s drive to subjugate Ukraine is what blocks peace, against 12% who blamed an inflexible Ukrainian government, and 92% said Russia strikes economic sites to wreck the economy and force capitulation, not in retaliation.
“The enemy, with its vile strikes by ballistic missiles and drones, is unable to break the spirit and will of Ukrainians,” KIIS executive director Anton Hrushetskyi says.
He argues that what Ukraine needs is “packages of interceptors for Patriot systems,” not an election or one-sided concessions dressed up as peace. The survey polled 1,031 adults across government-controlled Ukraine from 8-16 October.
