articles.title: Japan, US launch major military drills with new long-range missiles
articles.body:
Faisal Mahmud
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
Japan and the US launched a major joint military exercise Monday involving approximately 56,000 personnel, with Japan's new long-range anti-ship missiles participating for the first time.
The 11-day Keen Sword 2027 exercise began with an opening ceremony on Japan's Ishigaki Island and will run through Oct. 29, according to a statement published by DVIDS, an official US military media and information distribution platform.
Around 45,000 Japanese Self-Defense Forces personnel and 11,000 US troops are taking part, alongside forces from Australia, Canada, France, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand, and the Philippines.
South Korea and the UK have sent observers.
The biennial exercise, now in its 18th iteration, includes air and missile defense, facility protection, logistics, casualty evacuation, and maritime operations.
“Today, it is a great privilege and significance to commence Keen Sword 27 in Ishigaki, Japan's western-most point,” said Adm. Tawara Tateki, commander of Japan's Joint Operations Command.
Japanese daily Yomiuri Shimbun reported that Japan's Type 25 surface-to-ship guided missile is participating for the first time.
The missile, with a reported range of around 1,000 kilometers (621 miles), will be used in simulated operations without live firing.
US Marines are also deploying NMESIS anti-ship missile systems and MADIS air defense equipment on Japan's southwestern islands near Taiwan.
The exercise comes amid tensions between China and Japan over Taiwan, as well as China's expanding military and economic influence in the wider Asia-Pacific region.
Japan, South Korea, and the Philippines are military allies of the US in the region, with Tokyo and Seoul hosting some 50,000 and 39,000 American troops, respectively, while Manila has granted the Pentagon access to its military bases.

articles.title: Trump Endorses Netanyahu Days Before Israeli Election as Iran War Tests Friendship
articles.body:
With days to go before a crucial general election in Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu received a last-minute endorsement for re-election on Sunday from his longtime friend, U.S. President Donald Trump.
“Bibi Netanyahu has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump posted on Truth Social Sunday. “Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel.”
It’s a ringing, albeit late, recommendation for someone Trump hasn’t seen eye-to-eye with in recent months over how Netanyahu’s government has navigated the Middle East conflict. Trump explained his delayed endorsement to Axios reporter Barak Ravid, saying that he’d always meant to endorse Netanyahu because they “have a good relationship, and because we’ll continue to do good things together.”
Trump said in his post that, if Israel were to have “the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi,” the U.S. would be left alone to face the Iran threat. The U.S. and Israel jointly struck Iran in late February, kickstarting a conflict that has not only upended global markets but also thrust Middle Eastern regional security into turmoil.
“Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself,” Trump added, in apparent reference to Netanyahu’s domestic challenges, including a corruption trial, some of which the U.S. President has previously tried to influence. “Despite all of that, he has endured and, in fact, he has thrived!”
Trump’s endorsement comes just before Israelis head to the polling booths on Oct. 27, some three years after the country’s war with terror group Hamas ignited. Since then, Netanyahu has been criticized by opponents for failing to deliver on his promise of restoring regional security.
Public disillusionment with Netanyahu was among several factors that led to the formation of the Yashar! (“Straight!”) Party, whose founder, former Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, is challenging Netanyahu for the premiership. Eisenkot’s son and nephews were killed in the war in the Gaza Strip.
It’s unclear how big of an electoral boost Netanyahu will get from Trump’s endorsement. An opinion poll from nonprofit The Jewish People Policy Institute in Jerusalem released this month shows that most Israelis still see Trump as a great friend of Israel. A separate opinion poll from JPPI, however, shows their trust in him has eroded. Eisenkot, reacting to Trump’s endorsement, said at an event in Tel Aviv that while he appreciates Trump, only Israelis will decide on their next Prime Minister. Some surveys show Yashar! is in a tight race with Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud party.
Netanyahu nonetheless thanked his “dear friend Donald” in a video posted on social media, saying he was “honored” and “humbled” by Trump’s backing, adding that the U.S. was “fortunate” to have Trump as its leader in the fight to denuclearize Iran.
Trump and Netanyahu’s fraught friendship
Even before Trump became U.S. President, he had publicly endorsed Netanyahu, though Trump, still only a TV personality in 2013, said that the Israeli politician asked for it. Since Trump was first elected, the two have been political allies and friends. Their relationship, however, has seen a number of ups and downs since Trump returned to the White House last year.
Netanyahu was the first foreign leader invited to the White House during Trump’s second-term Administration, and he has met with Trump repeatedly since. Netanyahu pushed Trump to target three key Iranian nuclear facilities in June last year. Last November, Trump sent a letter to Israeli President Isaac Herzog, asking him to pardon Netanyahu on his drawn out corruption trial, which the U.S. President deemed to be “political, unjustified prosecution.”
On Feb. 11, when Trump and Netanyahu met in a closed-door meeting at the White House, Israel and the U.S. failed to reach an agreement on how to proceed with Iran. Netanyahu has long sought to decapitate the Iranian leadership, but Trump at the time insisted on negotiations. Netanyahu, nonetheless, reportedly pressed Trump to launch the Iran operation later that month.
Since their last meeting, their relationship has markedly shifted. Trump has since tried to find an off-ramp to the war in Iran, but Israel’s actions made such peace deal talks thorny.
In March, after Israel attacked Iran’s South Pars gas field in the Persian Gulf, Trump said he told Netanyahu to stop such attacks. Then, on April 17, Trump declared on Truth Social that Israel was “PROHIBITED” from further bombing Lebanon, where it was at war with the militant group Hezbollah. Netanyahu, however, insisted that Israeli troops would remain in southern Lebanon and that security threats persisted—complicating Washington’s efforts toward peace as Tehran indicated that any deal would need to include a halt of the attacks in Lebanon.
When Netanyahu in June ordered strikes on a Hezbollah stronghold in Beirut to retaliate against the group’s alleged attacks on Israel, Trump phoned and excoriated the Israeli Prime Minister, reportedly calling him “f-cking crazy.” Asked by CNBC about the call, Netanyahu said: “We have common goals. Sometimes we have, as in the best of families, you have these tactical disagreements. We always find a way to work them out, and we do so as great friends.”
During Netanyahu’s seventh U.S. visit in July, Trump went public with his frustration. During a telephone interview on Fox News, Trump criticized Netanyahu over reports that the Israeli leader planned to share intelligence showing Iran rebuilding its nuclear program. The U.S. President said: “I don’t need Bibi to tell me that. Bibi is telling me that because he wants me to stay involved.”
Netanyahu is part of Trump’s U.N. alternative called the Board of Peace, though Israel broke again with the U.S. President by rejecting having Turkish and Qatari representatives on the board’s subpanel, the Gaza Executive Board, which is tasked with overseeing post-war reconstruction in the Gaza Strip.
Then Netanyahu rejected the Board of Peace’s 15-point plan to advance a cease-fire in the Gaza Strip and insisted that Israel would not withdraw before Hamas fully disarmed.
In Trump’s extensive interview with TIME in late September, Trump did not answer directly when asked repeatedly if the Israeli population should give Netanyahu another term. “I can only say that I’m not involved in politics anymore,” the U.S. President said.
But despite the lack of clear endorsement then, Trump seemed confident that “Bibi” could still win. “People have written off Bibi many, many times, just like they’ve written off me many, many times,” Trump told TIME. “I wouldn’t underestimate Bibi.”

articles.title: Egypt parliament delays vote on military support to Saudi Arabia
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Egypt parliament delays vote on military support to Saudi Arabia
Egypt's parliament on Sunday postponed a vote on President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's request to authorise military support for Saudi Arabia, two lawmakers told AFP, with deliberations set to continue on Monday.
The session was convened after Sisi asked lawmakers to approve support for Saudi Arabia's defence if requested by the kingdom, which has come under near-daily attacks from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis since early October.
"The session was extended to give all lawmakers the opportunity to speak and express their views," lawmaker Ibrahim Kholeif told AFP, adding that parliamentarians were mostly in support of the move.
Another member, Maha Abdel Nasser, said proceedings would resume Monday "to allow all lawmakers to be heard".
Egyptian media reported that deliberations would continue into Tuesday.
Both lawmakers said no details were being discussed about what form Egypt's military support for Saudi Arabia could take.
Sisi on Saturday requested parliamentary authorisation to help defend Saudi Arabia "if requested", saying it was "inconceivable" for Cairo to stand by as Saudi Arabia's security and stability are threatened.
The decade-plus war between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen's internationally-recognised government reignited in July.
The Houthis seized Yemen's Red Sea coastline in September and have since launched attacks on Saudi Arabia, including state oil giant Aramco and Riyadh's international airport, where 13 people were killed a week ago.
On Saturday, Sisi called for an end to the fighting and said Egypt was not seeking to "confront or attack anyone. We are speaking only about defence".
Houthi threats to Egypt
Egypt's constitution requires the approval of both parliament and the National Defence Council -- which includes the leaders of Egypt's security apparatus -- before troops can be deployed on combat missions abroad.
Shortly before the parliamentary session, the council, chaired by Sisi, approved providing Saudi Arabia with "all necessary and available forms of support" to help defend its security, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites, the presidency said.
Potential military involvement would constitute a break from Egypt's historically conservative foreign policy, which has prioritised protecting its own national security.
For years Cairo has positioned itself as a regional mediator with channels open across conflict lines, including with Hamas, Israel and Iran.
In response to Sisi's call on Saturday, Houthi parliament speaker Yehia Ali al-Rai addressed a letter of warning to his Egyptian counterpart.
"Egypt's slide down this path would pose a grave danger to its own national security and internal stability before anyone else's," he wrote, according to the Houthis' Saba news agency.
Throughout this year, as its Gulf allies have come under attack in the war between Iran and the US, Cairo has repeatedly preached caution.
The Arab world's largest military did not issue a response even when its own Damietta port was struck by an unidentified drone in July.
It has not joined the Mecca defence pact signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan in August, according to experts to maintain its strategic autonomy.
But Riyadh is one of Cairo's strongest allies, and a key financial backer to Sisi's administration for over a decade.
Egypt joined the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen in 2015, contributing naval and air forces and deploying warships to the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Along with Saudi Arabia, Egypt is hardest hit by disruptions through Bab al-Mandab, the southern gateway to its Suez Canal, revenues from which have not recovered since Houthi attacks began in 2023.
Military expert Samir Farag told AFP that Egyptian assistance could take several forms, ranging from intelligence, military advisers, ammunition and spare parts to weapons and, ultimately, troop deployments.

articles.title: Ukraine and Russia should focus on ending war: Rubio
articles.body:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that Ukraine and Russia should focus on ending their war, as Washington continues efforts to broker a peace deal.
Asked during a visit to Uzbekistan about a possible meeting between US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to discuss the four-year-old conflict, Rubio said the meeting had not been confirmed.
“There’s been talks of a meeting. I don’t know whether it’s been finalized, but the president has been clear. He’d like the war in Ukraine and Russia to end,” Rubio told reporters.
Rubio also denied that Washington had suspended intelligence sharing with Ukraine, contrary to claims from Kiev. He called President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to "focus" on ending the war with Russia.
"What he should be focused on and what we want to be focused on is bringing an end to this war," he said.
Rubio arrived in Samarkand on Sunday night to meet senior officials from the C5+1 grouping, which brings together the US and five Central Asian countries: Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.
Trump hosted the leaders of the five countries at the White House last November.
“We see nothing good coming from this war,” Rubio said, warning of the risk of escalation and the conflict spreading into neighbouring countries.
He cited the possibility of a failed sabotage attack or drones affected by electronic warfare straying across borders.
Peace efforts amid renewed attacks
The US has been seeking to mediate an agreement to end the war. Trump has also secured a deal allowing Russian diesel imports and waived some sanctions on Moscow, saying the moves could help keep the Kremlin at the negotiating table.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has criticised the moves.
Meanwhile, a fresh Russian air strike killed a woman in Kiev overnight and hit a subway station, while also damaging a 25-storey residential building, according to the supplied report.

articles.title: US resumes intelligence-sharing with Ukraine after pause, Zelensky says
articles.body:
The United States has resumed providing Ukraine with critical intelligence to help defend against Russian missile strikes after a brief pause, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in comments published on Sunday.
Ukraine has relied on US intelligence to spot the fast-moving ballistic missiles that Russia has fired in waves at its cities.
Speaking to NBC's Meet the Press, Zelensky said intelligence-sharing had been interrupted but later "de-blocked."
"We are very thankful for this," he said. "Now it works."
US President Donald Trump had said earlier this week that Washington was still sharing intelligence, despite Ukrainian officials saying some Russian strikes had occurred without warning.
Zelensky in talks with Trump envoys over new peace meeting this week
Zelensky said he is holding talks with US President Donald Trump’s envoys with a view to arranging a new peace meeting as early as this week, Bloomberg News reported on Sunday, citing an interview with the Ukrainian president.
Zelensky also said on Sunday he had spoken with US peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as part of "virtually nonstop communication" between the two countries' teams aimed at the "next steps in diplomacy."
"Had a conversation with the American President's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Peace comes only through strength and cooperation built on trust," he wrote on X.
"In particular, we discussed the results of our teams' meeting in Florida. Our teams maintain virtually nonstop communication. We are also preparing the next steps in diplomacy."

articles.title: The very stable genius, nine years later
articles.body:
In January 2018, after a book questioned his mental fitness, the president of the United States sat down and wrote his own diagnosis.
“My two greatest assets have been mental stability and being, like, really smart,” he tweeted. “I think that would qualify as not smart, but genius. And a very stable genius at that!”
He was 71 years old.
Nearly nine years and one reelection later, the self-assessment has not moved an inch. The facts around it have.
Start with the war he promised would never happen.
Trump campaigned twice on ending American wars, not starting them. In January, the US military struck targets across Venezuela and extracted President Nicolás Maduro, who now sits in a New York jail awaiting trial on narco-terrorism charges.
The operation followed months of strikes on small boats in the Caribbean. Well over 100 people were killed on suspicion, never proof, of drug trafficking.
Months later came Iran, a war the administration still calls “Operation Epic Fury.”
Trump recently told a rally crowd that the United States had lost “18 incredible people” in that war. Reporting by The Washington Post placed the true figure at 22 or higher.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth called the Post’s reporting “a complete LIE.”
The two numbers have never been reconciled.
Then there is the money.
Qatar gave Trump’s government a $400 million Boeing 747 to use as Air Force One. The aircraft was painted navy and gold to suit his taste. Trump has said it will eventually go to his presidential library when he leaves office.
READ: Lavrov says Trump’s Gaza plan remains ‘ink on paper,’ calls for Palestinian statehood
At home, he gutted the East Wing of the White House to make room for a gold-leafed ballroom costing $300 million. He covered the Oval Office in gilt cherubs and molding, creating what his own press secretary called “a golden office for the golden age.”
Critics have used different words: tacky, gaudy, a monument to ego.
On the campaign trail this fall, Trump has promised every American adult a $5,000 “dividend” if Republicans retain control of Congress in November.
It echoes two earlier promises. One offered Americans $2,000 from tariff revenue. The other promised an unspecified share of “DOGE savings.” Both were announced with fanfare. Neither was paid.
Polling suggests that most Americans do not believe this dividend will be paid either. In one recent survey, only 17 percent of adults said Trump generally keeps his promises.
His relationship with the truth is not incidental to his politics. It is the engine of it.
For decades, Trump has told audiences that he graduated first in his class at the Wharton School. The university’s own records from 1968 show that he made neither the Dean’s List nor any honors roll.
He has also said repeatedly, including as recently as this March during a meeting with Germany’s chancellor, that his father was born in “a very wonderful place in Germany.”
Fred Trump was born in the Bronx. It was Trump’s grandfather who emigrated from Germany.
These are not policy disagreements or competing interpretations of history. They are verifiable facts about his own life. He has overwritten them in public, repeatedly, at no apparent cost.
The self-praise runs in a straight line from that 2018 tweet to the present.
Trump has told voters for years, in one formulation after another, that he knows more than America’s generals, more than its diplomats, more than its intelligence agencies.
In 2018, standing beside Vladimir Putin in Helsinki, Trump was asked whether he believed the conclusion of his own intelligence community that Russia had interfered in the 2016 election, or Putin’s denial.
“I don’t see any reason why it would be,” Russia, he replied.
He spent the following week trying, unconvincingly, to recast the remark as a simple misstatement.
The pattern recurs across his biography and in matters of war and peace: a confident assertion, a contradiction from the record, and no meaningful reckoning with the distance between them.
Three wars into a presidency that promised none, Trump’s instinct to trust his own judgment over everyone else’s has survived every piece of evidence that might have revised it.
That pattern is what a group of mental health professionals has spent nine years trying to name.
In 2017, Yale psychiatrist Bandy Lee assembled 27 colleagues for “The Dangerous Case of Donald Trump.” They argued that they had a “duty to warn” the public, despite professional norms against diagnosing public figures from a distance.
OPINION: Trump could lose Congress and still expand the US war on Iran
Psychologist John Gartner, one of the contributors, has been more direct. For years, he has described Trump as a “malignant narcissist,” a term coined by psychoanalyst Erich Fromm to describe leaders who are grandiose, paranoid, and remorseless.
In 2024, more than 230 mental health professionals signed a public letter repeating the warning ahead of the election.
None of this constitutes a formal diagnosis. The signatories are explicit that it cannot. Trump has never submitted to an evaluation.
Yet the consistency of the assessment, sustained across nine years and echoed by dozens of credentialed observers, is itself a kind of data point.
So is the legal record.
Trump was indicted four times in 2023 on a combined 88 felony counts. He became the first former American president ever charged with a crime.
In New York, he was convicted on all 34 counts in the hush-money case.
He did not go to prison.
Having won reelection in the meantime, Trump received an unconditional discharge: no fine, no probation, no punishment beyond the conviction itself. The judge said it was the only sentence available for a sitting president.
The two federal cases were dropped after Trump’s victory. The Georgia case was dismissed last November.
He did not defeat the charges.
He outlasted the clock.
None of it cost him the presidency.
Trump won the Electoral College in 2024 by 312 votes to 226. He also won the popular vote by 1.5 points. It was a real victory, if a modest one by historical standards, and the second-narrowest popular-vote margin since 1960.
Enough Americans, in other words, looked at all of it: the boasting, the contradicted facts, the criminal indictments, the wars he promised never to fight. Then they voted for him anyway.
That may be the harder question, more troubling than any diagnosis.
Presidential falsehoods are not new in American life. What is new is a public that increasingly treats them as beside the point.
There was once an expectation that a president’s word could be taken to the bank.
Whether that was ever entirely true, the pretense itself is now gone.

articles.title: Ukrainian air defenses fail to intercept single Russian ballistic missile overnight
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 19. /TASS/. The air defense systems deployed by Ukraine overnight night failed to intercept a single Russian ballistic missile, according to data published by the Ukrainian Air Force on its Telegram channel.
On Monday morning, the Russian Defense Ministry reported that strikes had been carried out overnight against targets in Ukraine, including military-industrial facilities, storage sites for cruise missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles, and a data center in Kiev and the Kiev Region.
Earlier, The Washington Post reported that the Ukrainian military had nearly depleted its stockpile of Patriot missiles, and that deliveries have been irregular since May. For its part, CNN reported that Kiev had been warning its partners for several months that it was running out of Patriot interceptor missiles, which are currently in short supply everywhere.

articles.title: US Secretary of State Rubio Denies Any Pause in Intelligence Sharing With Ukraine
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
US Secretary of State Rubio Denies Any Pause in Intelligence Sharing With Ukraine
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied that Washington paused intelligence sharing with Ukraine, Reuters reported on October 19.
This contradicted Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s account that the flow had briefly been interrupted before being restored.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“We are very thankful for this,” Zelenskyy stated. “Now it works.”
Rubio rejected that account during a visit to Uzbekistan on October 19, telling reporters in Samarkand that intelligence sharing had never been interrupted.
“I don’t know where he’s getting these things or why he’s saying these things to the press,” Rubio stated, according to Reuters. “You should go back and ask him. There’s been no pause.”
“What he should be focused on, and what we want to be focused on, is bringing an end to this war. That’s what he should be focused on,” Rubio added.
On October 18, Zelenskyy stated that recent US moves, including Starlink restrictions and delays in Patriot deliveries, increasingly looked like pressure on Ukraine to capitulate to Russia, while stressing that he did not believe Washington necessarily intended that outcome.
Reuters noted that the dispute is the latest in a series of public contradictions between Washington and Kyiv as relations have deteriorated sharply in recent days.
Zelenskyy has also stated that he believes the US government was behind recent restrictions affecting Ukraine’s use of SpaceX’s Starshield system, which plays an important role in defending against Russian drones and missiles.
US officials have denied that claim as well, Reuters reported.
Ukraine relies heavily on US intelligence to detect fast-moving Russian ballistic missiles launched against Ukrainian cities.
The dispute over intelligence sharing comes days after Zelenskyy reported that Ukraine received no advance warning before five Russian ballistic missiles struck civilian infrastructure in Kyiv. He stressed that early intelligence on ballistic launches is critical because the short flight time leaves civilians and air-defense crews only minutes to react.
Discuss this article:

articles.title: Bessent warns Zelenskyy to 'be very careful' about claims U.S. is throttling Starlink
articles.body:
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday to "be careful" in public statements about U.S. support for Ukraine.
U.S.-provided Starlink internet was recently restricted in Ukraine, hindering the war-torn country's ability to respond to Russian assaults. Ukraine uses Starshield, the military and government-controlled version of the commercial Starlink, to conduct military operations.
In an earlier interview on NBC's "Meet the Press," Zelenskyy said he believed the U.S. government was responsible for the slowdown, and that Ukraine was "blocked" from U.S. intelligence for a period of time. Zelenskyy said Starshield-linked vehicles and drones are still being restricted in speed.
Bessent cautioned Zelenskyy about making those claims.
"President [Donald] Trump and Secretary [Marco] Rubio have categorically said that no one under the Trump administration did that, and I think it is very reckless for President Zelenskyy to make such a charge," Bessent said on "Meet the Press."
"President Zelenskyy should be very careful about making statements like this that aren't true," he added.
Starlink, high-speed satellite internet provided by Elon Musk's SpaceX, is critical to Ukraine's defense. Musk himself said in a post on X last week that the U.S. government and President Donald Trump are "ultimately" responsible for any slowdowns to the military version of Starlink known as Starshield.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," Musk wrote. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment from CNBC.
Reuters reported last week that the White House ordered the technology restrictions, but Trump has denied responsibility for the slowdown.
"Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," the president said last week. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been."
The U.S. relationship with Ukraine has been highly scrutinized throughout Trump's second term, as he has frequently antagonized the war-torn country while pushing for a peace deal.
Trump has recently expressed frustration over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries as he faces pressure from voters over sky-high gasoline and diesel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. The president has even personally blamed Zelenskyy for the rise in energy prices: "He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel," Trump said.
Soaring energy prices are largely due to the U.S. war with Iran, which severely disrupted the Strait of Hormuz and choked oil shipments from the Persian Gulf. The national average for a gallon of gas in the U.S. was nearly $4.30 on Sunday, according to AAA. Diesel was roughly $6.32 per gallon, about 20 cents off September's record high.
Trump has tried to offset the energy pinch by importing Russian diesel. In a post on Truth Social earlier in the month, he said: "Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!"
Many U.S. lawmakers, including Republicans, have condemned the president's plan to buy Russian diesel. Congress recently sent Trump an overwhelmingly bipartisan sanctions package aimed at crippling Russia's energy industry. Trump signed the bill into law, but waived portions of it over the weekend, citing the national interest in an explanation to Congress.
"Beyond irresponsible. What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?" Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said in a post on X. "It's unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day."

articles.title: Zelenskyy Says Washington’s Latest Moves Suggest Pressure on Ukraine to Capitulate to Russia
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Zelenskyy Says Washington’s Latest Moves Suggest Pressure on Ukraine to Capitulate to Russia
Starlink restrictions and delayed Patriot deliveries are making Washington’s pressure on Kyiv look increasingly like an attempt to push Ukraine toward capitulation.
Recent decisions by Washington increasingly look like an attempt to pressure Ukraine into capitulating to Russia, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an interview with Bloomberg on October 18.
“I believe steps were taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate,” Zelenskyy said.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
But the Ukrainian President also stressed that he does not believe Ukraine’s US partners necessarily intend that outcome.
He clarified that he was describing the effect of recent US actions rather than accusing Washington of explicitly pursuing Ukraine’s surrender.
“I don’t want to think that our American partners believe the war can be ended faster at Ukraine’s expense. But that is what it looks like,” he said.
Among the measures Zelenskyy cited were deliberate restrictions on Starlink connectivity and delays in supplying Patriot interceptor missiles that Ukraine had already paid for.
Both have become increasingly sensitive issues as Russia intensifies ballistic missile and drone strikes against Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
In addition, Ukraine received no warning from its partners before Russian ballistic missiles struck civilian infrastructure in Kyiv.
Zelenskyy also said US President Donald Trump maintains a genuinely good relationship with Russian leader Vladimir Putin, but argued that the relationship has so far failed to produce the result Washington wants.
“But one thing does not work here: right now Trump cannot force Putin to end the war,” Zelenskyy said.
Despite the growing tensions, the Ukrainian leader said he believes relations with Washington could stabilize after the US midterm elections on November 3.
“During elections, politics is very aggressive. I think what we are seeing now is agony, but after the elections life will continue, and I believe things will become calmer,” he said.
Zelenskyy warned, however, that Ukraine cannot afford to wait until political disagreements develop into much larger strategic problems.
“When Ukraine faces risks on the scale of a tsunami, you have to intervene while it is still only a light storm. I think far more is at stake than a diesel fuel deal,” he said.
The Ukrainian president added that he is likely to meet again this week with Trump envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff as Kyiv continues efforts to repair relations and secure military support.
Recently, US President Donald Trump blocked the implementation of sweeping sanctions and tariffs against Russia and buyers of Russian energy under a law championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, just weeks after signing the legislation himself.

articles.title: Lavrov visits Iran as Russia explores role in US-Tehran talks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Lavrov visits Iran as Russia explores mediation role in US-Tehran talks
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov arrived in Tehran on Monday for talks with senior Iranian officials, raising questions over whether Moscow could play a greater role in mediating between Iran and the United States amid fears of renewed war.
The visit comes as diplomatic efforts to avert another confrontation intensify, with The New Arab reporting on Monday that a breakthrough in US-Iran mediation efforts could be announced this week.
Senior sources familiar with negotiations told The New Arab that Qatar and Pakistan were working to narrow differences between Washington and Tehran and secure mutual concessions, while ruling out an immediate military escalation.
Lavrov's visit, his first to Iran since the US-Israeli war began on 28 February, follows Moscow's recent involvement in exchanging messages between the two countries.
It also comes ahead of a possible visit to Tehran by Pakistan's army chief, General Asim Munir, who has been involved in mediation efforts between Washington and Tehran.
The timing has raised speculation that Lavrov could be carrying messages from Washington, while his arrival from Bahrain on Sunday has also prompted questions about whether he could be conveying messages from Gulf states amid heightened regional tensions.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei described the visit as part of ongoing consultations between Tehran and Moscow aimed at following up on bilateral agreements and discussing regional and international developments.
Russia's foreign ministry said the talks would involve a "frank and in-depth" exchange of views on bilateral cooperation, major international issues and developments in the Gulf, including possible ways to resolve the crisis stemming from the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Ahead of his arrival, Lavrov criticised US President Donald Trump's approach towards Tehran as "wrong", arguing that it would not help achieve an agreement based on mutual respect and international law.
Can Russia mediate between Iran and the US?
Russia's potential mediation role began taking shape earlier this month, amid growing contacts between Moscow and Washington over the war in Ukraine.
On 10 October, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov revealed that Russian President Vladimir Putin had informed his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian of an upcoming telephone conversation with Trump.
The exchange followed a meeting between Putin and Pezeshkian in Turkmenistan on 9 October.
The Kremlin subsequently announced that Putin had conveyed Iran's position on a possible settlement to Trump, raising expectations that Moscow could become another diplomatic channel between Washington and Tehran.
However, Iranian officials have stopped short of recognising Russia as a formal mediator.
Baghaei said last week that, "technically, in the strict sense of the word", Pakistan and Qatar remained the actual mediators between Iran and the United States.
He added that consultations between Tehran and Moscow, particularly on the nuclear issue, were nothing new.
Experts question prospects of Russian mediation
Iranian analyst Hadi Mohammadi told The New Arab that Lavrov's visit reflected growing Russian concerns about developments in the Gulf and the possibility of further escalation.
He said Moscow appeared to be intensifying its diplomatic activities in an attempt to contain tensions, noting that the US-Iran confrontation had become closely linked to the war in Ukraine amid renewed contacts between Washington and Moscow.
Mohammadi suggested that Lavrov could be carrying messages from Washington or Israel during what he described as an extremely sensitive period.
He recalled that Putin had previously conveyed messages between Tehran and Israel, including an Israeli assurance before the latest war that it did not intend to attack Iran.
However, Mohammadi expressed limited confidence in Russia's ability to secure a breakthrough.
He argued that some international actors were making a fundamental mistake by pressuring Iran alone to accept the other side's conditions, while overlooking Tehran's position that it had been attacked and had complied with the Islamabad memorandum of understanding reached in June, which Iran accuses Washington of violating.
Mohammadi said Lavrov's visit could help reduce regional tensions but was unlikely to resolve the crisis on its own.
At best, he suggested, it could mark the beginning of further diplomatic exchanges, although he did not rule out the possibility that it represented a final attempt to avert another war.
Iranian analyst Abbas Aslani similarly told The New Arab that Lavrov's visit reflected the depth of cooperation between Tehran and Moscow in confronting Western pressure.
He said shared economic, political and military challenges had strengthened the importance of bilateral and regional coordination.
Aslani considered it possible that Lavrov was carrying a response or message from Washington, although he cautioned against drawing conclusions before the talks took place.
He also suggested that Moscow could use the visit to assess the Trump administration's position ahead of the US midterm elections on 3 November.
According to Aslani, Russia was already familiar with Iran's strategic red lines, including the conditions outlined in Tehran's seven-day proposal, and was unlikely to persuade Iranian officials to make substantial changes.
He described the visit as a potential opportunity to exchange "hard truths", but argued that any genuine breakthrough would depend on Washington accepting the new balance of power and security in the Gulf.

articles.title: Lebanon must refuse Hezbollah’s demand to return seized explosives - editorial
articles.body:
Lebanese security forces recently seized hundreds of kilograms of explosives from a vehicle at a checkpoint on the highway linking Beirut and the Bekaa Valley. Hezbollah admitted the shipment belonged to the organization and demanded its return.
“The vehicle and its cargo belong to the resistance,” Hezbollah lawmaker Hassan Fadlallah said, also demanding the release of those arrested. The Iran-backed organization said the material was intended for attacks against Israeli forces in Lebanon.
The Lebanese government should reject that demand. Its security forces have taken a concrete step toward enforcing state authority. Returning the explosives would undermine their work and confirm Hezbollah’s assumption that it can overrule them.
Lebanon has repeatedly said that weapons should be held by the state alone. In March, the government specifically banned Hezbollah’s military activities. Lebanese President Joseph Aoun has reiterated the state’s commitment to seizing illegal weapons and combating smuggling. The issue now is whether Beirut will enforce those decisions when Hezbollah openly challenges them.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who pressed Aoun to retain the explosives, was right. According to a US State Department official’s account of their call, Rubio said returning them should be “out of the question” and urged accountability for those who ordered, financed, and directed the shipment.
No sovereign government should accept an armed group moving hundreds of kilograms of explosives around the country without state authorization.
Lebanese military delegation to participate in US-hosted trilateral talks
A Lebanese military delegation is expected to participate on Tuesday in US-hosted trilateral talks in Tampa, Florida. Beirut plans to press for an end to Israeli attacks in Lebanon. Under the US-brokered framework, Hezbollah’s disarmament is linked to a gradual Israeli withdrawal. Hezbollah continues to refuse to disarm while Israeli forces remain on Lebanese territory.
Lebanon’s demand deserves to be taken seriously. Israel should seek a security arrangement that will allow its troops to withdraw. An indefinite military presence carries costs, while repeated strikes cannot provide a permanent solution.
Any withdrawal must also prevent a return to the conditions that existed before the war. For years, agreements intended to keep Hezbollah’s forces away from Israel’s border went unenforced. Hezbollah accumulated missiles, built military infrastructure, and maintained an armed organization stronger than the Lebanese state itself.
Israel cannot responsibly ask residents of the North to return to that reality.
Full disarmament will take time. Lebanon can begin with the weapons already in its possession: retain the explosives, preserve the evidence needed for the investigation, and arrange their safe destruction.
Authorities should investigate the shipment, prosecute anyone proven to have violated Lebanese law, and apply the same policy to future seizures regardless of who claims ownership.
Such action would strengthen Lebanon’s position at the negotiating table. If Beirut wants Israel to cease its strikes and withdraw its forces, it needs to demonstrate that Lebanese territory will remain secure against renewed preparations for attacks on Israel.
Supporting Lebanon to assert sovereignty over its borders
Israel also has a responsibility to support progress. Jerusalem says it wants the Lebanese government and Lebanese Armed Forces to replace Hezbollah as the effective authority in the south.
Sustained, independently verified progress toward disarmament, preventing smuggling, and extending state control should be matched by phased Israeli steps under the agreed framework, consistent with the security of northern communities.
A single seizure cannot establish that those conditions have been met. It can, however, help demonstrate whether Lebanese authorities intend to enforce their decisions consistently.
Verification should include access to suspected weapons sites, clear reporting on confiscations, and evidence that dismantled outposts remain closed. Lebanon’s partners should help its army carry out those tasks and insist that political pressure never determines which shipments pass through a checkpoint.
The European Union’s newly approved mission to train and advise Lebanon’s military and internal security forces offers further support. Its deployment remains pending. Foreign assistance will have limited effect unless Beirut is prepared to uphold its authority against Hezbollah’s demands.
Who decides which armed forces operate on Lebanese soil? If the answer is the Lebanese state, then Beirut already knows what to do with Hezbollah’s explosives.

articles.title: Exclusive: Breakthrough expected in US-Iran mediation efforts
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Breakthrough expected in US-Iran mediation efforts this week
A breakthrough in mediation efforts between the United States and Iran is expected to be announced this week, sources familiar with the negotiations told The New Arab on Monday, as Qatar and Pakistan continue diplomatic efforts to prevent a renewed war between Washington and Tehran.
Senior sources familiar with the mediation efforts, speaking to The New Arab on condition of anonymity, said negotiations were continuing to narrow differences and encourage mutual concessions aimed at preventing another military confrontation.
Despite ongoing threats exchanged between Washington and Tehran, and concerns that the war with Iran could resume after the US midterm elections on 3 November, the sources ruled out an immediate escalation in the region.
The anticipated breakthrough comes amid mounting tensions over Iran's nuclear programme, the continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz and US demands for Tehran to curb its uranium enrichment capabilities.
On Saturday evening, US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth warned that Iran would face "destruction" unless it abandoned its nuclear ambitions at the negotiating table.
Speaking at the University of Tennessee in Knoxville, Hegseth accused Iran of building a "large arsenal" of conventional missiles and attempting to pursue a strategy similar to that of North Korea.
Meanwhile, US embassies across the region have warned of the possibility of rapidly developing security threats, including potential attacks by Iran and its regional allies.
Iran accuses Netanyahu of pushing for another war
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Sunday accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of attempting to drag the United States into another war with Tehran to avoid imprisonment.
Responding to remarks made by Netanyahu about Iran, Araghchi wrote on X that the Israeli leader was "dragging the United States into a new war to avoid going to prison", while disregarding the potential consequences for Israel and the US president.
The Iranian foreign minister also reiterated Tehran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, provided Washington meets several Iranian demands.
These include lifting the blockade on Iranian ports, easing restrictions on Iranian oil exports and halting hostilities across regional fronts.
Araghchi said Tehran had received US feedback on the proposal and was reviewing it, although significant disagreements continued to obstruct progress.
According to Reuters, one of the main sticking points remains Washington's insistence on placing Iran's nuclear programme at the centre of negotiations, including demands for substantial reductions in Tehran's uranium enrichment capabilities.
Iran, however, wants to prioritise reopening the Strait of Hormuz and addressing the economic and security restrictions imposed on the country.
Qatar and Pakistan intensify mediation efforts
Qatar and Pakistan have continued diplomatic efforts to bridge differences between Washington and Tehran, although political and security obstacles have so far prevented an agreement that could end the confrontation and restore regional stability.
The talks come amid growing concerns over the consequences of the Strait of Hormuz remaining closed, with disruptions to shipping and global energy supplies adding urgency to efforts to reach a settlement.
Iran's ISNA news agency reported on Sunday that Pakistan's army chief, Asim Munir, could visit Tehran this week as part of ongoing cooperation between the two countries and discussions concerning regional developments and US-Iran negotiations.
The Strait of Hormuz remains one of the central issues in the crisis because of its strategic importance to global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments.
Reopening the waterway could serve not only as a measure to restore maritime traffic but also as an initial confidence-building step towards reducing tensions and restarting negotiations on broader disputes.
However, Tehran's proposal remains conditional on Washington meeting its demands, while the United States continues to insist that concerns over Iran's nuclear programme must be addressed.
Disagreements over sanctions, the blockade on Iranian ports and mechanisms for ending hostilities across the region also remain unresolved.
The latest mediation efforts therefore present Qatar and Pakistan with a critical challenge of preventing the collapse of diplomatic contacts while securing reciprocal confidence-building measures that could pave the way for broader negotiations on Iran's nuclear programme, sanctions and regional security arrangements.
The sources' assessment that an immediate escalation is unlikely offers a potential opening for diplomacy, despite the continued exchange of threats and the absence of a comprehensive agreement between Washington and Tehran.

articles.title: Russia and India wrap up joint naval drills in Pacific (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Russia and India wrap up joint naval drills in Pacific (VIDEO)
Russian and Indian warships have completed joint naval drills off Russia’s Pacific coast, conducting live-fire exercises and practicing defenses against drone attacks as part of the wider Indra-2026 military exercise.
The maritime phase of the drills took place in the Gulf of Peter the Great near Vladivostok, involving the Russian Pacific Fleet corvette Aldar Tsydenzhapov and the Indian Navy frigate INS Sahyadri, the Russian Defense Ministry said on Saturday.
INS Sahyadri arrived in Vladivostok on October 10 and conducted harbor engagements before operations at sea.
The crews fired naval artillery at surface and aerial targets, carried out coordinated maneuvers, and tested communications between the vessels. They also practiced repelling attacks by unmanned boats and aerial drones representing a simulated enemy. The Russian corvette used 30mm automatic guns, small arms, and electronic warfare systems to counter the simulated threats.
The exercises culminated in a simulated joint operation to rescue a civilian vessel seized by pirates. Russian and Indian naval counterterrorism units boarded the vessel and neutralized the attackers, with drone operators coordinating their movements.
The two navies also practiced helicopter operations, including reconnaissance, cross-deck landings, and medical evacuations.
An Indian helicopter landed aboard the Russian corvette shortly after a Russian helicopter took off. The crews then exchanged mannequins representing wounded sailors as part of a casualty evacuation exercise, RT correspondent Igor Zhdanov reported from aboard the Russian warship.
Indra-2026 began on October 14 and involves land, naval, and air forces from both countries.
The land component will continue in Russia’s Chelyabinsk Region until October 23, with troops practicing joint command and control and operations against simulated armed groups. Russian and Indian aircrews are also conducting exercises involving Su-30SM fighter jets and Mi-8 helicopters.
The previous edition of the exercise was held off the coast of the southern Indian city of Chennai.
The deployment builds on the longstanding defense partnership between Moscow and New Delhi and carries forward cooperation discussed during Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to India last December, India’s Defense Ministry said.

articles.title: Qatar unveils plans for new defence centre amid regional tension
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Qatar announces plans for new defence centre amid regional tensions
Qatar will soon announce the establishment of a new defence centre as part of efforts to strengthen its military capabilities amid heightened regional tensions, the country's deputy prime minister and minister of state for defence affairs said on Monday.
Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani made the announcement at the opening of the Global Security Forum in Doha, revealing that Qatar was working with regional partners, the United States, Britain and France to enhance its capabilities in ammunition, air defence, counter-drone systems and cybersecurity.
The minister said Qatar was also exploring domestic production and investment opportunities in certain defence sectors, while maintaining a state of readiness for potential crises in coordination with the Ministry of Interior and other security agencies.
His remarks come amid continuing regional tensions and efforts to prevent further instability from the US-Israeli war involving Iran.
Addressing developments in the region, Sheikh Saoud stressed the importance of diplomatic coordination, saying that mediation efforts by Qatar, Pakistan and Oman complemented one another and required close cooperation to achieve their objectives.
He also called for regional dialogue involving Turkey and Pakistan once the war ends.
The Qatari official reaffirmed that Doha had maintained communication with Iran despite disagreements between the two countries, expressing hope that Qatar would not face another attack following the strike on Ras Laffan.
In March, Iran launched missile attacks on Qatar's Ras Laffan Industrial City, triggering fires and causing material damage.
Qatar's foreign ministry condemned the attack at the time as a dangerous escalation and a flagrant violation of its sovereignty, warning that it posed a direct threat to national security and regional stability.
The announcement comes as Doha hosts the Global Security Forum from 19 to 21 October under the theme "The Future of Alliances".
The annual international gathering brings together leaders and experts from around the world to discuss shifting global dynamics, emerging security challenges and international cooperation.
The forum provides a platform for policymakers and security specialists to examine major threats facing the international community and explore opportunities for dialogue and collaboration.

articles.title: Sudan drone strike kills 11 at displacement camp – official
articles.body:
Sudan drone strike kills 11 at displacement camp – official
Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have killed at least 11 people, including nine children, in a drone attack on a displacement camp in West Darfur, according to the region’s Health and Social Welfare Minister, Babiker Hamdin.
In a statement published on Sunday, Hamdin said that the attack targeted displaced civilians on the Sudan-Chad border. According to preliminary figures, the victims included nine children aged between five and ten and two women aged 23 and 36. Five others were injured.
The victims had reportedly fled their villages last year after RSF fighters allegedly burned and looted their homes. They subsequently sought refuge in Sanakit, near the Chadian border, where they were living in difficult humanitarian conditions before the latest attack.
Hamdin condemned the strike as “a horrific crime and a grave violation of international humanitarian law, reflecting the militia’s indifference to the lives of innocent people.”
He called on the international community to hold those responsible accountable and designate the paramilitary group as a terrorist organization.
Sudan was plunged into a civil war three years ago after a struggle for power broke out between the SAF and the RSF.
Sudan descended into chaos in April 2023 when fighting erupted between the national army, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The conflict followed months of tension between their commanders, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti, over a planned transition to civilian rule. What began in the capital, Khartoum, as a power struggle has devastated the country, killing tens of thousands, displacing millions, and pushing parts of Sudan into famine.
Regional and international peace efforts, including African Union mediation and Saudi-US talks in Jeddah, have repeatedly stalled. In September 2025, the Quad group – the US, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and the United Arab Emirates – proposed a three-month humanitarian truce leading to a permanent ceasefire and a civilian-led political transition. Burhan rejected a subsequent US-led proposal that November, arguing it would dismantle state security institutions while leaving the RSF in place. The paramilitaries said they accepted the truce.
The UAE’s involvement has deepened mistrust of mediation. Sudan’s army-backed government severed diplomatic ties with Abu Dhabi in May 2025, accusing it of supporting the RSF. The UAE denies supplying weapons to the paramilitaries. Relations with Washington deteriorated further in September 2026 after the US questioned both factions’ legitimacy. Sudan rejected the remarks and called for peace efforts free from foreign dictates.
Meanwhile, rival administrations have entrenched Sudan’s divisions. Burhan’s government returned to Khartoum in January 2026 after the army recaptured the capital, having operated from Port Sudan during the fighting. In July 2025, the RSF-aligned TASIS coalition announced a rival government based in Nyala, Darfur, with Dagalo heading its governing council. The UN Security Council and African Union rejected the move.
The RSF has faced similar accusations from rights groups over attacks on civilians. In September, the Sudanese Alliance for Rights reported that five people were killed in an attack on a market in North Kordofan, while the Committee for Justice blamed the group for a courthouse strike that killed ten. On October 9, the Sudan Doctors Network accused the rebels of a drone attack on a displacement camp in Blue Nile state that killed 31 people, including four children.
Earlier this month, Russian diplomat Yulia Zhdanova said that Sudanese troops recovered US-supplied weapons intended for Ukraine from RSF fighters near Bara. Their markings indicated that they had been transferred to Kiev in December 2024, she said, according to TASS.

articles.title: Deadly Russian strike hits Kiev subway station: official
articles.body:
A Russian air strike killed a woman in Ukraine's Kiev overnight, while also hitting a subway station on the left bank of the capital city and damaging a 25-storey residential building, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram on Monday.
The attack, which also saw non-residential buildings and a medical facility hit, injured three other people in Kiev, he said.
A Reuters witness heard explosions in the city.
After a brief pause, the US has resumed sharing critical intelligence to help Ukraine defend against Russian missile strikes, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, a key to providing warning of the fast-moving missiles that Moscow has fired in waves.
Zelenskyy spoke with US peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner after the two visited Kiev earlier this month as the US administration tries to mediate a deal to end the war which Russia started by invading its neighbour in 2022.

articles.title: Putin suggests meeting with Trump, Xi to discuss Ukraine war resolution - report
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin proposed a meeting with US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping next month to discuss ending the Russia-Ukraine war, the Wall Street Journal reported Sunday night, citing people familiar with the discussions.
The talks would not involve Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, an unprecedented move which would be expected to alarm many European countries, WSJ wrote.
According to the report, the Kremlin suggested the three leaders meet on the sidelines of the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, which takes place Nov. 18 and 19 in Shenzhen, southern China.
Putin first suggested the meeting while speaking to Trump on October 9, in the same conversation in which the two leaders agreed that the US would buy Russian diesel fuel and facilitate its sale, a former Russian intelligence officer told WSJ.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov confirmed that discussions over a potential meeting were ongoing.
“There is no clear understanding yet regarding the meeting itself or its potential agenda, although all three parties acknowledge the hypothetical possibility of such a meeting taking place,” he told WSJ.
A senior US official told WSJ that Trump hadn't agreed to the meeting but may be receptive to the idea due to his desire to end the war.
Trump, Zelensky clash over Ukrainian attacks, US sanctions
This comes as Trump and Zelensky publicly criticize the other's decisions, with Zelensky saying on Saturday that Trump's decision to waive sanctions on Russia and tariffs on its goods days before they were to take effect will embolden Moscow to keep attacking Ukraine, and Trump suggesting that Ukraine needs a new president.
Trump claimed that Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did," in a post on Truth Social earlier on Sunday, calling on the Ukrainian leader to stop attacking Russian diesel refineries.
Neither the White House nor the Chinese Embassy in Washington has commented on the report, but analysts told WSJ that a meeting between Trump, Xi, and Putin could advance Xi's ambitions for China's place in global diplomacy.
“China wants to be seen as the pivot of the great powers, and potentially as a mediator between the US and Russia,” Yun Sun, director of the China program at the Stimson Center, a Washington think tank, told WSJ.
However, Chinese officials have expressed concern that the meeting could overshadow China's role in the region at APEC, according to the report.
People familiar with the discussions told WSJ that Xi is also trying to balance support for Putin and economic ties with Europe. A meeting with Putin and Trump to discuss Ukraine could raise the risk of European backlash.
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

articles.title: At least 18 killed in Houthi attack on military camp in Yemen’s Shabwa
articles.body:
Houthi attack on Yemen army camp in Shabwa reportedly kills at least 53
Houthis launch ballistic missiles at camp in southern governorate during training exercise, government forces spokesman says.
A Houthi missile attack on the al-AIam military camp in southern Yemen has killed at least 50 people, according to local authorities.
The Houthis launched three ballistic missiles on Monday at the camp in Shabwa governorate during a training exercise, a spokesperson for the Yemeni government forces said.
Officials for the internationally-recognised government and medical sources initially said at least 18 people were killed and more than 30 wounded when the strike hit the facility, at which new security recruits were undergoing training.
However, the numbers have now risen dramatically. The local authority in Shabwa said later on Monday that 53 people had been killed and 200 injured, news agencies reported.
‘Hostile threat’
The attack was carried out as fighting continued to rage across Yemen. The civil war with between the Saudi-backed government and rebel Houthis was frozen for some years before the United States and Israel’s war on Iran provoked a return to conflict.
The hostilities escalated rapidly when the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), seized strategic territory from forces loyal to the government along the Red Sea coast last month.
Government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, responded with a counteroffensive and then launched the “Dawn of Yemen” operation, which aims to recapture Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the Iran-aligned group seized in 2014.
The Houthis, meanwhile, have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, including on Riyadh’s international airport and the state oil company Aramco.
On Monday, Saudi authorities sent alerts to residents of the capital Riyadh warning of “a hostile aerial threat”.
New recruits
Rashad al-Alimi, the head of the Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council, said those killed in Shabwa were new recruits and promised a “firm response”.
“Targeting recruits reflects the Houthi militia’s approach of resorting to terrorist attacks when under pressure,” he said.
Reporting from Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said the Houthis claimed responsibility for the attack.
“The Houthis said the attack targeted what they called a ‘Saudi-backed’ military base, referring to Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces who are stationed at military camps across the country,” he said.
“The Houthis say they will continue to target those bases. Spokesperson Yahya Saree says anywhere with a Saudi-backed military presence will be considered a legitimate target.”
Earlier, Yemeni government forces said they targeted Houthi gatherings, vehicles and weapons in al-Aqroudh, al-Shaqab and al-Sarari, south of Taiz, which is suffering from fuel shortages and soaring prices.

articles.title: Ukrainian Sea Drones Could Extend US Army Strike Range Without Risking Crewed Vessels
articles.body:
- Category
- Defense Tech
Ukrainian Sea Drones Could Extend US Army Strike Range Without Risking Crewed Vessels
Ukraine’s Magura-type MV7 uncrewed surface vessels were tested as aerial drone carriers during a US Army exercise in Michigan, Defence Blog reported on October 18.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The vessels participated in Bayonet Quest 26, held from September 26 through October 6 by the 7th Infantry Division, part of Multi-Domain Command-Pacific. The division described the exercise as testing autonomous systems and uncrewed aircraft to extend sensing, operational reach, and decision-making.
Images and materials released by the division showed the Ukrainian-built vessels carrying dedicated platforms on their forward hulls, allowing aerial drones to launch directly from the boats. The exercise also paired autonomous maritime systems with a crewed Mk VI patrol boat.
The 7th Infantry Division did not disclose how many MV7 vessels participated, their exact configuration, or the type of aerial drones launched from them. Using an uncrewed boat as a drone carrier can extend aerial reconnaissance and strike range while keeping larger crewed vessels farther from potential threats.
Magura vessels became prominent through Ukrainian operations against Russia’s Black Sea Fleet near temporarily occupied Crimea. Ukraine later fielded variants equipped with missiles and machine guns, while Ukrainian military intelligence reported in 2025 that missile-armed Magura boats had downed Russian combat aircraft over the Black Sea.
The Michigan trials come as Ukrainian expertise in uncrewed maritime systems is increasingly built into allied exercises.
Days earlier, Ukraine used its DELTA battlefield management system to coordinate aerial, surface, and underwater drones with radar systems during NATO's REPMUS 2026 exercises, led by the Portuguese Navy.
It was Ukraine's third time taking part. Every system transmitting telemetry under NATO's STANAG 4817 standard was integrated into DELTA, which kept operating without interruption despite unstable communications.
