articles.title: Trump defends Russian sanctions relief, lashes out at Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Trump defends Russian sanctions relief, lashes out at Zelenskyy
US president accuses Ukrainian leader of not wanting to end the war, as Zelenskyy speaks with Washington envoys.
United States President Donald Trump has defended sanction waivers for Russia, saying he wants to keep Moscow at the bargaining table and accusing his counterpart in Kyiv of not wanting to end the war in Ukraine.
Trump made the comments on Truth Social on Sunday in response to criticism of his decision to block numerous sanctions on Russia just days before they were due to take effect.
“My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” he said.
The move has triggered a significant diplomatic fallout between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy over the past week.
Zelenskyy said that waiving sanctions on Russia, which launched a full-scale invasion of its neighbour in 2022, “will hurt Ukraine”, telling NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday that it would strengthen Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war effort.
“We can’t compare me and Putin. He’s [an] aggressor. He occupied us. He killed adults and children, his soldiers. He’s a terrorist, and that’s why I hope that President Trump will be very clear with this position.”
Trump reiterated his claim that Zelenskyy does not want the war on his country to end, saying on Truth Social that Kyiv was launching attacks on diesel refineries in Russia despite knowing it was “seriously hurting the world diesel markets”.
“Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him… he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” Trump wrote.
Trump announced plans on October 9 for Russia to supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel to US and global markets to tackle fuel prices that have soared since the US and Israel launched war on Iran in late February. The move led Tehran to effectively close the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of global energy exports transited before the war.
Trump’s embrace of Russian energy has angered not only Kyiv, but also European partners and many US officials, who say the move rewards Moscow while it continues its four-and-a-half-year war against Ukraine.
US-Ukraine talks continue
The Ukrainian president said on X on Sunday that he has spoken with US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as part of “virtually non-stop communication” between the two countries’ teams aimed at the “next steps in diplomacy”.
“We are doing everything on our part to make this happen, and to ensure that America’s position is strong and helps bring peace closer. Peace that everyone, except Russia, has been waiting for over the past four and a half years,” Zelenskyy wrote.
Zelenskyy spoke with Witkoff and Kushner as Russia and Ukraine continued to strike each other’s energy sites, with Moscow leaving thousands without power, and Kyiv carrying out the largest drone attack on Russia, in St Petersburg, since the war began.

articles.title: What It Took to Deliver a Legendary F-117A Stealth Aircraft to the Smithsonian
articles.body:
EDWARDS AIR FORCE BASE, Ca.—The flat-black fuselage rolled forward on its landing gear, pulled from its hanger at Lockheed Martin’s secretive Skunk Works compound by an aircraft tug.
More than a mile away, a giant C-5M Super Galaxy waited, its nose cone open and waiting for its unique cargo. Against a desert backdrop, the dramatic angles of the wingless airframe cut an unmistakable silhouette, a shining example of America’s first stealth aircraft, this one dubbed “the Overachiever” because it was the only Nighthawk to fly in all four major conflicts in which the jets participated.
More than 40 years after the original YF-117 operational prototype flew test runs from the shadowy Lockheed facility, the Overachiever returned to its Palmdale birthplace for a $1 million refurbishment to look its best when it assumes its place in history alongside other iconic aircraft on permanent exhibit at the National Air and Space Museum’s Stephen F. Udvar-Hazy Center in Chantilly, Va., beside Washington Dulles International Airport.
Air & Space Forces Magazine was on hand to witness the F-117’s 2,254-mile journey across the United States as a passenger aboard the C-5M from Air Force Reserve Command’s 512th Airlift Wing.
Conceived to give the Air Force an edge against the Soviet Union in the 1970s, the radar-evading F-117 was developed to sneak past the Russian-made, radar-guided antiaircraft missiles that had so vexed the U.S. Air Force in Vietnam.
The aircraft’s faceted exterior design radically reduced the F-117’s radar cross section, allowing it to evade radar detection during testing. While their first use in combat, in 1989’s Operation Just Cause in Panama, had been a disappointment, the Nighthawks’ performance in Operation Desert Storm proved stunning: On Jan. 17, 1991, the Nighthawks flew unobserved into heavily defended Iraqi airspace and destroyed their targets to mark the opening salvo of the Gulf War.
“This aircraft was specifically designed to be able to penetrate heavily defended areas that have radar-based defenses … which gave it a huge tactical advantage on the battlefield,” Michael Hankins, curator of modern military aviation at the Udvar-Hazy Center, told Air & Space Forces Magazine. “This will be the [museum’s] first example of the earliest generation of stealth aircraft. A lot of new aircraft that are in service today—like the F-22 Raptor, the F-35 lightning—really built on the foundation that was set by the F-117.”
The Air Force officially retired its F-117 fleet in 2008 after the F-22 Raptor achieved initial operating capability in 2005. But Nighthawks remained in “flyable storage,”and since around 2020 have participated in exercises such as Red Flag and in undisclosed activities.
Securing The Overachiever for the Air and Space Museum was the result of months of coordination between the Air Force, the Smithsonian, and Lockheed. Jeffrey Corbets, who oversaw the plane’s restoration at the Skunk Works Special Systems department, said preparing Tail No. 818 to become a museum showpiece required months of tedious restoration work by a dedicated team of more than a dozen Skunk Works employees.
The specialists who did the work aren’t standard-issue aircraft technicians. “They’re kind of different people,” Corbets said. “The team that’s actually working the bulk of this also supports our U-2 program, so they’re really familiar with supporting some of our longer-term, historical legacy products.”
Because of its highly classified status, the F-117 could not fly into Dulles and taxi over to the Udvar-Hazy Center as some other historical aircraft have done. It had to be completely de-militarized, which involved stripping away its most guarded secrets, Corbets said. From late January to early August, the Skunk Works team bead-blasted off the jet’s radar absorbing coating, known as RAM, leaving bare metal. The unique edges on the wings and rudders were replaced with “all new fake edges,” Corbets added.
“It’s a lot of manual labor,” he explained. “The first thing you have to do is actually get access to all the connectors, the bolts, and whatnot that hold edges on” These were hidden beneath the stealth coating. “You have to very carefully dig out the RAM, so you can get to those to take them off. And then once you have all the edges removed, then we can actually go into a bead blasting type operation to get the rest of the coatings off.”
The de-mil process also involved removing classified technical “components” in the cockpit, said Corbets, who would not elaborate on the systems that were removed.
“The cockpit is mostly intact, so they have, I’d say, 95 percent of the avionics are still in there—the screens and the displays are still in there, the hub system is still in there, the ejection seat, etc., etc. To even the educated observer, it would look like an operational F-117,” Corbets said. “The museum wanted it to be as representative a configuration as we could leave it, so if it didn’t absolutely have to come out, we didn’t take it out.”
Other F-117s are already in museums, including at the Museum of the U.S. Air Force in Dayton, Ohio. Lockheed’s Skunk Works performed a similar job in 2019 so a Nighthawk could go on display at the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library and Museum in Simi Valley, Calif.
To fit the Nighthawk into the C-5 transport, the F-117’s wings had to be removed, secured to wheeled dollies and loaded separately onto the aircraft. Air Force loadmasters used an electric winch and cable to gently pull each dolly onto the ramp and back to the rear of the plane. Airmen completed the slow, tedious task in the desert heat without incident.
But loading The Overachiever’s freshly painted fuselage onto the plane, so it could be safely secured for flight, was not without surprises. The wings and fuselage together weighed about 24,000 pounds, an easy lift for the C-5, which has a maximum cargo capacity of 285,000 pounds—enough to carry not just one, but two M1A2 Abrams tanks.
But there’s more to moving a disabled plane than weight. A miscommunication during the restoration process meant the aircraft lacked the proper amount of bolt-on anchoring points when it was time to tie it down in the cargo bay. That meant special anchoring collars had to be attached to each of the three landing gear struts to keep the jet from shifting during flight.
“We decided to use the collars that we use on the struts to help secure it down, but in order for that to work, we had to raise the struts so we get the right angle to use the collar,” a maintenance technician said. Getting clearance to make raise each strut roughly four inches and mount the collars took time.
Air Force Reserve Senior Master Sgt. Vasean Townsend, a C-5 loadmaster for the past 13 years, said it was nothing he hadn’t seen before.
“Basically, one of the tie-down points was missing on each side,” said Townsend, who helped transport another F-117 some years earlier. “We as loadmasters have to find a way to create other tie-down points. “If something is missing … we’ve just got to be creative. That’s part of the job.”
With the problem solved, Lockheed staff and aircrew silently watched as The Overachiever was lashed down for its flight to Dulles.
For C-5 pilot Maj. Dean Mouritzen, the mission was “humbling.”
“This is my last flight in the military,” he said. “It’s my last mission, and doing something this—taking an F-117 to a museum and being able to tell my kids, my grandkids, that I was just one of the peons to take it some place where it’s going to sit forever—it’s pretty awesome.”
To Corbets and the Lockheed team, “it’s a little bit like watching a friend leave you, because obviously everyone’s been really excited to be part of the project, and now it’s going off to its new home.”
After hours in the air, the C-5 landed at Dulles and finally lowered its ramp at 8:38 p.m. local time, and the crew quickly offloaded The Overachiever’s fuselage and wings onto the chilly ramp by 9:16 p.m. From there, museum officials whisked it away to the nearby Mary Baker Engen Restoration Hangar, where it will be reassembled before going on exhibit.
The Overachiever was scheduled to be unveiled for public viewing at the Udvar-Hazy Center late this month.
“The current plan is to have this airplane on the floor next to all the other aircraft in our Cold War modern military section,” Hankins said. “It’ll be right next to the F-15 Eagle, which it flew with during Operation Desert Storm. There’s a lot of a lot of historical significance there to having those two together on the floor.”
“This is a really big step and a very historic and important aircraft in the history of U.S. aviation,” said Hankins, who said he had been working on the project for “several years.”
“We’re so excited to have this on the floor,” he said, “and be able to show the public why this airplane is so unique and special and important and iconic.”
Shaun Barrows, senior multimedia manager at Air & Space Forces Association, contributed to this story.

articles.title: Tehran's dilemma: Is there a growing Baloch insurgency in Iran?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Tehran's dilemma: Is there a growing Baloch insurgency in Iran?
Armed clashes in Iran’s southeastern province of Sistan-Baluchestan have intensified in recent weeks, reaching their highest level in a decade.
With the US-Israel war threatening to enter an even more volatile phase, such tensions have raised growing concern in Tehran.
At the centre of the escalation is the emergence of a coalition of diverse Baloch militant factions, the Popular Fighters Front (PFF), also known by its Persian acronym JMM (Jebhe-ye-Mobarezin-e Mardomi).
Consisting of Jaish-ul-Adl, PADA Baluch, Harakate Nasr Baluchestan, and the Mohammad Rasulullah Brigade, the militant umbrella was formed in December 2025.
Though they claim to fight for all of Iran, which they say has been “held hostage,” at least one faction among them has advocated Baloch separatism in the past.
But despite their differing political ambitions, the groups share a conservative Sunni Muslim identity, providing common ground in Shia-dominant Iran where the Sunni population is less than 9%.
Tehran's security dilemma
Suddenly, Sistan-Baluchestan has become dangerous.
Since January 2026, at least 37 armed attacks have been reported on police stations, military bases, and checkpoints, while security patrols have been targeted as they move through cities.
Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) personnel are a primary target. There have been high-ranking assassinations, and last month, a regime-linked Sunni cleric was shot dead.
If this continues, the Iranian government may have to send large reinforcements from other parts of the country to contain the unrest, stretching the security infrastructure at a time when it is prepared for a return to war.
Such instability in Sistan-Baluchestan could have consequences for Iran in the coming months.
As per the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), approximately 70 armed confrontations took place between Iranian security forces and armed groups in Sistan and Baluchestan during 2026, the highest annual level in a decade. Thirteen occurred in the past two weeks alone.
ACLED’s assessments suggest that although Tehran has intensified efforts to dismantle the militant network, raids have often turned into “prolonged battles”, with some lasting as long as nine hours.
Pointing towards a more entrenched insurgency, it says that the “key risk” would be convergence, and a full-scale resumption of the US-Israeli war on Iran could “stretch Tehran’s security forces thin.”
Meanwhile, the human toll is also mounting, according to the US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA), with at least 94 people killed and 33 wounded in 63 armed incidents between 31 March and 10 October.
On 13 October, more than 20 Fatemiyoun brigade members were reported killed or wounded in fighting that lasted for seven hours in the mountainous Taftan area.
The Fatemiyoun are an Iran-backed Shia militia composed largely of Afghan fighters and organised to fight alongside the IRGC. Their reported involvement underscores the extent to which Tehran is drawing on its wider security network to confront the violence.
The use of drones, artillery, and armoured vehicles by government forces in recent clashes further indicates the intensity of the fighting and raises concerns about the consequences of expanded operations in populated areas.
Consequently, Tehran faces a difficult strategic dilemma, and while a forceful response could disrupt militant networks, it may result in deepening local alienation.
While the Iranian government is not losing its grip, chronic instability constrains its ability to respond to war.
Rebranding a Baloch uprising?
Ridden by poverty, plagued by unemployment, and the least developed region in Iran, Sistan-Baluchestan has been tense for decades.
Since their unification as the PFF, however, the region’s militants have changed their narrative, pointing not only to Baloch grievances but also calling for broader political change in Iran.
So far, it cannot be determined whether this consolidation has increased their capabilities, but the ongoing war with Washington has created space for the militants to regroup in Iran.
Dr Farzan Sabet, an Iran expert at the Geneva Graduate Institute, told The New Arab that when “conditions for ordinary people are deteriorating, and the regime is perceived as vulnerable, there are surges of opposition hoping to overthrow the regime, or extract concessions”.
He highlighted the convergence during the 12-day war in June 2025 amid the so-called ‘Lion and Sun’ protests among “leading opposition organisations including the nationwide Pahlavi movement, the coalition of political forces of Iranian Kurdistan in majority Kurdish-speaking areas of Iran, and the PFF in Sistan-Baluchestan”.
Sabet said that Iranian security forces in this province have “historically been poorly equipped and trained, experiencing greater disarray due to the assassination of Iranian security leaders and personnel” during the war.
Militancy in the province has also received a boost from deteriorating material conditions, the dire state of human rights, a disproportionate degree of executions and violations, and, possibly, foreign support.
According to Sabet, the political dynamics in Sistan-Baluchestan are often distinct from those in the core of the country, and there are fewer sensitive population centres and economic hubs.
“It is seen as less of a threat than, say, a comparable event in Tehran or another major city in the core, and there is a lower risk that discontent and instability spread from the periphery to the core than the other way around,” he added.
The impact of such peripheral insurgencies is usually geographically and politically contained in Iran, even though the PFF is “targeting its discourse toward the broader Iranian nation”.
However, “given the recent successes of Balochi militants, the regime may want to surge further security forces into the area,” Sabet said, such as the Fatemiyoun Division - an IRGC-backed militia of Afghan Shia whose members died in recent clashes.
The US-Israel war has added a new dimension to the fragile situation in Sistan-Baluchestan as Iran’s security establishment has diverted away resources and armed groups have seen it as “an opportunity to intensify their activities and test the state’s capacity to respond”, Babak Vahdad, an independent researcher and Iran analyst, told The New Arab.
In his view, the escalation is not an immediate threat to the survival of the Islamic Republic, as Baloch militancy remains geographically concentrated and is not a broader national uprising.
But the situation has exposed “some of the structural weaknesses of the Iranian state, particularly its difficult relationship with ethnic and religious minorities, and a predominantly military response may contain the insurgency in the short term without addressing its underlying causes”.
Meanwhile, according to Iran’s narrative, “certain regional actors” might be encouraging instability there to “divert Tehran’s military and security resources away from the main confrontation in the Gulf, possibly even preparing the ground for a future military attack against Iran”, Vahdad added.
Fractious borders, wider risks
The security issue is made worse by geography. Across mountainous terrain, the porous 900 km Iran-Pakistan border stretches from a tripoint with Afghanistan to the northern Arabian Sea, and policing it is an arduous task for Tehran as deserted, interconnected frontiers with low populations create fertile ground for armed groups and mercenaries.
Even the Pakistani province of Baluchistan across the border has separatist outfits, mercenaries, a smuggling nexus, and long-standing political and socio-economic issues.
Currently, border crossings along the Pakistan-Iran border have been closed by Islamabad.
Naveed Ali Sheikh, an Islamabad-based military analyst, told The New Arab that Pakistan has been facing terrorist attacks originating from the Iranian border region of Sistan and Baluchestan, where banned militant outfits operate and carry out “hit-and-run” [back across the border] attacks.
These groups have targeted Iranian and Pakistani government forces, as well as civilian infrastructure, he said. Noting that a surge in such attacks was observed recently, Sheikh said the border required better security infrastructure, upgraded surveillance systems, and more effective mechanisms to prevent further incursions.
However, border security was not the primary reason behind the recent closure of cross-border trade, as “shadow banking networks are being used by smugglers and black-market operators, which the United States alleges are helping finance Iran's sanctioned military establishment”.
And the temporary closure of border crossings may be intended to manage the anticipated backlog of transactions and documentation if the banking and trade standstill continues.
Sabena Siddiqui is a foreign affairs journalist, lawyer and geopolitical analyst specialising in modern China, the Belt and Road Initiative, the Middle East, and South Asia.
Follow her on X: @sabena_siddiqi

articles.title: Three-Barrel Gatling Gun and Guided Missiles: Slovenia Unveils New Skythunder Air Defense System
articles.body:
Slovenian company Valhalla Turrets has announced a new version of the Skythunder air defense system, armed with a 20 mm M197 Gatling gun and 70 mm laser-guided missiles.
The manufacturer announced the system on the social media platform X.
The new system is designed to engage UAVs and other low-altitude aerial targets and protect critical infrastructure against mass attacks.
The system’s primary armament will be the 20 mm M197 Gatling three-barrel automatic cannon manufactured by General Dynamics. It will be complemented by guided 70 mm missiles designed to engage targets at longer ranges.
According to the cannon’s manufacturer, the M197 is a lightweight, three-barrel variant of the six-barrel M61A1 Vulcan. It has a rate of fire of up to 1,500 rounds per minute, weighs approximately 60 kg, and achieves a muzzle velocity of 1,030 m/s.
The cannon also powers the U.S. Marine Corps’ AH-1Z Viper attack helicopters.
The system will also feature 360-degree radar coverage, as well as automated target detection and tracking capabilities.
In June, the company presented another system configuration, the Skythunder 300, at the Eurosatory 2026 exhibition.
It builds on the technologies of the Mangart 30 remotely operated weapon station and includes a Northrop Grumman MK44S Bushmaster 30 mm automatic cannon, a separate turret mounting a Dillon Aero M134D 7.62 mm six-barrel machine gun, and Arnold Defense LAND-LGR4 70 mm guided rockets.
According to the published technical specifications, the Skythunder 300 is equipped with three Hensoldt Spexer 2000 radars, providing 360-degree airspace surveillance.
According to the manufacturer, the 30 mm cannon can engage larger UAVs out to 2.5 km, while the machine gun can engage small drones out to 1 km. The missile armament has an engagement range of up to 6 km.
However, equivalent performance figures for the new 20 mm Skythunder configuration have not yet been released.
Valhalla Turrets is also developing other remotely operated weapon stations for air defense systems.
In June 2025, Militarnyi reported on testing of the Wolf 25 AD anti-aircraft system, developed at Ukraine’s request. It is equipped with a weapon station manufactured by the Slovenian company and armed with a 25 mm Oerlikon KBA cannon.
In October of the same year, the Wolf 25 AD system was deployed in Ukraine to carry out air defense missions.

articles.body:
- Category

Russia Admits Its Air Defenses Cannot Shield Vast Industrial Empire From Ukrainian Drone Strikes
Russia cannot provide comprehensive air defense coverage for its vast industrial infrastructure, with many of the country’s largest factories and production complexes too extensive to be fully protected against Ukrainian drone strikes.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Alexander Shokhin, head of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs (RSPP), acknowledged these limitations, according to Russian state news agency TASS on October 17. He explained that the scale and layout of Soviet-era industrial facilities present significant challenges for Russia’s air defense systems.
Many of Russia’s largest industrial enterprises were originally designed during the Soviet period with the possibility of nuclear war in mind. Production facilities were deliberately spread across large areas to reduce the risk of an entire industrial complex being destroyed in a single attack.
However, the same design principles have created vulnerabilities in modern warfare, particularly as Ukraine continues using long-range drones to strike industrial and military-related infrastructure deep inside Russian territory.
Metallurgical plants, chemical factories, and other major industrial facilities can stretch across several kilometers, making it difficult to establish comprehensive protection over their entire territory.
Shokhin noted that Soviet planners placed individual workshops far apart to improve the chances of maintaining production following a nuclear strike. While this approach offered certain advantages, it also required extensive infrastructure connecting different sections of industrial complexes.
These dispersed facilities now present a major challenge for Russia, as protecting individual production buildings does not necessarily guarantee the security of the wider industrial site.
The acknowledgment comes amid Ukraine’s continuing campaign of long-range strikes against Russian oil refineries, military production facilities, airfields, chemical plants, and other strategically important infrastructure.
In September, five Russian oil refineries, including the Moscow Oil Refinery, suspended processing operations following damage and fires.
On October 18, Ukrainian drones also struck the Petersburg Oil Terminal, triggering a fire, while separate attacks targeted a VKontakte data center and electrical infrastructure in the surrounding Leningrad region.

articles.title: US miscalculated Iran’s resilience in war: Basij chief
articles.body:
Speaking at a meeting in Tehran on Sunday, Taeb said the United States and Israel had expected Iran to capitulate within days or weeks, but the Iranian nation and Armed Forces had stood firm.
“They thought that if they could not achieve their objectives in three days, Iran’s resilience in the war would last no more than six weeks,” Taeb said.
He said the US and Israel had expected Iran to run short of ammunition and missiles, face economic disruption and experience domestic security pressures, forcing it to negotiate from a position of weakness.
“Those assessments proved wrong,” Taeb said, adding that the United States and Israel had also faced limitations in ammunition supplies and air defense capabilities, including dwindling stocks of THAAD interceptor missiles.
Taeb said Iran’s missile operations had become increasingly effective as the war progressed, with a growing proportion of missiles reaching their intended targets in Israeli-occupied territories.
He added that the United States and Israel had sought a ceasefire through European and regional intermediaries, expecting Iran to make concessions in subsequent negotiations.
Taeb said Washington and Tel Aviv were then forced to shift their strategy from direct, full-scale warfare toward proxy forces, regional and international alliances, and economic pressure after Iran gained full control over the Strait of Hormuz.
He described the conflict as a contest of endurance, stressing that the closure of the Strait of Hormuz had also imposed significant costs on the US and global economies.
Citing polls, Taeb said more than 70% of Americans believed the war with Iran had brought their country no meaningful benefits while imposing heavy costs. He also pointed to rising diesel prices and transportation costs as factors increasing the economic burden on American households, adding that European countries were beginning to experience the consequences as well.
Taeb called on Iranians to support the Armed Forces and strengthen the country’s deterrence capabilities, warning that any renewed aggression would be met with an unpredictable response.

articles.title: Two killed and seven injured in Russian strike on Kryvyi Rih
articles.body:
Two killed and seven injured in Russian strike on Kryvyi Rih
Two men have been killed and seven people, including a 15-year-old boy, have been injured after Russian forces attacked an industrial business in the Pokrovskyi district of Kryvyi Rih.
Source: Oleksandr Vilkul, Head of Kryvyi Rih Defence Council; Oleksandr Hanzha, Head of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Military Administration; Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Prosecutor's Office
Quote from Vilkul: "Sadly, two men have been killed by an enemy strike using a Banderol [drone-launched cruise missile] on the Pokrovskyi district. Seven more people have been injured, including a 15-year-old boy. One 39-year-old man is in a serious condition. Four others are in a moderate condition."
Details: Vilkul said that the Russians struck using a Banderol. He released the figure of seven injured as of 12:30, having previously reported three and subsequently four casualties.
The attack also damaged 17 multi-storey buildings, shattering nearly 50 windows and damaging three roofs. An industrial building, a post office, a bank, a college, shops and cars were also affected.
Inspections of the damage are ongoing.
An assistance headquarters has been set up at the school closest to the impact site, where residents can receive building materials for emergency repairs and submit applications for municipal financial aid.
Prosecutors are documenting the aftermath of the Russian war crime.
Under the procedural guidance of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Prosecutor's Office, criminal proceedings have been initiated under Article 438 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine concerning the commission of a war crime.

Kyiv • UNN
Since the beginning of 2026, courts have handed down 75 convictions for disseminating videos of shelling and air defense operations. The SBU also exposed three Kyiv residents.
Since the beginning of 2026, 75 people in Ukraine have received court sentences for disseminating photos and videos of enemy attacks, including materials about the location and operation of Ukrainian air defense. This was reported by the Security Service of Ukraine, UNN writes.
Thus, over the past week, the Security Service exposed three Kyiv residents who had published the positions of air defense units. They are currently suspects under Article 114-2 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (unauthorized dissemination of information about the Armed Forces of Ukraine or other military formations)
The SBU once again emphasizes that the unauthorized dissemination of information about the geolocations, combat operations of the Defense Forces, and the aftermath of enemy attacks not only helps the enemy prepare and adjust repeated strikes, but also provides Russian propaganda with new opportunities to work against our state.
The Security Service of Ukraine urges citizens not to film or disseminate photos and videos of enemy attacks. In particular, it is prohibited to publish content documenting the operation of Ukrainian air defense, occupiers' strikes on military facilities and critical infrastructure, the movement of equipment and personnel of the Defense Forces, and so on
The Ukrainian special service also calls on people to report any information about such offenses by calling 1516, emailing [email protected], or writing to the "Spaly FSB Officer" chatbot or t.me/spaly_fsb_bot

articles.title: French Nuclear Submarine Rubis Prepared for Launch
articles.body:
In France, the nuclear submarine Rubis, the fifth in the Suffren class, was moved from the construction hall to a special launch site.
The French Directorate General of Armaments (DGA) reported this.
This stage took place on October 16 at the Naval Group shipyard in Cherbourg. The submarine is scheduled to be launched in 2027.
After its launch, the submarine will undergo sea trials before joining the French Navy. The Rubis is scheduled to be handed over to the fleet in 2028.
The Rubis is part of the Barracuda program, which calls for the construction of six Suffren-class nuclear-powered attack submarines.
They are intended to replace the previous-generation Rubis-class submarines, which the French Navy began receiving in the 1980s.
The French nuclear-powered submarine Rubis was ordered on May 7, 2018, as part of the Barracuda program, which calls for the construction of six Suffren-class nuclear-powered attack submarines for the French Navy.
At the same time, Naval Group is developing a separate Orka project for the Netherlands based on the Barracuda family, which also includes the French Suffren-class submarines.
On September 30, 2024, the Netherlands signed a contract with the French company to deliver four Orka submarines. They are intended to replace the previous-generation Walrus-class submarines, which the Dutch Navy has been operating since the 1990s.
Unlike the nuclear-powered Suffren-class submarines, the Dutch submarines will not have a nuclear propulsion system. The project calls for modern battery systems.
Dutch industry will also be involved in the program. Local companies will supply hull structures, living quarters modules, hydraulic systems, and other equipment. The Dutch side has allocated approximately 1 billion euros in orders for its own companies.
Under the plan, the Dutch Navy is set to receive the first submarine in 2033 and the last by 2037.
Specifications:
Displacement: 4,700 metric tons on the surface and 5,300 metric tons submerged.
Length: 99 m.
Hull diameter: 8.8 m.
Maximum speed: approximately 25 knots (46 km/h) submerged.
Maximum diving depth: over 300 m.
Endurance: approximately 70 days.
Crew: 65 sailors; the submarine can also carry special operations forces.
Propulsion system: YASU, K15 reactor.
Armament:
Torpedo armament: F21 heavy torpedoes for engaging submarines and surface ships.
Anti-ship armament: Exocet SM39 missiles.
Strike armament: MdCN sea-launched cruise missiles for engaging land targets at long range.
Additional armament: sea mines.
Torpedo tubes: four 533-mm torpedo tubes.

articles.title: Hundreds arrested in Paris as rioters defy Macron (VIDEOS)
articles.body:
Hundreds arrested in Paris as rioters defy Macron (VIDEOS)
Nearly 350 people were arrested in Paris on Sunday and overnight amid violent unrest sweeping France despite President Emmanuel Macron’s appeals for calm, the authorities said on Monday.
Hundreds of thousands protested rising living costs and education funding cuts over the weekend, with demonstrations escalating into clashes with police, arson and looting.
The violence erupted Saturday as Yellow Vest demonstrations merged with student protests that began last month at a high school in Creteil, near Paris, over teacher shortages and deteriorating facilities. The movement has since broadened into protests against inequality and rising living costs, with labor unions joining in opposition to the government’s proposed 2027 budget and spending cuts.
Despite Macron’s Friday appeal for “calm and respect,” Paris endured two days of rioting. On Sunday, protesters clashed with police near Place de la Republique as vehicles and trach cans burned, shops were looted and officers deployed tear gas and water cannons.
Footage showed charred wreckage, shattered storefronts, smashed advertising signs and graffiti-covered businesses.
🇫🇷 Paris? Its looks like a third world country 😢 Writer: Samuel https://t.co/rbd0fwCwm6
— Mario Nawfal (@MarioNawfal) October 19, 2026
A crowd also attacked RT Arabic correspondent Wafa Fakkani while she was filming the protests. Her cameraman captured the incident before the crew escaped and resumed reporting.
A day prior, violence hit some of the capital’s wealthiest shopping districts, where luxury retailers were targeted by vandals and looters. Paris Mayor Emmanuel Gregoire said “entire streets” had been “systematically devastated.”
Galeries Lafayette in Paris is being looted tonight. It’s the French equivalent of Harrods in London or Bergdorf Goodman in NYC https://t.co/F5jZU4bswZ
— Visegrád 24 (@visegrad24) October 17, 2026
Clashes also erupted in Marseille, Lyon, Lille, Bordeaux, Angers, and Limoges, damaging businesses and public buildings. Alain Di Crescenzo, head of the CCI France chamber of commerce network, estimated that more than 2,000 businesses were affected, with damage reaching “hundreds of millions of euros.”
Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin put nationwide turnout at 550,000, including 110,000 in Paris, while organizing trade unions, including the CGT, and student groups estimated that 800,000 people took part. Darmanin told France 2 on Monday that, in total, more than 2,330 people had been detained over the weekend, including around 855 in the capital. Nearly 1,000 police officers and gendarmes were reportedly injured.
Although the worst rioting had subsided by Monday morning, students and union activists blocked access to the iconic Louvre Museum, denouncing “police repression.” Footage showed demonstrators gathering outside the museum’s glass pyramid after passing security, prompting its temporary closure.
🚨🇫🇷 ALERTE INFO ! "ACAB, ACAB, ACAB !" Devant la pyramide du Louvre à Paris, des étudiants d’écoles d’art et de culture manifestent et bloquent l’entrée du musée. (@JBSemerdjian / Le Figaro) https://t.co/zpH7KcHPX4
— Impact (@ImpactMediaFR) October 19, 2026
Action and reaction
Politicians across France’s political spectrum blamed Macron and his government for the unrest, accusing the administration of undermining public services and failing to maintain order.
Marine Le Pen, who leads first-round polling for the 2027 presidential election, called Macron a president “without credibility or authority,” describing his administration as “a government on its last legs.” Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of the left-wing France Unbowed party, blamed “ten disastrous years” of Macron weakening public services. The mayors of Paris, Marseille and Limoges accused Interior Minister Laurent Nunez and police commanders of incompetence in maintaining public order.
Nunez initially blamed “opportunistic troublemakers” for the unrest, but admitted Monday that police had suffered “a loss of control” due to poor planning. He said he offered his resignation Sunday, but Macron refused, instead ordering a new policing strategy, faster deployment and transparency over intelligence failures. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu ordered partial curfews in several cities.
Macron condemned the rioting, insisting there was “no place for violence” and promising punishment for vandals and looters. In a televised address Sunday, he said “nothing justifies” the destruction, but pledged to address students’ complaints over school conditions. Meanwhile, he portrayed the unrest as an attempt by political opponents to disrupt the democratic process and influence voters ahead of the presidential election in six months.
Despite the unrest, Macron departed on Monday for a three-day visit to the Middle East, leaving his government to deal with the fallout at home.
The crisis comes as Macron’s approval ratings hit record lows. An October Ipsos BVA-CESI poll for La Tribune Dimanche put his approval at 15%, with 82% disapproving, the lowest since he took office in 2017. An Ifop survey recorded 17% approval and 83% dissaproval. Le Pen leads first-round polling for the April 2027 election with 32-36% support.
Protests spread beyond France
France was not alone in facing unrest over the weekend, as tens of thousands protested living costs, housing shortages and government policies across Europe. Demonstrations in several countries escalated into clashes, vandalism and arson.
In Belgium, students opposed rising education costs and reforms they say threaten access to higher education. In Italy, marches against living costs and wars turned violent in Milan and Bologna. In Portugal, tens of thousands protested low wages, rising rents and housing shortages. In Albania, student-led protests entered a fifth day, with demonstrators demanding Prime Minister Edi Rama’s resignation over corruption allegations, unemployment and poor prospects for young people.
Former Austrian Chancellor Sebastian Kurz described the unrest across Europe over the weekend as resembling “scenes from a civil war,” warning in a post on X that “we risk seeing the same scenes soon in Berlin, Vienna and Munich.”
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov described the European unrest as “bordering on chaos,” calling it a major crisis.
“It’s hard to say whether the crisis is systemic or not, but it is obvious that it is a big crisis,” he told reporters on Monday.
Some experts who spoke to RT linked the unrest to EU’s confrontation with Russia. Italian journalist Davide Carbonaro called the severing of economic ties with Moscow “economic and political suicide,” saying that young Europeans felt betrayed and deprived of a future. Serbian journalist Nebojsa Malic accused Western leaders of scapegoating Russia to hide their failures.
RT’s Chay Bowes examined how Europe’s continued support for Ukraine and sanctions against Russia are fueling economic pressures and public discontent as unrest spreads across the continent.

articles.title: Musk’s tech used in strike that killed Russian students – investigators
articles.body:
Musk’s tech used in strike that killed Russian students – investigators
Two of at least seven Ukrainian drones used in a strike on a Russian college which killed 21 people earlier this year were equipped with Starlink terminals, investigators have established.
The nighttime attack on a college dormitory in Starobelsk in the Lugansk People’s Republic took place in May and was classified as a deliberate terrorist attack by Russia’s Investigative Committee. Its chairman, Aleksandr Bastrykin, discussed findings from the investigation in an interview with RIA Novosti published on Monday.
“The Ukrainian armed forces used at least seven drones identified as Fire Point 1, Fire Point 2, Sichen and RZ-100, two of which were controlled via the Starlink satellite communication system,” he said.
The strike also injured scores of civilians and caused an estimated $14.5 million in damage, according to Bastrykin. Investigators identified Robert Brodi, commander of Ukraine’s drone forces, Oleg Ivashchenko, head of Ukrainian military intelligence, and Andrey Klimenko, commander of the 414th drone brigade, as the main suspects, he added.
Kiev’s use of Starlink in territory that Washington recognizes as part of Ukraine became a source of friction with the US this month after Ukrainian officials claimed new restrictions had been imposed on faster-moving platforms. If true, the limitations would disrupt so-called “middle-strike” operations against targets behind the front line but within Starlink’s permitted coverage area, including Starobelsk.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has denied imposing such restrictions, accusing Vladimir Zelensky of making false claims and suggesting the Ukrainian leader does not know “what he’s talking about.” Starlink owner Elon Musk has also rejected the Ukrainian allegations.
Rubio further stated that Ukraine has no access to Starshield, Starlink’s military-grade sister service.
Bloomberg reported that Kiev had obtained access to Starshield years earlier, with a contract signed in 2024 to expand connectivity through regular Starlink terminals. Recent Reuters reporting suggests Starshield access remained active as of last week, albeit with new restrictions affecting its use in Ukrainian drone operations.

articles.title: Iran to answer 'mother of all bombs' with 'father of bombs': senior IRGC commander
articles.body:
Iran to answer 'mother of all bombs' with 'father of bombs': senior IRGC commander
TEHRAN – Deputy Coordinator of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps, Brigadier General Mohammad Reza Naqdi, has warned the United States against any military miscalculation against Iran, saying Tehran would respond to Washington's "mother of all bombs" with the "father of bombs."
Speaking on Sunday afternoon at the "Self-Sacrificers for Iran" rally in Sari, Naqdi was referring to recent threats by US President Donald Trump to use the GBU-43/B massive ordnance, widely known as the mother of all bombs, against Iran.
"If you make a wrong move, we will come for you with the father of bombs, and all your assets will be at risk," Naqdi said.
He described Trump's remarks as a sign of fatigue and depleted patience in confronting a nation that resists pressure, arguing that the threats reflect the difficulty of dealing with Iran.
Criticizing the threats to use heavy bombs, Naqdi said the enemy had already used heavy weaponry in the past, but those actions had failed to achieve US objectives. He also claimed that parts of the technology used in some of the weapons deployed against Iran are now in the hands of Iranian forces and are under examination.
Warning of the consequences of any military action, he said any miscalculation and escalation could jeopardize the security of US investments and economic activities in the region, including American technology, artificial intelligence and oil companies operating in the region.
On Iran's deterrent power, Naqdi said the country's defense capability in land and naval domains is not limited to military hardware alone, stressing that the will of a people who stand to defend their land is a key element of that power.
"The enemy may be able to take certain actions, but the fundamental question is whether it can achieve its goals. Our defensive readiness and the will of the Iranian people have complicated the enemy's calculations," he said.
He added that US military movements in the region have been affected by Iran's defense capabilities.
Naqdi said such threats may pursue different objectives, including creating division among the people, weakening the resolve of officials and reducing the readiness of the Armed Forces. He stressed the need to preserve national unity, stay vigilant against psychological warfare, and prevent internal disputes.
Maintaining the country's defense preparedness, solidarity between the people and officials, and cohesion of the Armed Forces play a decisive role in countering foreign threats, he said, adding that threats should not cause any doubt in defending national interests.

Putin Wants Trump and Xi to Decide Ukraine’s Future at Three-Way Summit in China, WSJ Reports
Russian leader Vladimir Putin has proposed holding a trilateral summit with US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in November to discuss the war in Ukraine and pursue a potential settlement favorable to Moscow, according to Suspilne on October 19, citing The Wall Street Journal.
The proposed meeting would take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, scheduled for November 18–19 in Shenzhen, China, the newspaper reported.

According to one source, Putin raised the proposal during a phone conversation with Trump on October 9, during which the two leaders reportedly reached an agreement on US purchases of Russian diesel fuel and assistance in facilitating its sales on international markets.
Peskov confirmed that discussions about a possible trilateral meeting were underway but stressed that neither the format nor the agenda had been finalized.
However, a senior US official said Trump had not agreed to participate in the proposed summit. The official suggested that the American president might nevertheless be receptive to the idea, given his stated commitment to fulfilling his campaign promise to resolve the war in Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Russian officials have reportedly presented the proposal to Beijing through diplomatic channels. According to sources cited by the newspaper, Chinese representatives indicated they would not oppose the meeting if Trump supported the initiative.
According to Suspilne, for Moscow, the proposed summit represents an opportunity to reinforce Russia’s position among the world's major powers while potentially shaping negotiations over Ukraine without direct European participation.
The Kremlin views Europe as a major obstacle to achieving its objectives in Ukraine, making a trilateral format involving Washington and Beijing particularly attractive to Moscow, the outlet reported.
The potential summit could also strengthen Xi’s efforts to position China as an influential diplomatic mediator, particularly if Beijing hosts discussions involving the leaders of the United States and Russia.
However, the proposed format presents diplomatic challenges for China, whose officials reportedly fear that discussions about Ukraine could overshadow Beijing’s broader objectives for the APEC summit.
According to the report, Chinese authorities are concerned that the war in Ukraine, which they regard as a secondary geopolitical issue in the context of the summit, could divert attention from their plans to showcase China's regional influence.
A trilateral meeting could also draw Beijing more directly into diplomatic efforts surrounding the war and provoke criticism from European governments already concerned about China's increasingly close relationship with Moscow.
The discussions come amid renewed debate over Washington’s approach to pressuring Russia into negotiations, particularly following Trump's decision to delay additional sanctions against Moscow.
According to BBC News on October 19, the US president blocked several sanctions targeting Russia just two days before they were scheduled to take effect, arguing that further economic restrictions could jeopardize ongoing peace efforts.
Trump defended the decision as necessary to preserve the possibility of a negotiated settlement. Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed concern that Washington’s recent actions increasingly appeared to place pressure on Kyiv to accept Moscow’s demands rather than intensify pressure on Russia.

Russia Keeps Attacking, but Ukraine Has Liberated More Territory Than Moscow Captured Since Autumn
Ukrainian forces have liberated more territory than Russian troops have managed to capture since the beginning of autumn, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said following a briefing on the frontline situation by Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Mykhailo Drapatyi.

articles.title: No new outsourcing at Fylingdales, minister says
articles.body:
The Ministry of Defence has refused to publish a risk assessment of private sector involvement in running the Solid State Phased Array Radar at RAF Fylingdales, saying the recent contract activity continues arrangements that have been in place for years, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Mark Pritchard, the Conservative member for The Wrekin, asked whether a risk assessment of outsourcing the operation and maintenance of the radar would be published.
Louise Sandher-Jones, Parliamentary Under-Secretary and Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “Private-sector support to the Solid State Phased Array Radar at RAF Fylingdales is longstanding. The recent contract activity represents the continuation and re-let of existing support arrangements, rather than a new decision to outsource the capability.
“The contractual re-lets were subject to the Ministry of Defence’s established investment, commercial, security, safety and risk-assurance processes. Operational command of, and accountability for, the radar remain with the Ministry of Defence. Contractor personnel provide defined operational, maintenance and sustainment support within established contractual, security and technical governance arrangements.”
RAF Fylingdales stands on the North York Moors and has provided ballistic missile early warning since 1963, originally through three radomes that gave the station its nickname of the golf balls. They were replaced in 1992 by the present solid state phased array, a truncated pyramid with three faces each covering 120 degrees, which watches continuously without moving parts. The station feeds the United States Ballistic Missile Early Warning System as well as British users, and contributes to space surveillance.

articles.title: Trump’s Policies Upping the Pressure on Zelensky
articles.body:
Ten days after announcing his diesel deal with Vladimir Putin, criticism of Donald Trump is mounting. The US President has now called on Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian refineries and is stepping up the pressure on President Zelensky. Europe’s press debates whether Trump is thus promoting Russia’s interests, and how Europe should respond.
The end of the West

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Former EU Commissioner Paolo Gentiloni (Italy) fears the worst in La Repubblica:
“Over the last ten days, Donald Trump first struck a deal with Putin on exports of Russian diesel, then called for Urkaine’s attacks on Russian refineries to cease, and finally scrapped the new package of sanctions against Moscow passed by the US Senate. Desperate decisions. And pointless too, given that it was the war in the Gulf that triggered the surge in prices. But their pointlessness does not make them any less serious. Europeans find themselves confronted with a US President who presented himself as a ‘neutral’ party between the attacked and the attacker but now seems to have chosen to side with the attacker. And if Trump openly sides with Putin, what will remain of the West?”
US president overemotional
There may be subjective reasons behind Trump’s behaviour, political scientist Abbas Gallyamov suggests on Facebook (Russia) :
“Trump undoubtedly has rational motives. In particular, the desire to bring down fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections. But his constant quest to find yet another excuse for attacking Zelensky comes across as far too emotional. ... Trump needs to prove to himself that by acting against Ukraine’s interests, he is doing the right thing. After all, acknowledging the legitimacy of Zelensky’s actions would mean calling his own decisions into question. It’s far easier to portray Zelensky as a bad person who only has himself to blame for what is happening now.”
Russian Airports Begin Checking Military Registration Statuses, Activists Report
Europeans must stand firm
Ukraine cannot simply ignore the pressure from Washington, argues Der Tagesspiegel (Germany) :
“While it no longer receives direct financial aid from Washington, it remains dependent on the US for air defence, satellites and reconnaissance. Even before Trump’s latest interference the Ukrainians were facing their harshest winter since the start of the full-scale Russian invasion. Now it’s likely to be even harsher. The Europeans must therefore stand firm, continue to support Ukraine and make it clear to Trump that this approach will not bring peace, but at best a Ukrainian defeat followed by civil war.”
Hesitant Europe is the real problem
In the Sunday Times (UK), columnist Matthew Syed counters the criticism of Donald Trump’s deal with Vladimir Putin:
“I recognise that the diesel deal was designed to distract from his calamitous war in Iran. I know he doesn’t give a fig about Ukraine, justice or sovereignty. But given his accurate conclusion that Europe will never give Ukraine what it takes to win, what’s the point of one, two or four more years of a frozen front line, while thousands more Ukrainians perish (more Russian soldiers are dying each day than the UK lost over the entire Iraq war, not that Putin cares) when we will end up in much the same place?”

articles.title: EU paid Russia 682 million euros for steel in eight months, with slab loophole keeping money flowing, and big consumers lobbying to keep it open — analysis
articles.body:
Four years of sanctions have not closed the door through which Russian metal still reaches Europe. The EU imported 1.6 million tons of Russian iron and steel products in the first eight months of 2026, paying 682 million euros, down 54% in value year on year, GMK Center, a Ukrainian-based consulting company, reports, citing Eurostat data.
Every euro spent on Russian metal is revenue for a state waging war on Ukraine, and the EU has banned most of it: pig iron, direct-reduced iron, iron ore and ferroalloys. Yet one category still flows almost untouched: semi-finished steel, mostly slabs, which made up 97.8% of the imports, or 1.56 million tons worth 670 million euros.
Volumes dropped 55% year on year after the full ban on Russian pig iron and DRI took effect on 1 January 2026, and no pig iron, ferroalloys, iron ore, or DRI reached the EU from Russia in the period, the center found. Iron ore and ferroalloys fall under sectoral limits, and the largest Russian producers are subject to corporate sanctions.
The slab loophole that keeps the money flowing
Slabs are the gap in the wall. Belgium took 767,700 tons of Russian semi-finished steel, nearly half the EU total, and Italy 191,800 tons, the center said.
Demand still outstrips the rules, with a slab quota for the year to September 2026 standing at nearly 3 million tons and effectively used up within four months, the data showed. Scrap was the only other notable inflow, at 41,300 tons worth 11.7 million euros, down about a third.
A ban that keeps getting postpone
The door is closing slowly, and not without a fight. The quota falls to 2.6 million tons for the year to September 2027б and to 2 million for the following year, the center added, yet attempts to halt Russian slab imports early have failed because the biggest consumer countries lobby against it.
Earlier, the Kiel Institute for the World Economy reported that the EU paid Russia €317 billion in goods since February 2022. The sum is €116 billion more than the €201 billion the bloc extended to Ukraine in financial aid over the same period.

articles.title: F-35C makes first arrested landing on Ford carrier
articles.body:
A US Navy F-35C Lightning II has completed the first arrested landing by the type aboard a Gerald R. Ford-class aircraft carrier, with the milestone taking place aboard the future USS John F. Kennedy during aircraft compatibility testing in the Atlantic, according to the US Navy.
The landing took place on 13 October aboard Pre-Commissioning Unit John F. Kennedy, designated CVN 79, as the second carrier of the Ford class continues testing ahead of its planned delivery to the Navy.
Aircraft from Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 23, known as the “Salty Dogs”, have been operating from the carrier during the trials. Imagery released the following day shows an F-35C conducting a touch-and-go from John F. Kennedy’s flight deck as testing continued on 14 October.
The current programme is focused on Aircraft Compatibility Testing, which assesses whether the ship’s launch and recovery equipment can safely and reliably support the different aircraft expected to operate from the carrier during service. For the F-35C, that means operating with two of the defining systems introduced by the Ford class: the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System, or EMALS, and Advanced Arresting Gear.
EMALS replaces the steam catapults used aboard the preceding Nimitz-class carriers with an electrically driven system for accelerating aircraft from the flight deck. Advanced Arresting Gear performs the other half of the carrier aviation cycle, absorbing the energy of an arriving aircraft when its tailhook catches one of the arresting wires stretched across the deck.
The F-35C is the carrier variant of the Joint Strike Fighter and was developed specifically for conventional US Navy aircraft carriers. It uses larger wings than the F-35A and F-35B, strengthened landing gear and a tailhook for arrested recoveries, allowing it to operate from carriers equipped with catapults and arresting gear.
Testing continued on 14 October with touch-and-go operations from the carrier. In imagery released by the US military, an F-35C from VX-23 is seen just above John F. Kennedy’s flight deck with its landing gear extended during one of the test sorties.
The US Navy said the carrier was underway conducting Aircraft Compatibility Testing, describing the work as an assessment of the operational capabilities of the ship’s aircraft launch and recovery equipment with Navy aircraft.
John F. Kennedy is the second Gerald R. Ford-class carrier, following USS Gerald R. Ford, which entered service in 2017. The class introduces a substantially redesigned aviation system compared with the Nimitz class, including EMALS, Advanced Arresting Gear, a revised flight deck layout and increased electrical generating capacity.
The carrier displaces around 100,000 tonnes at full load and is powered by two A1B nuclear reactors. Its flight deck measures more than 330 metres in length, with the class designed to operate a large embarked air wing including F/A-18E/F Super Hornets, EA-18G Growlers, E-2D Advanced Hawkeyes, helicopters and F-35Cs.
John F. Kennedy also differs from the lead ship in several areas, including its radar fit. From CVN 79 onwards, the class uses the AN/SPY-6(V)3 Enterprise Air Surveillance Radar together with the AN/SPQ-9B surface search radar rather than the dual-band arrangement installed aboard USS Gerald R. Ford. The ship remains in its pre-commissioning phase, with delivery expected in 2027. The latest aviation trials are part of the wider test programme required before the carrier can enter service and begin the process of integrating a full air wing.
The arrested landing on 13 October marked the first time an F-35C had completed a carrier recovery aboard a Ford-class ship, followed immediately by further flight deck testing as John F. Kennedy continues preparations for operational service.

articles.title: Sudanese army says it repelled RSF ground attack in Blue Nile, intercepted drones over Khartoum
articles.body:
Adel Abdel Rahim and Sahin Demir
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
The Sudanese army said Monday it had repelled a ground attack by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), in southeastern Blue Nile state, while its air defenses intercepted a drone attack east of the capital Khartoum.
In a statement, the army’s 14th Infantry Division said its forces thwarted an attack by the RSF and SPLM-N on the Al-Baraka area in the southern sector of Blue Nile state.
The division said its troops inflicted heavy casualties and equipment losses on the attacking forces, preventing them from advancing toward army positions.
It added that several military vehicles were destroyed and the attackers were forced to retreat under heavy fire.
The division said the operation demonstrated the army’s readiness to respond to any hostile movements threatening its positions or the security of civilians and their property.
There was no immediate comment from the RSF or SPLM-N on the army’s claims.
Blue Nile state has witnessed escalating military tensions in recent weeks following attacks by the RSF and SPLM-N on several areas.
 
Drone attack
In a separate development, military sources told Anadolu that army air defenses intercepted an RSF drone attack east of Khartoum on Monday, near Khartoum International Airport.
The sources said all attacking drones were shot down but did not specify their number.
Witnesses also told Anadolu that explosions were heard in the skies over eastern Khartoum on Monday morning.
Videos circulated on social media showed a drone flying over the Sudanese capital the same day.
There was no immediate comment from Sudanese authorities or the RSF on the reported drone attack.
On May 4, Sudan’s Information Ministry reported that a site within Khartoum International Airport had been targeted by a drone, without causing casualties or material damage.
Sudanese authorities and human rights organizations have accused the RSF of targeting civilian facilities. The group rarely comments on such accusations but maintains that it works to protect civilians.
Since April 2023, the Sudanese army and RSF have been engaged in a war that erupted over disagreements concerning the integration of the paramilitary group into the country’s military.
The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, while worsening famine and humanitarian conditions in what has become one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

articles.title: Putin, Trump and Xi could hold a three-way meeting next month

Kremlin says Putin, Trump and Xi could hold a three-way meeting in China next month
The Kremlin said on Monday that President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping could hold a three-way meeting on the sidelines of next month's APEC summit in China and that a potential meeting had come up in talks.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was commenting after being asked about a report in the Wall Street Journal which said that Putin had proposed such a meeting in order to discuss how to end the conflict in Ukraine.
"Given that all three heads of state may potentially take part in the summit in China, the subject of such a hypothetical meeting was indeed raised. It was raised, but no specific proposals or agreements were discussed or put forward by anyone, either regarding the meeting itself or the possible agenda and content of that meeting," said Peskov.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha criticised the idea of such a summit.
"A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Ukraine, the US, and Russia could help end the war sooner. A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China, and the US would do only the opposite: encourage Putin to continue this war," he said on X.
Peskov, who told reporters on a daily conference call that the US was continuing its mediation efforts to resolve the conflict and that Russia appreciated those efforts, said it was obvious that Ukraine would need to be involved in any final peace deal.
"Of course, a final settlement is impossible without the participation of someone in Kyiv who is prepared to take responsibility," he said.
The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February before the United States and Israel launched a war against Iran. Ukraine and Russia remain as far apart as ever when it comes to the terms of any possible peace deal.

articles.title: Espionage case on Army officer’s wife, lens on ‘China links’
articles.body:
JAMMU: J&K Police have filed a case and started a probe against a Jammu-based Army officer’s wife for allegedly collecting and sharing sensitive information with foreign intelligence operatives, including those linked to China, sources said Sunday.The woman is from Telangana, works as a freelance researcher and had a UN internship in 2023. She allegedly used AI tools ChatGPT and Claude to write papers on sensitive security issues for Chinese intelligence operatives suspected to have contacted her posing as academicians. The information was allegedly passed on through encrypted communication (online) mediums.The woman married the major-rank officer in 2023, a year after finishing a course in international governance from Geneva. She got a Master’s degree from a Bengaluru university in 2021.A joint team of officers, including some from a central intelligence agency, intercepted the woman at Jammu railway station on Oct 14 when she was reportedly preparing to board a train to Pathankot. She was stopped and taken to a nearby military station for questioning, officials said. This followed a case filed at Jammu’s Gandhi Nagar Police Station under Official Secrets Act, and BNS sections relating to criminal conspiracy and offences against national sovereignty.
A DSP assigned to lead the probe has questioned the woman, seizing her phone and extracting data that purportedly showed documents on sensitive subjects. The accused claimed her material was based entirely on open-source research supplemented by the AI platforms.The officials made it clear that despite being booked, the woman has not been arrested yet. Her interrogation indicated that she had interacted with several foreign nationals during her UN internship, including a Chinese national with whom she allegedly maintained contact through WhatsApp, the officials said. In 2024, she was in contact via social media with a Malaysian consultant allegedly working for Chinese intelligence agencies, the officials added.Preliminary investigations indicate the Chinese operatives initially made the woman write articles on environmental and geopolitics issues before gradually goading her to switch to defence matters. Investigators suspect she may have fallen into an “intellectual trap”, not realising that those approaching her as academicians were actually operatives trying to extract sensitive information.
Investigators are examining whether the woman engaged in systematic information-sharing under the guise of freelance research, adding a comprehensive forensic examination of her digital devices and financial transactions is on to establish the exact nature of the shared material, the officials said.(With inputs from agencies)

articles.title: The Domino Effect: How Strikes on Data Centers Paralyze Russian Businesses
articles.body:
The Domino Effect: How Strikes on Data Centers Paralyze Russian Businesses
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian drones attacked the data centers of Yandex, Sberbank, and VK. Expert Oleksandr Hlushchenko explained that strikes on server infrastructure paralyze business processes and harm the Russian economy.
The massive attack by Ukrainian drones on St. Petersburg on the night of October 18 targeted an oil terminal, energy infrastructure, and a data center. After the strike, Russians began massively complaining about disruptions to the operation of the "VKontakte" social network. However, the consequences of further attacks on data centers could prove much more serious—from disruptions to banking payments to interference with the operation of businesses. Read about what this threatens for the Russian economy in the UNN article.
The Russians themselves effectively created the conditions under which their digital infrastructure is becoming vulnerable to such strikes. Russia spent years building a centralized digital system, moving an increasing number of services online, concentrating enormous amounts of data in large technology companies, and at the same time requiring that the personal data of Russian citizens be stored on Russian territory. In peacetime, this model makes it possible to centrally manage services, scale them, and control information flows. But during wartime, it creates serious risks. When a significant part of digital infrastructure is concentrated within a single state, and its operation depends on a limited number of large technology platforms, damage to individual elements can have consequences far beyond a single enterprise
In fact, this concerns a threat not only to social networks but also to the entire system of digital services on which Russians' daily lives depend. Data centers ensure the storage of enormous volumes of information and the operation of applications, cloud platforms, and financial and corporate services. Damage to such facilities can deprive companies of part of their computing capacity and users of access to their usual services.
Repeated strikes pose a particular danger. Large technology companies have backup data centers capable of taking over the load of damaged facilities. However, their capabilities are limited. If several complexes go offline at once, the load on the remaining ones increases, along with the risk of large-scale disruptions.
At a certain point, servers can no longer fully process all requests. Some services begin operating more slowly, others periodically become unavailable, and some operations end in errors. And the less reserve capacity remains, the harder it is for the system to withstand even ordinary technical failures
How will strikes on data centers affect the Russian economy?
The consequences of such disruptions will be felt most acutely by Russian businesses. Modern enterprises simultaneously depend on banking, cloud, logistics, and other digital services.
You may have goods, employees, and customers, but be unable to make a payment on time, process documents, or organize supplies. In other words, economic activity slows down not because the goods or enterprises themselves have disappeared, but because the mechanisms connecting them have stopped working properly
Why is it difficult for Russia to restore data centers?
Another problem for Russia is replacing damaged equipment. Data centers require not only servers but also complex information-storage systems, networking equipment, power-supply and cooling systems. Due to technological sanctions, purchasing the necessary components may turn into a lengthy and expensive process.
A data center cannot be restored simply because a company has enough money in its account. Servers, storage devices, network switches, optical equipment, power-supply systems, cooling systems, and other components are required
According to the expert's assessment, the additional costs of restoring the infrastructure may ultimately also be felt by Russians themselves. Technology companies will be forced to spend more money on equipment, reserve capacity, and maintenance. This creates the conditions for services to become more expensive for end consumers.
At the same time, several damaged data centers do not mean the immediate collapse of the Russian internet. Large companies have backup systems, but their capabilities are not unlimited.
This does not necessarily mean an immediate collapse, but it may mean a gradual degradation in the quality of digital services
Therefore, if the attacks continue, Russia’s main problem may no longer be the temporary unavailability of individual websites, but the gradual depletion of digital infrastructure, the increasingly costly restoration of that infrastructure, and growing risks for the entire economy.

articles.title: Macron opens Gulf tour amid violent protests in France
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Macron opens tour of Gulf states amid violent protests in France
French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday began a Gulf tour aimed at securing oil and diesel supplies in an effort to bring down prices, after a weekend of violent protests sparked by soaring living costs.
Macron, just hours after slamming France's "unbridled" violence in an address late on Sunday, arrived in OPEC member Kuwait where he was welcomed by the emir, Sheikh Mishal Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah.
He will also visit the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Qatar by Wednesday on a trip aimed at strengthening "economic and defence partnerships" in the Gulf, which has been thrown into turmoil by the US-Iran war since February.
Macron acknowledged security and intelligence failures but refused his interior minister's resignation after more than 2,500 people were arrested in some of France's worst violence in years, with town halls and shops looted and set on fire.
Before flying to Kuwait, he said the visit was needed to "secure our supplies", pointing out that the demonstrators had expressed "concern" about fuel prices.
Macron's tour "may give an impression of normality... but may also appear out of touch and suggest a kind of power vacuum", said constitutional expert Benjamin Morel.
'Alternative' energy routes
During his trip, "the goal is to secure a certain number of commitments" on diesel and oil volumes, the French presidency said.
Macron is accompanied by senior executives from France's two biggest energy groups, TotalEnergies and Engie.
The G7 countries, chaired this year by France, agreed in early October to draw up to 100 million barrels of oil from their strategic reserves to ease pressure.
Crude oil prices have ballooned during the eight-month war, as Iran blockades the Strait of Hormuz -- the main exit route for the Gulf's energy exports.
Yemen's Houthis have compounded the pressure by firing on Saudi tankers in the Red Sea, striking the kingdom's oil sites and carrying out deadly attacks on Riyadh's international airport.
Francis Perrin, an energy expert at the French Institute for International and Strategic Relations, said he did not expect Macron's visit to have an impact on fuel prices.
"The Arab countries of the Gulf are very eager to supply the world, and the French market, but it is difficult for them to make firm commitments until the region has been stabilised," he said.
Macron will hold talks with Gulf leaders including the UAE's president and Qatar's emir on ways to "secure" maritime shipments and find "alternative and bypass routes" for energy exports, the presidency said.
France and Britain have assembled an international mission to help reopen the Strait of Hormuz, mainly through demining operations, once the United States and Iran reach agreement on the waterway.
However, the two sides remain at an impasse, eight months since the start of hostilities.
The French president will also hold talks on defence cooperation, after the Gulf countries were targeted by thousands of Iranian missiles and drones.
France deployed its aircraft carrier Charles de Gaulle in the spring, along with Rafale fighter jets, a frigate and air defence assets.
Macron also sent French soldiers to protect Yanbu, an oil terminal on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast that has become a vital conduit for exports.

articles.title: Russians strike warehouse belonging to major pharmaceutical distributor in Rivne

Russians strike warehouse belonging to major pharmaceutical distributor in Rivne
Russian forces struck a warehouse belonging to BaDM, one of Ukraine's largest pharmaceutical distributors, during a drone attack on Rivne. No casualties have been reported.
Source: participants in the pharmaceutical market
Details: The warehouse covers an area of 2,370 sq m and was opened in Rivne in 2012.
This is not the first BaDM facility to be attacked by the Russians. Another BaDM warehouse was struck on 14 September. Reports at the time said it was the fourth pharmaceutical warehouse to be attacked since the beginning of September.

- On 7 October, Russian forces struck the Borshchahivka Chemical and Pharmaceutical Plant in Kyiv.
- On 4 October, a plant belonging to the pharmaceutical manufacturer Kusum in Sumy was destroyed in a Russian attack.
