articles.title: Five children from family killed in Russian missile strike laid to rest in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast
articles.body:
Five children from family killed in Russian missile strike laid to rest in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast
Five children from the Voronov family – 16-year-old Dominika, 14-year-old Viorika, 13-year-old Zakharii, nine-year-old Federika and 18-month-old Artem – have been laid to rest in Radushne, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast. Their lives were cut short on the night of 29-30 July when a Russian missile struck their family home.
Source: Suspilne Dnipro
Details: The children had been considered missing for around two and a half months, but forensic examinations have now confirmed their deaths.
The children's grandmother, Nelia, said that only the foundation remained of the house after the strike. Throughout this time, she had prayed that all those killed would be identified.
"We didn't know how they would be separated. But now they will all be together as one family there, in the cemetery. Nothing miraculous could have happened. The only thing I asked God for was that everyone would be found and identified. There was no one else there, only family members – 10 people," the woman said.
Inna lives near the site where the Voronov family's home once stood. She said she ran outside immediately after the explosion, but saw only rubble where the house had been.
Quote from Inna: "The missile hit right in the middle of the house, in the children's room, as we were told. We were putting out a fire in the neighbouring house, where two children had been trapped under the rubble. When we got them out and went to the [Voronovs'] house, there was no one left to look for… We knew them. All the children were friends with each other. They were good people."
Details: Their neighbour Mykola said the Voronovs had always been a close-knit and cheerful family.
"In a large family, everyone is like that – they help one another and live as one family. It is hard to comprehend what happened. Such pain," he said.
Dominika's best friend, Karina, also attended the funeral. She said they often spent time together.
Quote from Karina: "[Dominika] was a very kind and sincere person. She really loved beadwork. I even have a pendant from her. She was so wonderful that I don't even have any more words. She loved children so much. She even planned to have a family of her own one day. She wanted two children."
Details: Dominika's classmate, Sofiia, remembered her as a cheerful, smiling person.
"I didn't know her family, but Dominika was a very cheerful person who always smiled. I never saw her sad. It is so sad that this happened," Sofiia said.
Ihor Kozachenko, head of the school where Dominika studied, described her as a kind friend and an optimist who always had a smile on her face.
"She was the one who supported others during difficult times, when some people were in despair. She always had a kind word for others. This is a huge loss for our school. Her family was very close-knit – that is rare these days," the teacher said.
Tetiana Usenko, head of the school attended by Federika, Zakharii and Viorika, said that the children's classmates still cannot speak about them without tears.
What is known about the tragedy
On the night of 29-30 July, Russian forces attacked the Kryvyi Rih district. A ballistic missile struck a house in the settlement of Radushne, where the large Voronov family lived.
Artem Voronov, 47, and his wife Olena, 41, were raising 10 children. Seven of them were at home with their parents that night: 17-year-old Mark, 16-year-old Dominika, 14-year-old Viorika, 13-year-old Zakharii, 11-year-old Azarii-Ilai, nine-year-old Federika and six-year-old Emiliia.
Their 18-month-old grandson, Artem, was also visiting. He was the son of their eldest son, Danylo, a serviceman living in Mykolaiv. The boy was due to return home that weekend and had already been enrolled in nursery.
Before the latest forensic findings, the deaths of only five family members had been officially confirmed: the parents, Olena and Artem, and three children – Mark, Azarii-Ilai and Emiliia.

articles.title: ‘Father of Iranian missiles’ ready to hit enemy energy sites
articles.body:
Brigadier General Mohammad Reza Naqdi, a senior adviser to the IRGC commander-in-chief, made the remarks on Sunday while addressing thousands of participants in the “Sacrifice for Iran” campaign in the northern city of Sari.
“We have readied the father of our missiles, and should the enemy make any misstep, its attack is doomed to failure, and there will be no way out for them,” he said, according to Press TV EN website.
The “father of our missiles” remark was a direct rhetorical counter to US President Donald Trump’s public threat to use the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast—commonly known as the “mother of all bombs”—against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites.
“In case of any miscalculation, all infrastructure platforms and energy investments belonging to the aggressors in the region will be within operational range, and their security will be directly jeopardized,” Naqdi said.
He added that the Iranian armed forces had displayed high missile capabilities and deterrence in response to US military threats, enabling them to deliver a decisive response to any act of aggression.
Naqdi emphasized that Iran’s power and victories stem not primarily from military hardware but from the strong presence and readiness of the Iranian people.
The IRGC commander said the nation’s preparedness and resistance had prevented ground incursions and forced hostile vessels to retreat by 1,000 kilometers at sea.
Naqdi: Trump’s threats amount to admission of defeat against Iran
Elsewhere in his speech, Naqdi said US President Donald Trump’s recent statements about running out of patience and threatening tougher action against Iran were an “open admission of defeat” against the Iranian people.
He added that such remarks contradict Washington's claims of victory, saying that a side that claims to have won would not speak of having exhausted its patience.
Responding to US threats involving advanced weapons, including the “mother of all bombs,” the IRGC commander said 14-ton bombs had been dropped on Iran during the 12-day war, but some failed to detonate and were subsequently seized by Iranian forces.
Iran now possesses samples of the weapons in addition to the country that manufactured them, he explained.

articles.title: Araghchi’s Baghdad diplomacy: Hormuz, regional security and Muslim unity top Iran’s agenda
articles.body:
Araghchi’s Baghdad diplomacy: Hormuz, regional security and Muslim unity top Iran’s agenda
TEHRAN — Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has used a series of diplomatic meetings in Baghdad to press for an end to military escalation in West Asia, outline Iran’s conditions for restoring security in the Strait of Hormuz and call for a more active role for the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) in addressing disputes among Muslim countries.
Araghchi traveled to the Iraqi capital to attend the 52nd session of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers, where he held talks with Iraqi officials and counterparts from Lebanon, Egypt and Algeria, as well as the organization’s secretary-general. His engagements focused on regional security, the Palestinian issue, bilateral relations and diplomatic efforts to prevent further escalation.
In remarks on the sidelines of the meeting on Sunday, Araghchi reiterated that Iran remained prepared to defend its national interests while pursuing diplomacy, provided negotiations respected Iran’s rights and were conducted on an appropriate basis.
Strait of Hormuz: Iran sets out seven-point plan for reopening
Araghchi said the insecurity affecting the Strait of Hormuz and its economic consequences for regional countries and the wider international community were a direct result of US-Israeli military aggression against Iran.
He said Tehran had presented Washington with a seven-point plan setting out its conditions for resolving the confrontation. The United States had submitted its own views, which Iran was reviewing, he added.
According to Araghchi, the proposed framework provides a clear path toward restoring security in the strategic waterway if Washington meets Iran’s conditions.
“If our conditions are met, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen on the sixth day, and negotiations will begin on the seventh day,” he said.
The foreign minister stressed that Iran’s conditions were not extraordinary, arguing that they concerned commitments the United States had previously undertaken under an earlier memorandum of understanding and in other negotiations. He said Washington could implement the requirements within days if it genuinely sought to reopen the strait.
Araghchi also briefed Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein on ongoing diplomatic consultations related to regional peace and security. He reiterated that Iran remained committed to diplomacy as a means of preventing further escalation, even as it maintained its readiness to defend its national security.
The issue also featured in Araghchi’s meeting with Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty, during which the two officials discussed bilateral relations, regional and international developments, and diplomatic consultations conducted through mediators.
Araghchi told Abdelatty that Iran had consistently pursued diplomacy with the aim of reducing tensions, while accusing Washington of repeatedly violating its commitments. He cited a US breach of its pledge just two weeks after the signing of a memorandum of understanding intended to end the war.
Iraq ties and the need for regional dialogue
In his meeting with Hussein, Araghchi highlighted the importance of strengthening cooperation between Iran and Iraq, particularly in economic, trade and security affairs.
The two ministers also discussed developments in the Arabian Peninsula and ways to help end regional conflicts. Araghchi emphasized that Iran was prepared to facilitate dialogue between parties involved in regional disputes.
Araghchi also met Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi during his visit to Baghdad. No further details of their discussions were immediately available.
Beyond bilateral ties, Araghchi argued that Muslim countries needed to strengthen dialogue and solidarity to address shared challenges, particularly the Palestinian issue and the continued expansionism of the Israeli regime.
OIC urged to play a stronger role in resolving disputes
Araghchi called on the OIC to play a more effective role in resolving differences among Muslim countries and strengthening cooperation across the Islamic world.
He said he had raised the issue in meetings with the Iraqi prime minister, Hussein, and the organization’s newly appointed Secretary-General Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed.
During his meeting with Cheikh Ahmed, the secretary-general expressed the organization’s interest in drawing on Iran’s experience and capabilities to develop initiatives for mediation and dispute settlement among Muslim countries.
Araghchi welcomed the prospect of a more active OIC role, stressing that the organization’s secretariat should operate professionally and impartially and avoid any perception of bias toward or against member states.
He also emphasized the importance of strengthening solidarity among Muslim countries in confronting common challenges, particularly those arising from developments in occupied Palestine.
The foreign minister noted that the OIC had lost some of its influence in recent years and expressed hope that Iraq’s assumption of the rotating presidency, together with the appointment of a new secretary-general, would help revitalize the organization.
Yemen Resolution: Iran insists on fairness, balance and a political solution
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has warned that Iran will not join the consensus on a proposed resolution on Yemen at the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) unless the final text reflects fairness and balance, stressing that Tehran’s position will depend on the wording ultimately adopted.
Speaking to IRNA on Sunday on the sidelines of the annual session of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers in Baghdad, Araghchi said the organization’s resolutions had not yet been adopted and that the final communiqué was still being drafted. He noted that Iranian diplomats had engaged in extensive discussions in recent days to ensure that Iran’s views were reflected in the documents, adding that most of the proposed resolutions, with a few exceptions, repeated texts adopted the previous year.
On Yemen, Araghchi said serious discussions had taken place among member states, with Saudi Arabia, Iran and other countries presenting their respective positions. The draft resolution had yet to be finalized, he said, expressing hope that the final text would reflect a fair and balanced approach. If these principles were not upheld, Iran would be unable to join the consensus and would formally register its reservations or reject the resolution, depending on its final wording.
Araghchi acknowledged that countries aligned with Saudi Arabia constituted a sizable bloc within the OIC, but said Tehran had conducted extensive consultations and clearly outlined its position on a just solution to the conflict. He stressed that Yemen’s crisis could not be resolved through military force or blockade, calling instead for a political process grounded in the United Nations Charter, respect for Yemen’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and protection of the Yemeni people’s human rights. He also offered Iran’s assistance in facilitating dialogue among the parties.
Rejecting allegations that Yemen’s armed forces had attacked Mecca and Medina, Araghchi said repeating such accusations would neither serve the interests of the Muslim world nor strengthen unity among OIC member states. He emphasized that the sanctity of Islamic holy sites must be respected by all.
Lebanon: Iran stresses sovereignty while acknowledging political differences
Araghchi’s meeting with Lebanese Foreign Minister Youssef Rajji focused on bilateral relations, Lebanon’s sovereignty and national security, and regional developments.
Araghchi reaffirmed Iran’s support for Lebanon’s territorial integrity and its efforts to defend its sovereignty and national security against Israeli military action and expansionism.
Speaking separately to reporters, he described his meeting with Rajji as respectful but serious and frank, acknowledging differences between Tehran and the current Lebanese government over approaches to regional and domestic issues.
Nevertheless, he stressed that both countries had an interest in maintaining and developing relations.
“I emphasized that the Islamic Republic of Iran is interested in having comprehensive political, economic and cultural relations with Lebanon as a country,” Araghchi said.
He added that Lebanon’s internal affairs were for the Lebanese people to decide. Referring to Hezbollah, he described the movement as one of Lebanon’s most important political groups and an established part of the country’s political and social landscape.
Araghchi said decisions made by Lebanese political groups, including Hezbollah, should be treated as matters of Lebanon’s domestic affairs.
Algeria: Palestinian issue remains central to Muslim solidarity
In a meeting with Sofiane Chaib, Algeria’s secretary of state to the minister of foreign affairs, Araghchi discussed bilateral relations and developments affecting the Muslim world, with particular emphasis on Palestine.
He described Palestine as the foremost concern facing the Muslim world and humanity, citing the continued Israeli occupation and the situation in the occupied Palestinian territories.
Araghchi called for stronger unity and solidarity among Muslim countries to end Israel’s impunity and to confront its continued expansionism.
He also briefed the Algerian official on developments in West Asia and US interventionist and destabilizing actions in the Persian Gulf region.
Alongside his meetings in Baghdad, Araghchi held a telephone conversation on Sunday with Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar.
According to Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry, the two officials discussed bilateral relations and regional developments and stressed the importance of dialogue and diplomacy amid continuing regional tensions.
The conversation added to the diplomatic contacts surrounding efforts to prevent further escalation and address outstanding regional disputes.
Diplomacy and defense remain parallel priorities
Across his meetings and public remarks in Baghdad, Araghchi presented diplomacy as a central instrument for addressing regional crises, while maintaining that Iran would defend its national interests and security.
His message combined calls for stronger cooperation among neighboring countries, a more active OIC role in resolving disputes, and greater unity among Muslim states over Palestine with a clear warning that progress on the Strait of Hormuz depended on Washington meeting Tehran’s stated conditions.
The meetings also highlighted the range of issues confronting regional diplomacy, from maritime security and the economic repercussions of conflict to Yemen, Lebanon and the future of Palestinian territories.
For Tehran, Araghchi’s Baghdad engagements provided an opportunity to advance bilateral ties, engage regional counterparts and press for diplomatic solutions while reiterating Iran’s position that lasting security requires respect for national sovereignty and the fulfillment of commitments.

articles.title: Egypt unveils new laser system to intercept drones in Sinai
articles.body:
Israeli media outlets specialising in military affairs have reported the appearance of a new Egyptian laser system during Second Field Army exercises in Sinai, highlighting its ability to intercept drones and comparing it with similar systems worldwide.
The Israeli platform Nziv Net reported that the Egyptian laser system, named EGY-HEL 01, was officially unveiled this month during live-fire exercises conducted by Egypt’s Second Field Army. The name is likely an abbreviation for Egyptian High-Energy Laser, version one, it said.
The platform said the system was designed to intercept drones, primarily providing short-range air defence against unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), small drones and projectiles.
It added that the system was developed for installation on light vehicles, such as pick-up trucks or light tracked vehicles, allowing it to move quickly, change positions easily and operate alongside field units and ground forces to protect them from low-altitude threats.
The system was likely developed and manufactured locally in Egypt by the Egyptian army’s Technical Research Centre, the platform said.
It added that the system was cost-effective because it reduces reliance on expensive air defence missiles to intercept low-cost targets, helping preserve stocks of conventional ammunition.

articles.title: Majority of Ukrainians oppose ceding Donbas for security guarantees, ready to endure war – KIIS poll
articles.body:
An absolute majority (61%) of Ukrainians continue to consider it categorically unacceptable to cede full control of Donbas to the Russian Federation in exchange for security guarantees, while 35% are open to such a concession, according to a survey conducted on October 8–16 by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS).
It is noted that compared to late July–early August, when a similar survey was conducted, there were no statistically significant changes. However, on October 8–9, prior to the announcement of the "diesel deal" between the U.S and Russia and subsequent pressure on Ukraine, 57% were categorically opposed to giving up Donbas in exchange for security guarantees.
Across all macro-regions, a half or majority rejects the proposal to withdraw Ukrainian troops in exchange for security guarantees. The highest proportion of those willing to approve such an option is among residents of the East (primarily Kharkiv region), where 45% generally allow for approval, while 51% are categorically against. In other regions, including the South and Lower Dnipro region, 60–66% categorically reject the proposal. In Kyiv, 66% are opposed.
When asked how much longer Ukrainians are willing to endure the war, virtually the same percentage (62%) stated for as long as necessary. Another 4% spoke of 1 year. A shorter timeframe (several months to six months) was cited by 21%, while the remaining 13% were undecided. Among respondents surveyed on October 8–9, 60% answered that they were ready to endure as long as necessary.
Only 10% of respondents expect the war to end by the end of the current year, 2026. Another 13% expect the war to end in the first half of 2027, and 17% by the end of 2027 (bringing the total to 40%). Meanwhile, 39% expect the war to end in 2028 or later, with 21% holding no definite opinion on the matter.
"The results of our survey once again demonstrate that many in both the West and the East still have a limited understanding of Ukraine and Ukrainians (and still seem to view us through the lens of Russian expertise). As we can see, the Russian enemy, through its despicable ballistic missile and drone strikes, is unable to break the spirit and will of Ukrainians; Ukrainians still insist on continuing the resistance. The same applies to pressure from the other side—attempts by some of our partners to pressure Ukrainians into accepting terms of virtual surrender (blushing behind empty and unfulfillable promises of something in the future). Once again, Ukrainians want peace, but between surrender now with an almost inevitable risk of future Russian genocide and resistance now with the hope of achieving acceptable terms, Ukrainians choose to continue resisting," noted Anton Hrushetsky, Executive Director of KIIS.
The survey was conducted via computer-assisted telephone interviews (CATI) based on a random sample of mobile phone numbers across all government-controlled territories of Ukraine, surveying 1,031 respondents aged 18 and older. Under standard conditions, the formal statistical margin of error (with a probability of 0.95 and taking into account a design effect of 1.3) did not exceed 4% for indicators close to 50% and 1.7% for indicators close to 5%, though certain systematic deviations are added under war conditions.
